speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: I'm not going to set our goals low. I don't think all of those competitors are going to survive, I really don't, but a couple of them probably will.
finding: He sets ambitious share goals (about half the market) and predicts a shake-out among new entrants.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: I believe that this is an airplane we will probably do and that will complete the 787 family, as we know it, the -8, the -9 and the 10.
finding: He signalled the 787-10 stretch as a likely move in 2011; it was launched in 2013.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: Entering the service, which means completing flight test, getting our type cert. We understand now to do that. I think we're going to make it. I don't see any issues there.
finding: He committed in May 2011 to 787 certification and third-quarter entry into service; the first 787 was delivered to ANA on Sept 26 2011.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: And it's a deliberate process, and it's one where we're not going to be driven by a date to make an announcement. If you're holding your breath on the Paris air show, well, I'm not going to say we're not going to make that announcement, I would be very surprised if we did.
finding: He refuses to let air-show calendars force a product launch decision, framing the single-aisle choice as a deliberate, data-gathering process.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: I think what you'll see us do this time is take the time required to mature the technology and only then do we into detail, design and development. And then we'll follow a very disciplined gated process, where we don't travel design risk into the next phase of the design process.
finding: He commits to a gated development process that matures technology before detailed design, trading speed for schedule reliability.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: I don't have everybody ringing my phone off the hook, telling me that we have to have a decision in the ... next few weeks or the next couple of months.
finding: He judged there was no customer urgency on the narrowbody decision in May 2011, a read overtaken within weeks by the American Airlines neo order and the August MAX launch.

numbers.actual: re-engine announced Jul 20 2011 with AA order; board launch Aug 30 2011

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: Now we get in trouble when we went up in rate back in 1998, and there's a lot of scar tissue on the organization as a result of that. And we have very well-defined rules on how often you can make a rate break on a program. What you do is you break rate and you stabilize
finding: Albaugh runs rate increases by an explicit 'break rate, then stabilize' rule born of the 1998 Renton shutdown, so a rate move is never stacked on an unstable line.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: The other thing we try to stay away from is having rate breaks on 2 different programs at the same time, because a lot of resources are demanded as we go up.
finding: He avoids simultaneous rate breaks on two programs, treating factory and engineering bandwidth as the binding constraint on ramp speed.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: When we made the decision to go from 31.5 737 to 35, that took us 6 months to get comfortable, so that we could do it and manage the risk.
finding: He documents a long readiness review before each rate step, drilling down to every work cell and second-sourcing to manage risk.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: But in my mind, 7 years of backlog is too much. When a market comes back, you have to tell good customers that you'll deliver them an airplane, but they got to wait 6 or 7 years. And it's not about having the best airplane, it's about having the best airplane that's available.
finding: He sees an over-long backlog as a competitive weakness (customers defect to whoever has slots), which pushes him toward rate increases rather than banking orders.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: But we're not satisfied with the zero-margin airplane, we've investment too much and we're going to make some money with this airplane.
finding: He frames 787 profitability as non-negotiable after the investment, signalling cost-down pressure on the program and suppliers.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: Now I'll say this, we're going to do one of those last 2. We're going to do a re-engine or we're going to do a new airplane. In either case, we're going to provide our customer with great value. And as Jim mentioned earlier, we're probably leaning towards a new airplane, but we'll bring the re-engine along with us.
finding: In May 2011 he publicly leaned toward a clean-sheet narrowbody while keeping the re-engine alive as a parallel option.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: In the past, we've adapted airplanes to the production system. This time, we need to design an airplane and a production system together, and that's precisely what we're trying to do.
finding: For any new airplane he insists the production system be designed in parallel with the airframe, making high-rate producibility a gating criterion.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: My speech to the team is we need to build something of everything. We need to know how this airplane works better than the competition. ... but we need to build enough of everything, so we can go and help our suppliers when they get in trouble or we can bring the work back, if they really have an issue.
finding: His make/buy doctrine is to keep enough in-house capability in every major element to rescue or insource from a failing supplier.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: I think one of the unintended consequences of all the outsourcing we did is we paid people to develop IP that they now own. And we need to be very careful going forward of whether or not we're giving away things that's important to our success over the long haul.
finding: He treats outsourcing as an IP-leakage risk, favouring retention of critical intellectual property over capital-light partnering.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: And we think this is a program that if it’s real that will be towards the end of this decade, if not into the next decade. ... But we also have some major upgrades we could do in the event that we have to respond to a move by the competition.
finding: On the 777 he holds major upgrades in reserve and times them to Airbus's A350-1000 moves rather than pre-empting.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: What they want are lower operating costs, but what they're telling us is they want us to do something transformation. They want us to provide them with a step-function improvement in economics.
finding: He reads customer demand as wanting a step-change in economics, the argument he used for a clean sheet before switching to the re-engine.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: given the option of going higher which would require a capital investment, I’d opt for pushing the 8.3% rate out for a couple of more years and bypassing the capital expenditure that we’d have to make.
finding: Faced with strong 777 demand, he prefers extending a rate plateau over spending capital for a higher rate, avoiding the risk of having to come back down.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: Our view is if Airbus goes through and does the re-engine, that what that will do is just bring that airplane to parity with the 737-800NG.
finding: He initially dismissed the A320neo as merely catching up to the in-production 737NG, under-weighting the neo's threat.
response: incremental NG+ improvement while studying re-engine vs new airplane

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: And there's a very high cost to switching, and there's also a cost for complexity. And I really don't think that we're going to see too many customers really think about switching to a different type of airplane anytime soon.
finding: He relied on fleet-commonality switching costs to protect Boeing's narrowbody customers from the neo; within weeks American Airlines split its order with Airbus.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: The days of the duopoly are over. It's not just us and the Europeans, it's now the Boeing, the Europeans, the Russians, the Chinese, the Brazilians and the Canadians ... we're assuming that they're going to be able to bring to the market a credible airplane
finding: He plans against new entrants (COMAC, Bombardier, Embraer, Russia) as if they will succeed, using that to justify technology investment.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: they're building the C919. It will be a better airplane and, eventually, they'll get it right, and they will get some of the market share in China ... the market share around the world as the Chinese government calls in some of the IOUs they have with countries around the world. So we're taking them very, very seriously
finding: He expects COMAC to eventually win share in China and abroad through state leverage, and takes it seriously as a long-run threat.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: Airbus has been probably a little more innovative than we have been, in relative to the financing and deals. ... they have not been the swing producer we have. ... I think they also have competed on price, as we've competed on value
finding: He characterises Airbus as a price-and-financing competitor and Boeing as a value competitor, and rejects becoming the industry's swing producer again.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: They build a good airplane. They have 52% of the marketplace. ... but always have the most competitive airplane, and we will do that.
finding: He respects Airbus's product and share and commits to matching it deal-for-deal while relying on a capability edge.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Boeing Commercial Airplanes, Inc.
quote: And what I like about those people is that they brought great program management disciplines to the program, very solid integrated schedules and a real focus on risk management. ... they're all very paranoid about what can go wrong. And that's what you'll want in a program manager
finding: He selects program managers for risk paranoia and integrated-schedule discipline.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: And we can take the money that we didn't spend to do the new smaller airplane. And we can use that to do a 777 improvement in the event that we need to do that. And it also gives us some money to do a 787-10 or a stretch variant of the 787.
finding: He reallocated the R&D avoided by not doing a clean-sheet narrowbody toward 777 upgrades and a 787-10 stretch.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: if the investment that we had to make to go above 8.3 a month or tens of millions of dollars, we'd probably do that without thinking very long and hard about it. ... it's one that we're only going to do if we're very confident ... but for several years.
finding: He states a capex threshold for rate increases: tens of millions is a quick yes; larger outlays require confidence in several years of sustained demand.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: On the EIS, the 2017, I will tell you I'm driving our team to an earlier date than that. But one of the things that I want to do on this program is I want to under-promise and I want to over-deliver. ... Don't make promises you can't keep.
finding: He set a deliberately padded 2017 MAX EIS under an under-promise/over-deliver doctrine learned from 787/747 slips; the MAX entered service in May 2017.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: This is going to be profitable from the beginning. The margins are going to start out low. ... the expectation over the long haul is we make this program as profitable as the 737 and the 777 programs.
finding: He promised the 787 would be profitable from the start on a 1,100-unit accounting block; the program later carried tens of billions in deferred production costs and charges.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I'm an engineer, and I was looking forward to the opportunity to build that airplane. But the issues were really twofold. One, the nonrecurring cost. It was a cost estimate that I had some concerns about. ... Could we really build 60 all-composite airplanes a year?
finding: He reversed his own stated preference for a clean sheet once NRE uncertainty and high-rate composite producibility could not be resolved, putting the engineer's instinct below cost and production risk.
trigger: A320neo order momentum and customer demand for date certainty
response: launched 737 MAX re-engine (Aug 2011)
lag: about 2-3 months after the May 2011 lean toward a new airplane

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We're being conservative because we understand that our future to a large degree depends on the 737 and 777 to continue to deliver the performance that they have. So our approach is go up in rate and get stable, stay there; go up in rate, get stable and continue to march up
finding: He keeps ramp conservative on the cash-cow 737 and 777 because they fund development; stability comes before the next step.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: You think about 37 and 777, they drive the cash that we need to do our development programs. ... So we're going to be conservative as we come up to rate to make sure that we don't have any perturbation that could impact cash or profitability.
finding: He ranks protecting cash generation on the 737/777 above faster growth, accepting conservative ramps to avoid disruption.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: we gave away a lot of elements of work that we'd always done in the past. And then we didn't provide the kind of oversight necessary for some of the people that we're doing work that they've ever done before. ... So what we're trying to do is manage our suppliers like they're our factories
finding: After the 787, he built a large supplier-readiness organisation and manages suppliers like internal factories.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: And their view was improve, improve fuel burn now and date certainty was what they were after. So that drove us to the decision to do the MAX airplane.
finding: He credits customers' demand for near-term fuel burn and date certainty as decisive for choosing the MAX re-engine over a new airplane.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: 68 really is a sweet spot for us. It's a sweet spot in terms of fuel burn drag on the airplane and also additional weight to the airplane. ... And a lot of people I know get over-enamored with fan size. Fan size is important.
finding: He chose the MAX engine (CFM LEAP-1B, 68-inch fan, sole source GE/CFM) by integrated airplane-level optimisation and dismissed fan-size comparisons with the neo.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: At Boeing, I've reminded our team that we'd never want to use the word simple and reengine in the same sentence because there's nothing simple about doing a reengine. ... Other than that, anything else we do will have to earn its way onto the airplane. And we're going to keep this low risk.
finding: He imposed strict scope control on the MAX: anything beyond engines, structure and minimal aero must earn its way on, to keep the derivative low risk.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: The way I like to look at it with those decisions, we really have de-risked this decade in terms of doing things that we understand and doing things that will not drive your big swings in R&D or also put us in a position where we can't deliver on the promises that we make to our customers.
finding: He explicitly chose a low-risk, derivative-led product plan for the decade to avoid big R&D swings and broken customer promises.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: One thing we know is when things are good, they're not going to be good forever. ... we legitimize some of the competitors if we don't have the capacity to deliver what they need.
finding: He balances cycle risk against the strategic cost of capacity shortfalls, arguing that a lack of slots legitimises competitors.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: R&D spend next year and the following years will be down about $300 million to $500 million from where we are today
finding: He guided BCA R&D down as 787/747 development wound down, preferring derivatives over a costly new program.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I went into this year wanting to burn the backlog down and we have failed miserably at that.
finding: He candidly owns missing a self-set goal, framed positively as strong demand.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: that schedule has us still going to 10 a month by the end of 2013. And we don't put schedules out if we don't think that those are schedules that we can meet.
finding: He committed to 787 rate 10 by end-2013 and claimed Boeing only publishes schedules it can meet; rate 10 was reached in early 2014.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I feel very comfortable telling you that the book-to-bill will be well above one next year
finding: He forecast a 2012 book-to-bill well above one on MAX conversions; BCA booked over 1,200 net orders against 601 deliveries in 2012.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We actually announced this airplane before we went to the board. We went to the board at the end of August
finding: The MAX was announced to the market before formal board approval, showing that competitive urgency compressed the usual governance sequence.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: But one thing we won't do is try to go up in rate before we have stability at the rate that we're operating at right now. We want to make sure that we don't get in a situation where our factory can't handle all the work that's come again.
finding: He makes stability at the current rate a hard precondition for the next 787 rate step.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: 42 airplanes a month is the limit. ... And it's my hope that as we continue to lean out the 737 program, we could be in a similar position where we could go even higher than 42 if we chose to.
finding: He treats Renton's 42/month as the current ceiling but expects lean flow to lift it without major capital, as on the 777.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: we've had strikes 3 out of the last 4 times we've gone to the table with the union. And to me, it was a lose-lose for both of us.
finding: He treats IAM strikes as lose-lose and sought an early, cooperative labor settlement.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: we want to make sure that we don't get in a situation where we aren't delivering narrow-body airplanes for some period of time that might have a significant impact on profitability and cash. So we want to build the bridge to the 737 MAX
finding: He prioritises an uninterrupted NG-to-MAX transition to protect narrowbody cash and profit.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: we certainly are not in the business of building airplanes; we're in the business of making money selling airplanes
finding: He states that profit, not volume, is the objective.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I think there are 3 reasons why people buy ... They buy based on price, one; capability, two; and the relationship is three. ... And I like to win on the second 2 and maybe lose on the first one and people pay a premium.
finding: He would rather lose on price than discount, competing on capability and relationships to defend a premium.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: But one thing we're not going to do is we're not going to go in and give away the critical technologies that we have. We always want to build in tomorrow's airplane while other companies are building today's. And we're building very high walls around what we think are critical technologies
finding: In China he will localise supply chain and services for market access but not share critical technology, and has no final-assembly plans.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We wouldn't go up in rate if we didn't think we could sustain it for 2 to 3 years.
finding: He sets a demand-durability threshold for any rate increase: it must be sustainable for 2-3 years.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: If that's a real airplane and if it can really be delivered in 2018, 2019 that will drive us to making a decision sooner on the 777X. ... If it's not a real airplane and the entry in the service gets pushed out. We'll probably spend a little more time thinking about what the 777X is
finding: He explicitly ties 777X launch timing to the credibility and EIS of Airbus's A350-1000, a reactive trigger.
response: 777X launch timing

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We had an opportunity a couple of years back to sell quite a number of airplanes to Ryanair and we chose not to, because we didn't like the price point that they demanded. ... We're not going to give airplanes away.
finding: He walked away from a Ryanair deal on price and treats pricing discipline as a proven strategy, even against COMAC entry.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: This is the first time anybody has accused me of sandbagging going up in the rate on 787. ... we will sneak up on these rate changes as opposed to trying to force them. ... But I don't want to get ahead of myself and making commitments that we can't meet.
finding: He resists analyst pressure to accelerate and frames conservatism as protecting credibility.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I don't think I want to go out on a limb and tell you what I think the book to bill is going to be in 2013, I think there are too many uncertainties out there with the economic situation and also the price of oil.
finding: He gives firm near-term order calls but declines longer-range forecasts amid macro uncertainty.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I've see nothing to date that would lead me to believe that we won't deliver all the 787s that we have in our plan by the end of the year.
finding: Despite a South Carolina shimming issue, he reaffirmed the 2012 787 delivery plan (70-85 787/747 deliveries combined); Boeing delivered 46 787s and 31 747-8s in 2012.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: If we can figure out what the NRE is and we can satisfy ourselves that the risk is acceptable, we could be taking these programs to the board sometime later in the year.
finding: He gated the 787-10 and 777X on NRE clarity and acceptable risk, targeting a 2012 board decision; both were launched in 2013 (787-10 in June, 777X in November).

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: getting the labor issue off the table for us was a huge accomplishment. ... So we've got 5 years of peace, I think, with the IAM.
finding: He closed an early IAM contract extension (tied to building the MAX in Renton) and values labor peace through the rate ramps.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: Well, I'd love to go to 13 because we could sell them all. Our plan all along has been 10. ... But let's get to 10 first.
finding: He holds the 787 to its planned 10/month despite demand for more, deferring any higher rate until 10 is reached and supplier capacity is proven.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: No, we've looked at doing a brand-new airplane, and that's something that I don't think we will do. It's a huge investment, time and money.
finding: He ruled out a clean-sheet 777 replacement in favour of a new-engine, composite-wing derivative (the eventual 777X).

numbers.outcome: 777X launched 2013 with composite wing and GE9X

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We should have done it last time when the market softened. We didn't. We cut rates. And then when the market came back, we were in a position that we couldn't support all the demands from our customers. I don't want to be in that position again.
finding: He explicitly rejects cutting rates in a soft market, preferring to burn down backlog, because past cuts left Boeing short of capacity in the upturn.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: Well, I'm not sure I want to handicap the competition. We have enjoyed a duopoly. ... I think they'll struggle with the 919 but eventually they’ll probably get it right. And I think if you fast-forward another 10 years from now, that small airplane market in China will be split between Airbus, Boeing and Comac.
finding: He forecasts COMAC sharing China's narrowbody market with Airbus and Boeing within about 10 years, though slowly.

numbers.forecast: China small-airplane market split three ways

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: What I wanted to do is play to the strengths of both of these program managers. ... This has nothing to do with dissatisfaction with the performance of either one of them.
finding: He reassigns program leaders by skill fit (development vs production) and publicly frames moves as non-punitive.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: you don't tell me you need to have more capital to go up in rate. ... How can you work the other levers like Lean and flow ... we're going to spend very, very little capital
finding: He makes lean flow, not capex, the default route to higher rates.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: There has been some slippage. ... now we're looking at the first few months of 2014. ... the loads data that we needed to get from the -8 was late.
finding: He acknowledges a modest 787-9 slip (4Q13 to early 2014) and attributes it to late 787-8 loads data; the first 787-9 was delivered in mid-2014.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: our commitment to the shareholders, my commitment to Jim is, that over the next 5 years, we're going to make this program more profitable each and every year.
finding: He committed to year-over-year 787 profitability improvement over 5 years, with an internal plan he said must be beaten.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I think there's a lot more opportunity to do better than 13% than there are risks to do 13%.
finding: He signalled upside to the MAX's 13% fuel-burn target, consistent with his under-promise doctrine; the MAX met or slightly exceeded it at entry into service.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I fully expect by the end of this year, or sometime in the middle of next year, that if you look at the number of MAX airplanes on order versus the number of neos on order, you're going to see the kind of parity that we've had in years past.
finding: He forecast MAX-neo order parity by end-2012 or mid-2013; the neo kept a sizeable order lead through the decade.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We start looking at a rate increase 24 months before we make the change. And we take a hard look at our people, processes and tools, systems, capital, all the things that go in to a successful rate change and all the things that we've learned from rate changes over the last 95 years at the Boeing
finding: He plans each rate increase with a 24-month lead time across people, processes, tools, systems and capital.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: And this is all about getting in early, understanding the risks, taking action before the suppliers get in trouble and making sure that we don't fumble the ball as we go up in rate. And I don't think we will.
finding: He reviews supplier readiness metrics weekly and intervenes before suppliers fail.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I think there's long tail until we get comfortable that they have figured out how to support us better
finding: Suppliers that needed rescue stay under scrutiny long after the fix and are weighed in future sourcing.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: Program margins, never good enough. We've got to continue to work on productivity and taking costs out of what we do.
finding: He keeps continuous margin improvement among his standing priorities alongside rates and core-program health.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: I think you always want to have a book-to-bill of 1. I really believe that. I don't want to go backwards. ... if the demand is there, we've got to match the capacity with the demand. We're giving up market share if we don't.
finding: He treats book-to-bill below 1 as going backwards and capacity shortfall as surrendering share, so he keeps studying higher 737/777 rates.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We did make some bad decisions on the 787. We did outsource too much. And I think we did it because we were looking to maximize RONA.
finding: He attributes 787 over-outsourcing to a RONA-maximising mindset and now weighs capital efficiency against execution risk.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: And if anybody wants to do anything more, they've got to earn their way onto the airplane, and they got to get by Delaney first and then me next.
finding: He makes himself the final gate on any MAX scope growth.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We're also trying to limit what the liquidated damages would be. We're also, as we always do, where the supply chain doesn't perform, the impact is on them.
finding: On MAX contracts he caps customer liquidated damages and pushes supplier non-performance risk down the chain.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We really have not seen any evidence that would support the fact that we have a bubble. ... I think most of the discussion about that is really coming from the leasors ... They would like to see the supply go down, so prices will go up.
finding: He dismissed production-bubble warnings as lessor self-interest and kept raising rates.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: We understand what game they're playing, and it is a market share game. ... We do not want them to get to 60% and us, 40%. ... they come down the learning curve faster than we do, they have pricing power in the marketplace. It's a slippery slope for us to be on.
finding: He sees Airbus as playing for share and treats a 60/40 split as a strategic red line because of learning-curve and pricing-power effects.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: Now there is some predatory pricing out there. We'll admit that. ... But what we're not doing is losing margin. ... We've got to continue to cut costs so we can maintain the margins
finding: He answers Airbus's predatory pricing by cutting cost to defend margin rather than conceding on price.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: Well, it hasn't been lost on us. We need to go play in their sandbox, too. And we've targeted a few of those airlines.
finding: After losing AMR and others to the neo, he shifts to attacking traditional Airbus customers.
trigger: share losses to A320neo (AMR, Garuda, SAS)
response: target Airbus customers

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: if I reflect back on the organization that we had, 2.5 years ago, there are only 3 people that are currently in the same role.
finding: In about 2.5 years he turned over almost all of BCA's top team, matching people to roles.

speaker: Jim Albaugh, Former Executive Vice President and Member of Executive Council
quote: When we've got all of those things understood, we'll have a discussion with Jim, and we'll decide what we're going to do with this airplane. But right now, we're in the study phase.
finding: Launch decision rights for the 777X sit with the corporate CEO (McNerney) after BCA resolves the A350-1000 view, NRE and configuration.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We will buy accordingly, as long as the stock is undervalued as it is, we will continue to have a pretty active buyback program.
finding: In the 2006 up-cycle he ran a 'balanced cash deployment' with active, valuation-linked buybacks and planned to seek more authorization from the Board.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Well, clearly it's a competitive environment, but we're really pleased with the kinds of deals we're signing. We believe we have embedded in those deals a real opportunity to create real value going forward, Steve, so we're not having fire sales.
finding: He framed order-capture pricing as value-disciplined and denied buying market share with deep discounts.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We remain confident that we'll meet our customer commitments. We are on track to begin flight testing next year, followed by entry into service in 2008.
finding: As CFO he publicly committed to the 787 schedule (flight test 2007, EIS 2008), a commitment later broken by successive delays announced from October 2007 onward.

numbers.outcome: Oct 2007: ~35 deliveries moved from 2008 to 2009; Apr 2008: first delivery Q3 2009

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: It is a very complex, detailed study that has to take place, and generally, once you get through that, the implementation of it is in the future. It's not something that you can turn on immediately.
finding: He treats production-rate increases as slow, study-gated decisions integrated with the supply chain rather than quick responses to demand.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: our focus is on making sure that we can orderly increase our production ramp up, bring our supply chain along so that we can deliver on our commitments, and deliver on our commitments with excellent profitability. That's our first priority.
finding: Despite a sold-out 2007 he ranked an orderly, supply-chain-paced ramp with profitability ahead of chasing demand with faster rate increases.
trigger: Analyst asks about raising production given 98% sold-out 2007
response: Rate rises only after studies with supply chain

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: As you know, our performance score is based on how well we deliver economic profit for the corporation, and one of the levers there are assets, and working capital as well.
finding: He anchored management incentives on economic profit and working-capital efficiency, cascading the metric to executives and salaried staff.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We will continually be working with our customers, because that's where a product development decision is going to start and end ... Right now, Steve, we're just enjoying the success of the 737.
finding: Asked about a 737 replacement, he deferred any new narrowbody decision to customer-driven requirements and preferred to harvest the 737 backlog.
response: No decision; customer-led; deliver on 737 order book

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: we're pretty comfortable with the business case on that product that we're going to deliver good margins. As to whether it will ultimately be higher than the margins on other airplanes, that's yet to be seen.
finding: He backed the 787's new outsourced build model on business-case grounds but avoided promising superior margins.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We're well within the budget, well within the business case, and it really does look good. Stanley, all I can tell you is that right now, this looks like the best-run development program I've ever seen, but it is a development program.
finding: He was highly confident on the 787 in early 2006 while hedging that development risk remained; the program later suffered multi-year delays.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Now, beginning this year we have moved to a split of duties between our CEO, Jim McNerney, and myself on our earnings call. Jim will participate in the calls at mid-year and at year-end and other calls on a selected basis. Of course, I will continue to be on all of Boeing's quarterly earnings calls.
finding: From 2006 the CFO was the constant voice to investors on every quarterly call, with McNerney joining selectively, making Bell the main owner of guidance.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: However, if we do decide to divest or shutdown the business, the move would be accretive to our EPS in 2007 and beyond.
finding: He framed exiting a loss-making non-core business (Connexion) primarily through its EPS accretion, a willingness to cut losing bets.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We are increasing our R&D investment in BCA primarily to reduce risks on 787 program goals related to weight and schedule. The program remains on track to meet its performance commitments and entry into service.
finding: His response to emerging 787 weight and schedule pressure was to spend more R&D up front as risk insurance while reaffirming the schedule.
response: Raised R&D to ~$3B/yr; schedule reaffirmed

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: So again, with the problem with unit margins, I know you all like them, but they're volatile, because they can be affected by near-term things and doesn't take a program picture into effect. But it's a data point.
finding: He steered analysts away from unit margins toward program-accounting margins, downplaying near-term volatility.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: So, quite frankly if we were going to focus on something big happening, it would be something that would be totally unexpected like somebody dropping a big piece of hardware or a big piece of tooling or something having a major failure.
finding: In late 2006 he saw no major technical risk on the 787 beyond freak events; within a year the program announced the first of several delays.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We continue to expect that the 787 and the 747-A will be delivered on time and in accordance with our contractual obligations.
finding: He reaffirmed on-time delivery of both new programs; both the 787 and 747-8 later slipped and the 747-8 took a reach-forward loss in 2008.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: I think the key here is we've gotten out early and looked at what are the possible risks we can experience given where we are at this stage in the development program, and we decided that now is the time to resource those in case they're needed.
finding: He described a pre-emptive contingency approach: fund identified development risks early rather than wait for them to materialize.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We don't have the complexity on our airplane that the A380 is, we have a fifth of the electrical wiring in it. So I think if some of the concern is being driven by what you see out there in other places, then I think you have to understand there's some distinct differences in what we're doing here.
finding: He used Airbus's A380 wiring crisis as a contrast to argue the 787 carried less integration risk.
trigger: A380 delays raise investor concern about 787
response: Distinguished 787 from A380

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: The fact of the matter is, Jim and I are going to run this business from a conservative perspective, and we're going to make sure that we have in place plans early enough that we can implement, so that we can hold to schedule and meet our customer obligations
finding: He presented himself and CEO McNerney as a joint, conservative management team prioritising schedule and customer obligations over near-term earnings.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: And Cai we do feel comfortable. We will hit our guidance at greater than 10.
finding: He committed to BCA 2007 operating margin above 10%; BCA delivered 10.7% for 2007.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Obviously, it's the beginning of a new program, and although it will start out more probable than any new program, any new product introduced at least in our history. It will still dilute the margins that we experienced on our mature programs.
finding: He set expectations that the 787 would be margin-dilutive versus mature 737/777 programs into 2010 even if profitable from the start.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We continue to be a bit over where we want to be on weight, but we remain confident that we will deliver the unprecedented operating efficiency that our customers expect.
finding: He delivered bad 787 news (weight) in minimising terms paired with reassurance.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We are running slightly behind in certain areas. We need to add lab capacity to enable concurrent testing and we expect to hold on to testing resources longer than originally planned.
finding: In July 2007 he characterised 787 systems-development problems as 'slightly behind'; three months later the first major delay was announced.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Given the nature of development programs, there is upward pressure on the 2008 R&D number. However, we do not currently believe that that R&D pressure will effect the EPS guidance we have given you for 2008.
finding: He flagged R&D overrun risk while promising EPS protection; 2008 R&D was raised twice (to $3.6-3.8B) and 2008 EPS ended at $3.71 versus $5.70-5.85 guidance, mainly because of the strike.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Think about it in two ways -- it will be profitable from the first airplane, which is something that is different than what we have experienced in the past
finding: He promised the 787 would be profitable from the first unit; by 2008 Boeing booked it at zero margin and in 2009 wrote off early test airplanes.

numbers.outcome: Apr 2008: 0% program margin assumed for 2009 deliveries

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: where we would have to spend more resources in '08 than we are anticipating in order to support the first delivery in May.
finding: In mid-2007 he still worked to a May 2008 first 787 delivery, which slipped to 2011.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We will sort all this out once the airplane gets built. There could be some of that that is grey that we would look at but quite frankly, we are not planning on it right now. We are just trying to all get together as a team and get this airplane built on time.
finding: He deferred cost recovery from 787 partners to keep them focused on schedule, prioritising delivery over contractual claims.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: if you are asking is there something there for 777 in response YEN to an A-350, probably not distinctly. I think there is something that we would have to deal with generic kinds of things that could be devoted to that for some initial studies if needed
finding: He signalled no dedicated 777 response spending to the A350 in 2007, only generic study money, keeping R&D focused on the 787.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: In '08 we always had high risk on the R&D number, but what we've said is if in fact it has to go up, we would still be able to hold the current guidance on earnings per share and we are holding earnings per share guidance.
finding: When challenged on a missed R&D forecast he reframed the commitment as being about EPS, not R&D, and pointed to EPS being held.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Total Boeing revenue guides for 2008 is reduced to between $67.5 billion and $68.5 billion due to the moving approximately 35 Dreamliner deliveries from 2008 into 2009. Despite the revenue shift, our 2008 EPS guidance is unchanged
finding: On the first 787 delay he reset revenue and cash but held EPS guidance, relying on core-business productivity to absorb the slip.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: And it is important to note that nearly all the 2008 cash flow reduction will be added to 2009 along with the 787 delivery. We expect cash flow in 2009 to be very strong
finding: He framed the 787 delay as a timing shift of cash into 2009; 2009 cash guidance later fell to >$2.5B as delays mounted.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: On the customer side, we have obviously talked all of them. And they are not pleased but, and we are obviously disappointed that we are calling them not to be pleased but, on the other hand they are very,
finding: After the first 787 delay he acknowledged customer displeasure directly but stressed product support and no fatal customer issue.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: During the quarter, we used over $890 million of cash to repurchase 9.4 million shares. For the year, we repurchased 29 million shares or $2.8 million and we intend to remain very active in our share repurchase program.
finding: In January 2008 he committed to continued heavy buybacks plus a 14% dividend increase, a stance reversed a year later when buybacks were cut to ~$200M.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Boeing's debt levels continue to decline during the year as maturing debt was not refinanced due to our strong cash position.
finding: In the boom he let debt run off rather than refinance, prioritising balance-sheet strength and top credit ratings.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: I think the other side of that equation is that the schedule stretch out that we have experienced is going to allow us to work harder on finding opportunities for productivity that would also offset some of the cost we would experience as a result of the delay
finding: He framed a 787 schedule slip as an opportunity to find offsetting productivity, a characteristic positive spin on bad news.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: The order of totals get a lot of attention and that is great, but executing on our record backlog is what really counts. That is our focus for 2008 and for every year beyond that.
finding: At the peak of the order boom he explicitly ranked execution of the backlog above order capture.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: I can't predict what the number will be. I just know that our past history would suggest that we do a pretty good job of mitigating that and not having and roll through to be a significant impact to your financial performance.
finding: On 787 customer compensation he refused to quantify and instead relied on Boeing's track record of mitigating penalties.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: 2009 deliveries will grow to between 500 and 505 airplanes including approximately 25, 787 Dreamliners. We expect further growth in deliveries in 2010.
finding: He guided to ~25 787 deliveries in 2009 within 500-505 total; zero 787s delivered in 2009 and total 2009 guidance was cut to 480-485.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: For 2009, we expect EPS to grow approximately 20% to between $6.80 and $7 per share driven by higher airplane deliveries and progress on growth and productivity initiatives as well as lower R&D and pension
finding: His April 2008 2009 EPS guidance of $6.80-7.00 was cut to $5.05-5.35 in January 2009 and to $4.70-5.00 in April 2009.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: if the economic situation does not deteriorate into something that we don't currently anticipate, if that doesn't happen that the bias would be to the upside there, longer term after '08. But we have time to make that call. And so we will take that time to make that call
finding: On a 737 rate increase he showed an upside bias but explicitly used available time to delay commitment until the economic picture cleared.
response: Pause after series of increases; decide within ~12 months

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Well in the case of the 787 we are going to have probably a 1000, so by the time we deliver it. So we are going to be more constrained by which obviously, gives us great opportunity over a time period to product good earnings and value
finding: He argued the 787's unprecedented pre-delivery order book (vs ~100 typical) de-risked market and pricing and gave capacity to absorb unknowns.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Now in our 2009 financial guidance we have assumed that the 787s delivered during that year will have a zero percent program accounting margin. We believe this allows for sufficient reserved to deal with customers issues and other cost associated with the delay.
finding: After the third 787 delay he chose to book the program at zero margin as a conservative reserve against customer compensation and delay costs.
response: 0% margin assumption for 2009 787 deliveries

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We did have an estimate in there, which we obviously underestimated the disruption that would be caused relative to these costs being allocated to programs, and so we trued it up in second quarter.
finding: He openly admitted underestimating the infrastructure-cost disruption from the 787 slip and described the fix as a true-up.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Well, we think we're going to make our plan in commercial airplanes, but if we don't, we'll still make our earnings per share expectations and the guidance we provided you.
finding: He promised 2008 EPS guidance would hold even if BCA missed; the machinists' strike later drove 2008 EPS to $3.71 versus $5.70-5.85 guidance.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: And we have asked the BCA team and they have accepted the challenge and they're committed to going out to see what we can do to reduce some of the other cost in the infrastructure to moderate those as the base has diminished somewhat with the flying of the 787. So we believe it's doable.
finding: As CFO he set cost-reduction challenges for BCA to recover a first-half shortfall, and described BCA as owning the commitment.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Now due to the uncertain length of the labor strike, we are suspending financial guidance until the strike concludes and a complete assessment is made on further results.
finding: During the 2008 IAM strike he suspended guidance outright rather than give a speculative range.
response: Guidance suspended

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: if the strike continues, then we have to send people home and we have to start shutting down suppliers. Obviously, it will take longer.
finding: He tied the cost response to strike duration, raising the prospect of furloughs and supplier shutdowns if it dragged on.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: particularly for those suppliers that were producing and doing a good job to the original schedule, and we've already talked about that. We have provided some liquidity to them.
finding: He gave liquidity support selectively to suppliers harmed by the 787 delay who had performed to the original schedule.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We will be disciplined in this process and work with BCA to determine the deals that make the most sense. We will also be mindful of preserving our current credit ratings.
finding: He bounded customer-financing support by deal selectivity and protection of the credit rating.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: I'm not saying to you that I'm willing to take it back up to $12 billion, but I am saying we have capacity and we'll have to look and see what happens.
finding: He set an informal ceiling on Boeing Capital's portfolio well below its 2003 peak of $12B while signalling capacity from the ~$6B level.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Share repurchase will decrease significantly in 2009 to approximately 200 million, which will offset dilution from our compensation plans. We are forecasting total capital expenditures to be $1.4 billion in 2009, which is nearly 20% lower than in recent years
finding: In the 2009 cash squeeze he cut buybacks to anti-dilution level and capex by ~20% while protecting the dividend.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: This resulted in an equity adjustment of approximately $8 billion in the fourth quarter, which produced a negative book equity as of year-end. This accounting adjustment will not impact our ability to pay dividends or comply with our debt covenants.
finding: He disclosed negative book equity plainly and immediately bounded its consequences for dividends and covenants.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: However, we are expecting that in 2010 R&D to be down substantially. So this is the year, Howard, that we'll get through our major R&D expenditures.
finding: He forecast 2009 as the peak R&D year; repeated earlier forecasts of falling R&D (2007, 2008) had already been missed.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Late maturity of the 747-8 design drove substantial changes for our supply partners. This coupled with the already existing schedule pressure caused significant disruption throughout the supply chain resulting in the charge we took this quarter.
finding: He explained the $685M 747-8 reach-forward loss with a detailed root-cause breakdown, attributing it mainly to late design maturity.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We'll be looking at that closely and that's why we're delaying the 2010 guidance, because we want to understand better a little of those uncertainties
finding: He delayed out-year guidance until uncertainty narrowed rather than issue a number he might have to cut.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: So the baseline assumption in our operating plan is that these rates will stay stable throughout the planning period. The reason for that is obviously we're under contract to deliver airplanes that would require the stable rates in order to meet those obligations.
finding: In the 2009 recession he anchored production rates to contractual backlog rather than cutting pre-emptively, holding a contingency instead.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We're having daily cash calls where we're making sure we're monitoring advance pays and we're monitoring our disbursements to make sure that we're paying just in time in accords with our contract terms and that we are aggressively pursuing our payments as they are required by contract.
finding: In the 2009 cash squeeze he ran intensive, centralised daily cash management, cutting non-essential spend and capex.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Well we need about $2 billion for operation cash, so that's kind of it. Then in this environment you surely want a safety net, given the fact that we have two major development programs that haven't gotten through their flight certification programs yet
finding: He named roughly $2B as the minimum operating cash level, plus a safety buffer while the 787 and 747-8 remained uncertified.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Had the Twin-Isle production decision has been the only impact this quarter, we would have maintained our earnings per share guidance. However, the lower escalation forecast had a sizable impact on our results
finding: When cutting 2009 EPS guidance he attributed the cut to external escalation indices rather than the twin-aisle rate cuts, which he said were already covered.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: but generally I would say to you we are in much better shape on this program to avoid that than we have been on any prior program.
finding: He argued the 787 was well protected from a forward loss because the order book had fixed market and pricing; in Q3 2009 Boeing took a $2.5B charge on the first test airplanes.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: gives us reasonable confidence that we'll get through the year without a rate adjustment on 37. Now, could things change? It could, but we have not reserved against that at any subtenant level.
finding: He held the 737 rate through the 2009 downturn on the strength of oversold positions; the 737 rate was not cut.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We are not at a point where we are considering cutting our dividends. I want to be very clear on that. We are not there.
finding: Even at the trough of the 787 crisis he ruled out a dividend cut, using debt markets and spending control instead.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: So clearly it's going to be higher than what you've seen traditionally, but until we finally have to book financials on our P&L statements, we are not going to disclose what that number is.
finding: He refused to disclose the 787 accounting quantity until required, a pattern of withholding sensitive estimates until accounting forced disclosure.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Oh, I've never said we weren't concerned about it, Joe. I just said that when we have gone through and done our assessments, we still believe the program to be profitable.
finding: Pressed on 787 profitability, he pushed back on characterisations of his past statements and restated the process-based conclusion.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: The cumulative impact of scheduled delays including the current one being assessed is obviously putting pressure on the program's profitability.
finding: After the June 2009 787 side-of-body delay he conceded mounting pressure on 787 profitability while deferring the accounting conclusion.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: the underlining engine in this company is performing well and that's predominantly the basis of our guidance, and until we really have a clearer understanding of the impact of the fix on that performance, we think it's appropriate to hold it
finding: After the 787 side-of-body delay he held guidance unchanged pending assessment, disclosing that the fix was not yet included, rather than pre-emptively cutting.
response: Guidance held pending assessment

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: We are controlling pretty tightly any expenditure that doesn't directly support our priority which is obviously getting the 787 airplane, getting that development done and in the hands of our customers
finding: In mid-2009 he made finishing the 787 the single top priority for cash, with all other spending tightly controlled.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: but it does allow us to have better control over a significant element of the production process that supports the 787 and obviously our intent in going in and acquiring it is to drive better performance.
finding: He justified buying Vought's 787 fuselage operation as taking back control of a failing outsourced work package, a partial reversal of the 787 outsourcing model.

speaker: James Bell, Chief Financial Officer
quote: Well, we have sold 850 of these and we know we are way ahead of our competition and the market is still going to be robust over a timeframe that we think we have the ability to estimate
finding: He leaned on the 787's lead over the A350 in orders to argue the program's revenue stream was secure despite delays.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: While we recognize contributing stock would have a dilutative (sic) [dilutive] impact to existing shares, there would also be a net cash benefit to the company, and lower future pension expenses.
finding: To conserve cash he proposed funding the pension with stock, accepting dilution; Boeing then contributed ~29M shares ($1.5B) in Q4 2009.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Looking forward, we will have pressure on our 2010 cash flow, as inventory continues to build on the 787 program. We expect that cash flow will improve in 2011, when we deliver more 787s and the 747-8s.
finding: He pointed to 2011 for the cash recovery; 2011 operating cash guidance was later cut from >$5B to >$2.5B as 787 deliveries slipped again.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: BCA's third quarter operating loss of $2.8 billion reflects the 787 cost reclassification of $2.5 billion for costs incurred through July on the first three flight-test airplanes, $138 million of spending on those planes in August and September, and the $1 billion 747 charge.
finding: He disclosed the 787 test-aircraft write-off and a second 747-8 charge together, presenting them as reclassifications while maintaining the 787 was not in a loss position.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: The remaining 362 million relates to the challenging market conditions, and the company's decision to maintain the 747-8 production rate at 1.5 airplanes per month for nearly two years longer than previously planned.
finding: Facing weak 747-8 demand, management cut the planned rate ramp and took the cost hit up front rather than build to an over-optimistic rate.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Obviously, that is an open issue that we have a lot of attention focused on, but clearly we see it two ways. I mean, obviously we got to work our way through it, but it doesn't mean that the initial claim that they put forward is what we will ultimately settle on.
finding: He took a firm negotiating stance on 787 supplier cost assertions, treating initial claims as opening bids.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Yes, when you have two major development programs, I don't think there's any such thing as that.
finding: Asked about excess cash after raising $5B of debt, he denied any excess while two development programs were open and deferred buybacks to 2011 or later.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: At this point, we're not considering going back and repurchase, our share repurchase program, and we won't get back to that or start considering things like that probably until 2011. Once we get through the challenges we have on our books today.
finding: He explicitly sequenced shareholder returns after completion of the 787 and 747-8 development programs.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: It's prudent, not conservative. But let me just tell you what it is, Cai.
finding: A signature phrase: he rejected 'conservative' or 'cushion' labels for guidance and insisted it was 'prudent', then itemised the drivers.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: when you take all of that in consideration, it walks that 11.1 down to the range we're showing you between 6.5 and 7.5.
finding: His 2010 BCA margin guidance of 6.5-7.5% proved conservative: it was raised twice and BCA delivered 9.4% in 2010.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Let me remind you that initial deliveries for our new programs typically start out with lower zero margins and improve over time. We anticipate that 787 will follow the same pattern.
finding: By 2010 his 787 margin message had shifted from 'profitable from the first airplane' (2007) to zero initial margins, a quiet reset of expectations.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: We expect 2011 R&D expense to decrease by more than $500 million, a substantial reduction but one that retains funds that support the 787 and 747 derivatives and pursue potential investments in the 777 and the 737.
finding: Even while cutting R&D he kept money earmarked for 787/747 derivatives and future 777 and 737 investments.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: On 747-8, clearly it's still a program that's challenging for us. We do have issues that we've encountered on this program, literally every day.
finding: He candidly described the 747-8 as a daily struggle while noting opportunities had offset risks, so no further reach-forward loss.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: I would call it being prudent. The fact of the matter is that we still have two major programs that are in flight-test that we need to get certified. We do have a lot of units that are in production that, should something come out of that certification process that would have to require us to have to modify them.
finding: He reserved for concurrency risk: many 787/747-8 airplanes built before certification could require rework.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: We're going to be pricing those reasonably and trying to keep them stable. But obviously, we have some room so that we can really be competitive as necessary.
finding: With orders recovering in 2010 he aimed for stable pricing but signalled headroom to discount against Airbus where needed.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Operating cash flow for this two-year period is expected to be higher than prior guidance, with 2010 now expected to be greater than $1.5 billion, and 2011 expected to be greater than $4 billion.
finding: He re-phased cash between 2010 and 2011 as the 787 and 747-8 slipped; 2010 came in at $3B while 2011 was cut further to >$2.5B.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: We had no further reach in third quarter as a result of the schedule slide. Clearly, we've been working -- the risk items, clearly, we've been working our opportunities and we had a little reserved in the number in our assumptions already.
finding: He absorbed another 787 slip without a reach-forward loss by netting risks against opportunities and existing reserves.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: The 2011 commercial delivery forecast is between 485 and 500 airplanes and is sold out. This includes a combined 25 to 40 787s and 747-8 deliveries, split roughly equally between the two programs.
finding: His 2011 forecast of 25-40 787 and 747-8 deliveries was cut to 20-30 in July and 15-20 in October 2011.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: We found ourselves having issues on the original program, and we found some ways to improve on that, and so when we got into the development phase of the 787-9, we implemented those lessons learned and that's what it is.
finding: For the 787-9 Boeing took back design control and paid suppliers as it went, a lesson-learned shift away from partner-funded development on the 787-8.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: But I don't want to lose sight of the fact that we still have two major development programs that we need to deliver on mid-year and third quarter. And so I'm obviously cautious about, and aware of that, Howard
finding: After a strong quarter he declined to raise guidance until development deliveries were secured, a consistent wait-until-it's-real stance.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: By the end of this year, we should have a sharper view of new airplane versus re-engine. As you know, most of the data and customer feedback is suggesting to us that the new airplane option is the most favorable.
finding: In April 2011 (transcript attributes this to Bell; the wording resembles McNerney's) Boeing's stated lean was an all-new narrowbody for 2019-2020, reversed within months in favour of the 737 MAX re-engine.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: And so you can think your way through that the R&D spend at the height would be lower even on a new program whether it be re-engined or whether it be a new airplane, because we're only going to do one of those programs one at a time.
finding: After the 787/747-8 concurrency, he committed to running only one major development program at a time with a lower R&D peak.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: As we progress along these efforts, we will look more broadly at our cash deployment plans, including dividend increases and share repurchases. We will also continue to look at niche M&A opportunities to enhance capabilities and supplement our core organic growth strategy.
finding: He signalled a return to dividend increases and buybacks once the 787/747-8 entered delivery, with M&A limited to niche deals.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: So again, we won't be running $4 billion a year as we have the last couple, but we're not going to go down to $1.5 billion.
finding: He set an R&D floor above the pre-787 $1.5-1.7B level to pre-fund technology before the next program, avoiding concurrent technology and product development.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: I don't think you're going to see a lot of large things. I don't think you're going to see much more consolidation of primes in the aerospace industry. But there'll be small acquisitions, and they'll be something well within our financial ability to execute on.
finding: He ruled out large M&A in favour of small, affordable bolt-ons in defense and services.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Now as the program achieves a stable rate of 10 airplanes per month, which we expect to happen in late 2013, and maintains a healthy production system at that level, deferred production cost should begin to decline
finding: He committed to 787 rate 10 by late 2013 as the trigger for deferred-cost decline.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: but we will make the cash we've invested in this program back. Probably not as soon as I'd like, but we will get it back.
finding: He committed to recovering the 787 cash investment while conceding the timeline would be longer than he wanted.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Obviously, 2 years ago, I had to deal with that. We expected this program to be done and start deliveries, and we had to respond accordingly. And I think you saw that we responded reasonably well under the circumstances.
finding: Looking back on 2009, he characterised his crisis response (debt raising, cash control, stock pension contribution) as adequate and still carried risk in guidance.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Well, it would be 7%. But getting there has proved difficult because obviously, you got to get the Commercial business up to a pretty high level and you need the Defense business at double digits.
finding: He kept a 7% long-term net margin goal while admitting Boeing had repeatedly fallen short at 4-4.5%.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Looking ahead to future development efforts, I can assure you, and Jim has already done this as well, that we will take a much more disciplined approach in developing and executing those programs. We will continue to leverage things that have worked for us, such as risk-sharing arrangements with our partners.
finding: He promised more disciplined future development while keeping partner risk-sharing, the element of the 787 model he still endorsed.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Historically, R&D spending on a new airplane has started about 5 to 6 years in advance of first delivery, and for a new derivative, about 3 to 4 years before delivery. Now typically, R&D peaks about 1 to 2 years in advance of that first delivery.
finding: He gave explicit timing rules for R&D on clean-sheet versus derivative programs, useful for modelling launch-to-EIS spend.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: I mean, we're not going to enter into fixed-price contracts where we don't have good, defined requirements, where we don't have fidelity on, on what it takes to build the product, both from a spec standpoint and a price standpoint.
finding: He set a condition for fixed-price defense work: only with well-defined requirements and cost fidelity.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Now the sensitivity in terms of having a slip, I mean it's not that sensitive. I mean, I think we could absorb some slips in terms of the schedule and in the ramp up and still hold pretty much to what our profit assumptions are.
finding: He argued life-of-program fixed-price supplier contracts and a large order book made 787 profitability robust to further slips.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: So I'm not going to cut Dennis' business down to historically low rates either. So again, we won't be running $4 billion a year as we have the last couple
finding: As CFO he set R&D envelopes for both business units, explicitly protecting defense (Muilenburg's BDS) prototyping spend for competitive bidding.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: As we have previously stated we won this program by offering the best integrated solution to meet the customer needs with an aggressive yet responsible bid.
finding: He described the KC-46 bid as 'aggressive yet responsible' and not in a forward-loss position; later overruns led to large charges.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: The benefits of volume leverage and continued productivity improvements are balanced with the competitive pricing environment and investments in tooling and production systems necessary to achieve the higher production rates.
finding: With 737 rate 42 announced for 2014, he booked rate increases as margin-neutral given pricing competition from Airbus and ramp investment.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: On R&D, Rob, obviously, a derivative airplane is a lot less expensive, a lot less risk associated with than an all-new airplane. So we will see that the R&D impact to this will be a lot less.
finding: After the 737 MAX re-engine decision he framed the derivative's lower cost and risk as a financial benefit versus a clean sheet.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: We had always bid this contract thinking that on the EMD phase, it would be a very low profitability or breakeven and that the profit would be generated as we started producing the tankers, the 179.
finding: He accepted breakeven on fixed-price development in exchange for production profits, an explicit investment-style bid.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: And as Jim just talked about, we do have pricing pressure that we are assuming in the margins today, and we talked about that earlier, that there is going to be some pricing pressure and we understand that. So the plan would be going forward is to sustain the margins.
finding: Amid the A320neo-driven competition he targeted sustaining, not expanding, production margins.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: I would use another C word. I would use the conversion. Actually, they converted from the 787 to 737 as they concentrate on growing their capacity in the domestic markets
finding: He reframed a customer's 787 cancellation as a 'conversion' to the 737, minimising negative order news.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: Our initial gross margin booking rate on the 787 is in the low single digits, which takes in consideration the cumulative impacts of delays and near-term production challenges.
finding: The 787 opened with a low-single-digit margin on a 1,100-unit block, far from his 2007 'profitable from the first airplane' framing.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: So in terms of that assumption, I would look at late '14, early '15 for it to be stable.
finding: Five months after targeting 787 rate-10 stability in late 2013, he pushed the stable-rate point to late 2014/early 2015.

speaker: James A. Bell, Former Executive Vice President
quote: there are significantly more costs associated with these first 40 airplanes as we build them out of sequence. And so that's why we believe once we digest those, the learning curve will go down sharply to traditional learning curve levels earlier than you would normally see
finding: He attributed high early 787 unit costs to out-of-sequence concurrent production and predicted a steep learning-curve drop afterwards.

speaker: David L. Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: It is important to emphasize that this estimate should not be interpreted as an attempt to influence or interfere with the FAA and other regulators' absolute authority to determine the timing and conditions ... accurate financial reporting requires that we provide our latest and most informed schedule.
finding: When he gave a schedule, he said it existed only because the accounting required one and that it was not pressure on the FAA. Every later date he gave came with the same caveat.

speaker: David L. Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
