quote: And in some ways, this moment will accelerate recovery, not delay it.
finding: Forecasts the door-plug pause will speed recovery; by April 2024 he conceded it would slow the recovery timing.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: Whatever conclusions are reached, Boeing is accountable for what happened. Whatever the specific cause of the accident might turn out to be, an event like this simply must not happen on an airplane that leaves one of our factories.
finding: Accepts accountability for the Alaska 1282 door-plug blowout before the root cause is known.
response: own it; quality actions

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: We caused the problem, and we understand that.
finding: Plain admission of responsibility in the door-plug crisis.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: I'm sort of glad they called out a pause because that's a good excuse to just take our time, do it right, and I wish I had called that out in the first day
finding: Welcomes the FAA-imposed production pause and regrets not calling it himself.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: She had a way different argument for me, and it was right.
finding: Reversed course and withdrew the MAX 7 anti-ice exemption request after a senator's argument and customer consultation.
trigger: Senate pushback on MAX 7 time-limited exemption
response: withdraw exemption request

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: Today, we're producing 737s at a rate of 38 per month. And we will remain at that rate until the FAA and Boeing is satisfied with our quality and manufacturing process.
finding: Accepts the FAA production cap at 38 and freezes the ramp.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: I know that these moments that impact delivery schedules can frustrate our customers and our investors. But quality and safety must come above all else.
finding: After the door plug, ranks quality and safety explicitly above delivery schedules and investor expectations, displacing free cash flow as the headline priority.
response: quality over deliveries and cash

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: By the end of this year, we expect to have largely delivered our 737 and 787 inventory, effectively shutting down our 2 large shadow factories.
finding: Dated commitment to clear legacy inventory and close the shadow factories by end-2024.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: If we get ourselves to 38, which is our first objective, and we do it in a steady fashion moving up another 12 in my view, is doable in the window that we're talking about.
finding: Keeps the rate-50 by 2025-26 goal after the door-plug accident.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: We won't rate up. We won't do anything until it is under control, and that has to stay that way.
finding: Rate increases are conditional on the FAA-agreed control metrics.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: Effective March 1, we moved inspection and rework teams to Wichita. Since then, we have only allowed fully inspected fuselages to be shipped to Renton
finding: Pushed inspection upstream to Spirit and accepted only clean fuselages, trading near-term deliveries for quality.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: the FAA didn't demand that. We demanded it because it's -- we're determined to get ahead of it.
finding: Presents the traveled-work crackdown as Boeing's own choice, not regulator-imposed.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: if we get to a moment where the buffers exceed that requirement, we will curtail but not until they exceed that requirement.
finding: Keeps suppliers running at plan during the slowdown to build buffers for rate 50, curtailing only when buffers exceed need.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: On the other hand, when you get big development programs wrong, you pay a price, and you pay it for a long time, and I know an awful lot about that. So my view is that next leader has to be prepared to make smart long-term decisions and get the development programs right.
finding: His succession prescription: the decisive risk is new-airplane development, not production.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: we've identified an engineering solution for the engine anti-ice system for in-production aircraft that will be implemented and certified in 2025 to support the first delivery of our -7 and -10
finding: Resets MAX 7/10 first delivery to after a 2025 anti-ice fix certification.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: Every metric gets better when you slow things down.
finding: Signature conviction that slowing production improves every quality and flow metric.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: We know that ASKs will be big. We know wage ASKs will be big. We're not afraid to treat our employees well in this process.
finding: Signals willingness to pay up to avoid an IAM strike, while handing the negotiation to his successor.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: This is an important shift in strategic direction, and it would course correct the decision made decades ago.
finding: Reverses the decades-old Spirit divestiture by agreeing to reacquire Spirit AeroSystems and bring fuselage work back in-house.

speaker: David Calhoun, President, CEO & Director
quote: I don't think this is intended to be a large leadership overhaul.
finding: Expected his successor (Ortberg) to keep the team and complete the stabilisation plan.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we're in a $3.3 billion to $3.5 billion as a total company right now for 2012. I think you should kind of think about it very similarly for 2013. The Dash 9 is going to be coming down, and the MAX is going to be coming up.
finding: He guides R&D to stay flat by overlapping programs, with one program's spend falling as the next rises, rather than stacking new development spend.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So I'm feeling cautiously optimistic as we go into these rate ramps. Now rate ramps are always a big deal, and but they're the key piece of executing all the profitability and all the cash projections as we move forward. So if we hit these rate ramps, we're going to be doing really well, and we're going to hit them.
finding: His confidence language moves from a hedge ('cautiously optimistic') to a flat promise ('we're going to hit them'), tying profit and cash guidance to the rate ramps.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So the key for us now is to get out there, sell more and keep that thing at that 2 a month and then get the 8-I into the marketplace a little bit more now than what we've had in the past.
finding: In 2012 he committed to defending a 2-per-month 747-8 rate through sales, a target the slice shows was not held: by May 2015 the rate had been cut to 1.3.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We are at 5 a month in the supply chain today, and we are breaking back in our factories right now to 5. And we will end the year at 5 a month on the 787.
finding: He gave a dated rate commitment (787 at 5/month by end-2012) that the slice shows was met: in March 2013 he reported 5/month across the whole value stream.

numbers.outcome: 2013-03-04: 'We are producing at 5 a month today across the whole value stream'

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I think we're going to be kind of hanging right in there. Heidi, it's -- if it's not, it's going to be very, very close.
finding: He guided a 2013 book-to-bill near 1; the slice shows demand ran far stronger, with the backlog rising from 4,400 (May 2013) to 5,154 airplanes (May 2014), so his order forecast was conservative.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: once we get to a 42 a month to maintain that as we go forward, once we get to 8.3 on the 777, maintain that as we go forward. ... the 787 as we make that climb to 10 a month, then we're going to peg it and then we look at what we can do after that.
finding: His rate doctrine is step-and-hold: reach the target rate, peg it and only then consider the next increase.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I think it's better to be steady, and we really manage our skyline well now. ... in the single aisles, we did not take the rate down. ... We are managing skyline better than we have, I think, ever, and we over-quote when we feel like it's necessary.
finding: He prefers holding production rates steady through a soft cycle, using skyline management and deliberate overbooking (over-quote) rather than cutting rates.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We're focused on trying to move people towards that defined contribution, and we'll continue to work that. ... whatever we do, we are still going to be a market-leading compensation, benefits and salary.
finding: In labour talks he pushes the pension shift from defined benefit to defined contribution while framing total pay as market-leading.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we started aggregating all the demand across our entire value stream. ... And we've got about 600 people that are in the supply chain today that are monitoring rate ramp and making sure that we stay on track.
finding: After the 787 supply problems he put Boeing deep inside the supply chain, aggregating raw-material demand and assigning about 600 people to monitor supplier readiness for rate increases.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I have spent a tremendous amount of time kind of baselining with all the programmers exactly where we are, what we got to do and then creating our new operating rhythm, focused around executing the rates, driving the profitability and then what are we going to do for the future with respect particularly to widebody programs
finding: Three months into the BCA job his first move was to baseline every program and install an operating rhythm that ranks rate execution and profitability ahead of future widebody decisions.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: the rate and profitability are the 2 big things. We are driving the efficiencies through the supply chain to get to rate, but we're also putting a tremendous focus on the profitability of the program as well.
finding: On the 787 he treats rate and profitability as twin priorities that both depend on supplier efficiency, with gains shared with suppliers.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So we'll get ourselves through the MAX, get ourselves through the 9, get the production stable, look at where we're at. And then as we speak right now, we are defining the airplanes with our customer to make sure that we've got the right products when we are ready to go
finding: He sequences new launches (777X, 787-10) behind finishing current derivatives and stabilising production, while defining configurations with customers in parallel.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We're using that kind of an opportunity to de-risk a little bit into our rate ramp, and then in the outer years, we'll look at some of the opportunities out there, too.
finding: When a customer (Qantas) gave up near-term 787 slots he chose to keep them as buffer to de-risk the ramp rather than resell them immediately, though he said he could sell them.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we are still driving a great premium on the MAX over the NEO, and we're driving a great premium on the MAX over the classic, the current NG. So our pricing, I'm very comfortable with our pricing as it is today
finding: He asserts a price premium for the MAX over the A320neo and refuses to discuss breakeven, presenting pricing as a strength against Airbus.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: SilkAir was a great example of we won down there and actually flipped an all Airbus customer to an all Boeing customer now. ... because of the range of the MAX over the NEO, they felt like they could go in and open new markets into China much easier than they could with the Airbus product.
finding: He keeps score of 'flips' of Airbus operators and credits product performance (MAX range) for the wins.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: It's important that I think everybody recognizes that the batteries are not used in flight. That's one thing that's been -- I've been asked a number of times. So I'm just going to get that out of the way right now.
finding: During the 787 grounding he opened by framing the problem as limited in seriousness before describing the fix.
trigger: 787 lithium-ion battery incidents (JAL, ANA) and fleet grounding, Jan 2013
response: frame the battery as non-critical in flight

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: right now, we're on track to break to 7 and then go to 10. ... Now obviously, that could change if something were to go sideways with the FAA or something like that. But we'll cross that bridge when we get to it.
finding: Even mid-grounding he held the 787 ramp plan (7 then 10 per month); the slice shows 7/month rolled out in May 2013 and 10/month reached by May 2014.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: right now, with the battery, I think the guidance stays in place. The battery situation, we still will be able to pull that off given the time frames that we're looking at.
finding: He refused to cut guidance during the grounding, betting the fix timeline would let Boeing absorb the disruption; in May 2013 he reiterated delivery guidance of more than 60 787s.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: after the events of both the JAL and ANA event, we put together a group of about 200 of our very best engineers across the enterprise ... We've probably compiled 200,000 hours of analysis and tests, and we've come up with a very comprehensive solution to the battery issue.
finding: His crisis response was a large, engineering-led effort that pulled specialists from across the enterprise, and he cited its scale as evidence the fix was sound.
response: 200-engineer team; fix presented to FAA Feb 22

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We are, as you know, a stickler for safety, both from a standpoint of the airplane, passenger crew, the whole thing. And then we would not go forward unless we felt like we had it nailed, and I think we do.
finding: He expressed firm conviction that the battery fix was complete and presented safety as a precondition for returning to service.
response: assert confidence in fix

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we're just continuing to produce at 5 per month, and we haven't slowed that down a bit. And the airplanes are rolling out very clean to the field.
finding: Through the grounding he kept 787 production at rate, accepting a build-up of undelivered airplanes rather than slowing the line.
response: maintain 5/month production

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: But we've got to keep our eye on this thing, and we're going to go kind of month-to-month to watch and see how things go.
finding: On the cargo-dependent 747-8 he manages the rate month by month against demand signals rather than committing to a fixed plan.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: certainly, you don't ever want to do anything from a cost perspective that would put any strain on the quality or schedule because all it does is end up costing you money in the long run.
finding: He states that supplier cost-down must never compromise quality or schedule, which he sees as costlier in the long run.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: there are other instances where we are utilizing some competitive situations to drive cost down too without losing the schedule or quality side of this thing. So we've qualified some of the people, and now we have some new competition out there.
finding: Besides 'partnering', he uses second-sourcing and supplier competition as leverage to push costs down.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: for us, right now, the focus on execution is really important. I think as you -- from midyear last year to the end of the year, what I've -- what we did differently I think was the focus on pure execution of the rate breaks, of the deliveries.
finding: His defining priority as BCA CEO was 'pure execution' of rate breaks and deliveries.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: the initial launch deals can get a little bit more aggressive than what you see as you start to stabilize out, and I think what we're seeing now is a stabilization that's occurring in the marketplace. So hopefully, that's -- we're through some of that intense pricing pressure.
finding: He accepts aggressive launch-customer pricing on a new derivative and expects prices to firm once the airplane is established.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: one of the reasons why we do go down a sole source scenario is that we end up optimizing the engine, airplane -- airframe combination, and that's what gives us the performance that we do
finding: He backs sole-source engine deals (CFM LEAP-1B on the MAX) as a way to optimise the engine and airframe together, rather than offering an engine choice.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we want to maintain our market position ... I think we've got the airplane in the 777X that will do that. ... I think it only benefits the 777 for us to be there with the 777X, much like with the MAX. ... try to get the business case where it needs to be
finding: He justified the 777X as defending market position in the large twin-aisle segment and modelled it on the MAX, launching only once the business case was ready.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: even through all of the analysis and everything that we've done, we couldn't see any reason to make the switch back. ... It's much faster for us to get back into the air that way. But really, at the end of the day, we feel very comfortable with the technology as it stands.
finding: He kept the lithium-ion technology rather than switch back to older nickel-cadmium batteries, citing speed of return to service and confidence in the technology.
response: retain lithium-ion with containment fix

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We stepped into some of that risk knowingly, and we're not doing that again. And I think the MAX is a great example of how we've approached this thing.
finding: Learning from the 787, he explicitly rejects knowingly taking on development risk again and points to the MAX as his model of a lower-risk program.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I think Airbus was very clear, too, that they're going to -- it's not that they're moving away from the technology so much that they're -- they just wanted to give themselves an alternate path as they move forward. And I think that's -- from their standpoint, probably a prudent way to look at this thing, too.
finding: He described Airbus's A350 battery fallback without criticism, calling it prudent for Airbus while defending Boeing's different choice.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we were a little late getting into the marketplace ... we were about a year late. And so there were some head-to-heads that we were involved with that we had to be a little bit more aggressive on.
finding: He admitted that launching the MAX about a year after the NEO forced sharper pricing in head-to-head campaigns against Airbus.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: book-to-bill will be 1. So we're going to push real hard on that. ... some people get concerned about the A350. And clearly, that is a concern. But 3 out of the 6 customers have ordered 777s as well.
finding: He openly called the A350 a threat to the 777 but rebutted it with evidence that A350 buyers were also ordering 777s, and set a book-to-bill target of 1.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: because we potentially could have 5 development programs going on at any one time with the MAX, the Tanker, the Dash 9, Dash 10 and the 777X. We separated production and development. So now we have a leader over development side
finding: He reorganised BCA by separating production from development under its own leader, so that five overlapping programs could share teams and lessons learned.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: 787, yes, we've had some pretty tough years on the 787, to say the least. But I think now we are turning towards 7 a month, I would say, we have turned the corner.
finding: He admits past problems briefly, then declares a turning point ('turned the corner') tied to a rate milestone.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Today, we're at 38 737s, which is an increase of 37% since 1999, and we're going to ramp to 42 in mid 2014. And we're going to do it all the same footprint as we were back in 1999
finding: He committed to 737 rate 42 by mid-2014 in the same factory footprint; the slice shows 42/month reached by September 2014.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So our guidance is unchanged for more than 60 dream lines by the end of 2013, and the production system continues to get healthier and more productive. On May 9, we rolled out our 7 per month airplane, and we're on track to break to 10 per month by the end of the year.
finding: Right after the grounding he held 787 delivery guidance and the 10/month target; the slice shows 10/month reached in about 2.5 years by May 2014.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I think if we hadn't had the battery situation on the 10X, we would have probably gotten there a lot sooner in terms of the launch. But it's difficult for somebody to go forward and want to say, "Hey, I want to go buy a 10X when the airplanes on the ground."
finding: He acknowledged that the 787 grounding delayed the 787-10 launch because customers would not commit while the fleet was grounded.
response: 787-10 launch deferred

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: It's good for our suppliers to be healthy, that is an absolutely imperative. For them not to be healthy, puts us at ... risk, too.
finding: He treats supplier financial health as a strategic imperative, even when efficiency gains also benefit Airbus, which shares the suppliers.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We go from 137 seats all the way up to 460 seats, and our plan is to go with 15% -- 10% to 15% seating increments between them. ... the 8X really is the one that matches up with the A350 1000.
finding: His product doctrine is a full family in 10-15% seat steps, with each derivative positioned against a specific Airbus model.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We were still thinking about going with a new small airplane up to that point, but it was clear that our customers, they didn't want to wait that long for the new efficiency. So we always had a re engine as part of the option, and then we brought that forward with the American deal as an option.
finding: He describes the MAX re-engine as a customer-driven reversal from a clean-sheet plan, triggered by the NEO and the American Airlines order.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: it gives us time to go look at this new small airplane, it give us time to go think about where do you start in terms of the right size. What's the right size to start with? ... but we need to go address the widebodies first
finding: He uses the MAX's long life to postpone a new small airplane and put widebody launches (777X, 787-10) first.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We have carefully managed this backlog for size and breadth and diversity, particularly after 2001, where we ended up taking the production lines down because we were so concentrated in North America.
finding: Shaped by the post-2001 rate cuts, he manages the backlog for regional and customer diversity to reduce downturn risk.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we've got them boxed in on the A350 at the top and we've got them boxed in at the bottom with the 787. So we feel strongly that we've got a terrific lineup of products for the future, so now it's just going to be about getting them launched and moving on.
finding: He describes the widebody strategy as boxing in the A350 with the 777X above and the 787 below.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: would I have loved to have taken all the share? Absolutely. But we got half of it, we got lot of widebodies in there. And the NEO, I think got a little bit of a jump on us, frankly, and we're still playing a little bit of catch up, but I still like the quality of our backlog a lot.
finding: He admitted the NEO got ahead of the MAX and that Boeing was still catching up, and stressed backlog quality over share.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Airbus had some, a lot of early positions available, okay. That's 1. ... But we didn't have those early delivery positions that Rusdi wanted very desperately, and so we'll see. And we didn't have some of the things that they brought to market in terms of pricing and some of that other stuff.
finding: He explains losing the Lion Air mega-order by Airbus's early delivery slots and pricing, which shows a sold-out skyline limits Boeing in some campaigns.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Battle tested team, driving a lot of productivity gains and we're well positioned to transform this backlog into cash. We've taken all of the lessons learned, major painful lessons, I have to say.
finding: He presents the 787 ordeal as having produced a 'battle tested' team and frames the job as converting backlog to cash.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: reduce the capital investment that's necessary when we go to 12 and to 14. We would anticipate a reduction from what it would typically be, to take the rates up again by about 25%.
finding: He plans future 787 rate increases (12, 14) to need about 25% less capital, using flow-time gains in place of new capacity.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I'll tell you what, I would put our product strategy up against anything in the world. It's got the most comprehensive market coverage, and it's a product line that is absolutely customer-driven, customer-focused and customer-generated.
finding: He talks up the portfolio in sweeping, absolute terms and calls it customer-generated.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Long term, the single-aisle market is going to be met by the 737 MAX, which is on track to deliver in third quarter of 2017.
finding: He committed to first MAX delivery in Q3 2017; by May 2016 the slice shows it pulled forward to the first half of 2017.

numbers.outcome: 2016-05-11: 'deliver in the first half of ... next year'

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: within that union agreement, which goes out to 2024, we have significant productivity and quality and safety incentives in there for the individuals but also for the company, too. We share in these benefits
finding: He uses the long-term IAM contract, with shared productivity incentives tracked weekly, as a lever for productivity.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we continue to pull on 4 main levers, and that is execution of the rate increases; increasing our production system efficiency and productivity; and lowering our nonrecurring and recurring costs on our development programs. And I can't stress that enough ... and then, finally, delivering world-class customer support and services.
finding: His four profit levers were rate execution, productivity, lower development costs (which he stressed most) and services growth.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: What always frustrates me when we go through these development programs is having to go back and do redesigns to lower cost. We're going to do that right up front and get the airplane out here that is in the right cost structure right from the very beginning
finding: He insists on designing in the target cost from the start of a program rather than redesigning for cost later.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: much like the way we did the bridge strategy on the 737NG, we're going to do a similar approach with the 777X in terms of pairing orders ... It's not to say that's not going to be -- it's not easy, but I think we're in a very good position to fill the bridge as we move forward.
finding: His transition tactic is to pair current-model orders with orders for the new derivative (777 with 777X), copying the NG-to-MAX bridge.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We knew that the 747-8 was going to be a niche airplane. The neat thing about it is we have both cargo and passenger. We still see it as a very integral part of our product strategy as we move forward.
finding: He keeps the 747-8 in the lineup as a niche product rather than cancelling it, despite weak cargo demand.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: The good news about that is we've already done a composite wing with Mitsubishi, and we were the ones that pretty much set up that production system there ... But having it in Everett was a big advantage for us, and it significantly derisked the program.
finding: He sees in-house, co-located composite wing production for the 777X (Everett) as a way to reduce program risk.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: it's 8% better than a NEO. So we're still the most efficient in the market segment. So a little -- just a little saying that we like to have, the NG is better today and the 737 MAX will certainly be better tomorrow. I might want to say that to John Leahy here in a couple of days
finding: He taunts Airbus's sales chief with a slogan claiming a per-seat efficiency lead for the MAX over the NEO.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: since the A350-1000 was launched, the 300ER has outsold them 2:1, 2:1. It's still the best airplane out there, by far.
finding: He defends the current 777 against the A350-1000 with sales-ratio evidence.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we're going to continue to deploy our cash accordingly to both the investors and then into the new programs and those kinds of things. And we increased the dividend 50%, and I think that's -- we'll continue to go down that path.
finding: He backs the company's balanced deployment of cash to shareholders (a 50% dividend increase) and to new programs.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: what we've demonstrated over the course of the last several years is our ability to continue to be highly productive and continue to offset any pricing pressure that we may see with great productivity and great efficiency to our production systems.
finding: He meets questions about pricing pressure by pointing to productivity, never by admitting margin erosion.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We've got 150 options to fill that bridge. We fill like about 50 airplanes per year, and we've sold in firm deals already this year, 43. ... So I'm feeling pretty bullish on the bridge as we look forward.
finding: He was bullish on filling the 777 bridge, citing a run-rate of about 50 orders per year; the slice later shows 777 output being stepped down (May 2016).

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: The approximate $25 billion. Yes. ... as we take the rates up to 12 a month in 2016, that's when you'll start to see this thing come down
finding: He tied the peak and decline of 787 deferred production cost (about $25B) to reaching 12/month in 2016; the slice confirms 12/month was reached by May 2016.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: rate in that -- somewhat in that 2018 time frame. Now I can tell you that the demand is there for those airplanes, significant demand. And so I'm not uncomfortable with the timing or with the rate.
finding: He backed a 737 rate of 52 around 2018; by May 2015 the slice shows it formalised ('47 in 2017, 52 in 2018').

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Yes, I do. I mean, we wouldn't be thinking about that if we didn't think they were. ... And then we all prepared for something -- when we went to 47, we were preparing for the possibility of something higher, too.
finding: He builds options for higher rates into supply-chain preparation ahead of formal rate decisions.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So bringing those 2 things together now today is kind of where we're focused on stabilizing and getting the Dash 9 and the Dash 8 mixed together at that 10 a month rate. ... And then we'll increase the rate again as we stabilize and then bring the Dash 10 in there after that.
finding: He sequences one change at a time: stabilise the 787-8/-9 mix at 10/month, then raise the rate, then add the -10.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: It gets to be a point of you can't go chase market share and start to destroy your margins either, and we're playing -- we want to play for our margin and we also want to play for meeting the demand of our customers.
finding: He puts margin ahead of market share and accepts a roughly 50-50 narrowbody split rather than buying share.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: But the heart of the market is still in that 737-8, 320 ... when we did the new airplane that we just announced, it was just playing to that strength of the 8 and putting more seats into it for the low-cost carriers, which is a much lower-risk solution than trying to go all the way up to a 321.
finding: He chose a low-risk densified MAX 8 (MAX 200) over a bigger answer to the A321neo, betting the heart of the market is in the MAX 8 size.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Well, we don't have anything in play right now. We're pretty focused on getting the 737 MAX into the marketplace and those kinds of things. I think we'd be looking more into the next decade for that one.
finding: He pushed any new narrowbody to the 2020s to keep focus on bringing the MAX to market.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: there's a lot of things you can do on price, but that advantage is worth tens of millions of dollars over the course of the life of the airplane. ... Maybe if you're looking for a near-term solution, that would be the right one, but it's a check you have to write every single flight, every single day
finding: He dismisses the A330neo as a short-term, price-led product whose higher operating cost buyers pay on every flight, defending the 787's value premium.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So all in all, every one of those moves was a fantastic win-win solution, which we always are trying to do with our customers as we move through these things. Regardless though, our backlog remains the same across the board. American did not drop their orders.
finding: He presents customer deferrals and mix changes (American, United) as 'win-win' and stresses that the backlog is intact.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: XM still remains an important source of funding for our customers with about 15% of Boeing's deliveries are supported by XM in 2015, but we fully are optimistic that will be able to get an extension on the XM here over the course of the next few months.
finding: He forecast a quick Ex-Im Bank reauthorisation; the outcome is not shown in the slice.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Today, Charleston and Everett are running a combined rate of 10 per month. ... we still are on track to increase our production now to 12 a month next year
finding: He held the 787 rate-12-in-2016 commitment; the slice shows it was met ('12 a month on the 787', May 2016).

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: This is going to be a fourth-generation composite wing for us and the final assembly is going to begin in the 2018 time frame with first delivery in 2020.
finding: He committed to a dated 777X schedule (final assembly 2018, first delivery 2020); the slice ends in 2016 so the outcome is not shown.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: But we took the rates to 1.3, we feel -- the airplane program remains profitable even at a 1 per month, so I feel okay about 747 right now.
finding: After cutting the 747-8 rate he said the program stayed profitable even at 1 per month; a year later he said cargo weakness was still 'impacting programs like 747'.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we announced that we were going to retire the temporary surge line up in Everett at the end of the year. I think this is a great indication of how the production is going ... It's hard to run 2 lines in a production system like that
finding: He retired temporary capacity (the 787 surge line) once the main lines stabilised, preferring single integrated lines for stability.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We are focused on being the #1 player in this market. We just moved into being #2. And so now our sights are set on being #1
finding: In 2015 he aimed for services leadership (#1), an ambition he scaled back by 2016 to holding #2 unless Boeing made acquisitions.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: this is not real complicated stuff for us. Execute the backlog. Keep driving for market leadership in terms of capturing our market share. Keep driving the productivity, profitability, that's right up there.
finding: He sums up his agenda simply: execute the backlog, win share, drive productivity and profit.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Now that our product strategy is largely set for the foreseeable future, we're very focused on execution and meeting our existing commitments.
finding: Once MAX, 787-10 and 777X were launched he declared product strategy settled and shifted fully to execution.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: So through the development organization with the intense focus on commonality, reuse all those kinds of things. Producibility and still maintaining an airplane that could do what we sold, we went from 70% to 95%.
finding: He pushed derivative commonality hard (787-10 from 70% to 95% common with the -9) to reduce cost and production disruption.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: there's clearly a spot there between the MAX and the 787, and how do you go into that ... We want to make sure we understand the marketplace, what the market needs, how do you flow that back in, how do you then create a new family.
finding: He acknowledged a middle-of-the-market gap between MAX and 787 but kept it at the market-study stage.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: these are not real high-risk automation type things, these are proven things that we're doing. But again, bringing them in on the 777 existing a program and then transferring them over to the 777X is going to really derisk the 777X production system
finding: He de-risks new production technology by proving it on the current 777 before using it on the 777X.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: maybe we're being a little bit more conservative, but irrespective, I mean, when you look at all the engine development that's going on concurrently, I mean, those -- it's a combined schedule between ourselves and the engine companies too.
finding: He admits building schedule margin into MAX and 777X dates because engine development by suppliers runs at the same time.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: It's the fact that you don't take these massive technology jumps in one single fell swoop to create -- you take a jump that you know you can deliver, that you don't have to have multiple innovation processes going on at one particular point in time.
finding: He rejects 'moon shots' in favour of technology steps Boeing knows it can deliver, without several innovations running at once, even on a future new airplane.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: you may see a plateau, you may drop a little bit, but I don't see a big -- I don't see a huge -- I don't see one of those huge steep fall-offs, unless something that we don't have any control over happens
finding: He saw cycle risk as a plateau rather than a crash, with only outside shocks able to cause a steep fall.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I know that the other guy has talked about going to 60 month, we can go to 60 a month. We could do that. We got to just make sure that we've got the kind of demand necessary to take it up there. But we're going to watch and see how this thing goes.
finding: He answered Airbus's talk of rate 60 by claiming Boeing had the same capability, but would raise rates only on proven demand.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: GE is -- they're #1, and that's a little bit tough nut to crack ... I think if we can maintain a solid #2, that's really good. If we wanted to jump into the next tier, there we'd have to be -- I think that we would be looking at some type of inorganic growth to do that.
finding: He said becoming the #1 aerospace services provider would need acquisitions, and that organic growth would only hold #2.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We've been to hell and back a couple of times, and each time, we don't like it. It's not a great place to be. But we have got a -- really done a nice job with this, and we've maintained the stability throughout the rate increases.
finding: He speaks bluntly about past crises and uses them to support claims of present stability.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: They've all been through a lot of tough times. We know how to balance risk now in a much better way, and we're not going to let things get out of hand any -- one way or the other, and I think that, that's something that you can count on. You can count on me.
finding: He makes personal guarantees ('You can count on me') of risk discipline.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: The competition's been very tough. I mean, that's -- there is no question about that. Sometimes don't confuse motivation with -- totally with the facts, I guess. ... I use particular campaigns just to give people a real sense, bring it to life for them, so we can get this competitive mindset
finding: Asked about his earlier blunt pricing comments, he admitted using harsh competitive messages partly to motivate the workforce, not only to describe market facts.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: At BCA, we're also very focused on the near-term objective of double-digit margins and the long-term aspirational goal of mid-teens.
finding: He set BCA's margin targets: double digits near term and mid-teens as a long-term aspiration.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Although it'll be a slow kind of taking down of the 777, I think that's what you're asking?
finding: By 2016 he confirmed 777 output would step down during the transition to the 777X, an outcome of the bridge he had called 'pretty bullish' in 2014.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: I'm confident that the decisions that we're making today, sometimes they're very difficult, they're hard, but they're the right ones. They're the ones that are going to really put us in a position for our next 100 years. And they're really -- they're not always easy, and sometimes, they affect people.
finding: He frames hard 2016 cost decisions, including job cuts, as necessary for long-term competitiveness and stands firmly behind them.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We're gathering a lot of data. We're talking with a lot of customers. And we're going to make the right decision at the right time, but we're very mindful of providing the right kind of value to our shareholders as well.
finding: On new-airplane decisions he is data-gathering and patient, with shareholder value as an explicit test.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: On the 37, we were still burning off a backlog that had been built up because of a strike. And we did not take the rate up because we were less confident at that point, and we didn't have the overbookings to feel very confident, so we didn't take the rate up.
finding: He raises rates only when overbooking gives a demand cushion, and cites holding the 737 rate in 2008 as proof.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Just like it is about finishing on any development program. Extending them, it's the worst thing that can happen is when those things start to slide. So we've got to be really disciplined about hitting the mark
finding: He sees schedule slips as the worst outcome for a development program and stresses discipline in hitting milestones.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we're using the voluntary layoffs, not backfilling attrition to make those kinds of reductions. It's good for our people, and it's very good in terms of reducing risk in the production system.
finding: He cut headcount through voluntary layoffs and unfilled attrition rather than layoffs that would cause seniority 'bumping' in the factory, citing production-system risk.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: the whole thing here is not to overproduce and we'll make the adjustments necessary, but we've got to have a production system. ... having that production system that can kind of move kind of up and down and not get hit with these big swings in margins
finding: His production rule is to avoid overproducing and keep a system flexible enough to change rates without margin swings, watching twin-aisle demand more closely.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: And we look at every opportunity to take as much market share as ... is reasonable, and I stress reasonable.
finding: He caps share ambition at what is 'reasonable', so profitability limits how far Boeing chases campaigns.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Our priority right now is really on the MAX, completing the development on the MAX, completing the development and production of the 787-10 and then development of the 777. We are looking at a number of options on each of these, but no decisions have been made at this particular point in time.
finding: In 2016 he put finishing the current derivatives first and kept new options (middle of the market, MAX changes) undecided.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Now the competing factors will be used airplanes or somebody wanting to extend the lease. And some of that, we saw little bit of that in a couple of places.
finding: He named used aircraft and lease extensions, not Airbus, as the main threat to filling the 777 bridge.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: this is not a market that's addressed by either any of the single-aisles or with the twin-aisles are today. So it's a very unique marketplace. ... we're just receiving at this particular point in time, and then generating ideas off that, and then it's a kind of a catch ball at this particular point in time.
finding: He saw the middle of the market as a distinct segment but kept it at a customer back-and-forth ('catch ball') stage with no commitment.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: When we were in the marketplace early, we're going to give people a better airplane than what they initially purchased. Too bad I can't go back and get more money for it.
finding: He notes that the MAX would beat its sold performance, after early sales were priced on conservative specs.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We're in a position at the lower end to make an adjustment to the -7, if we choose to, because we haven't really -- we're not very far in the design. ... If we want to do something with MAX 7, that's it. That's something we could do very easily.
finding: He kept the MAX 7 open to redesign while it was still early in design, a cheap option he could use against competitive moves.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: Now when you do a similar analysis of our competitor in terms of orders to installed fleet, they've taken a much different approach in terms of being more aggressive with respect to growth than with growth and replacement. ... But at the end of the day though, guys, it's all about deliveries.
finding: He portrays Airbus's backlog as riskier and growth-heavy against Boeing's replacement-heavy quality, and says deliveries are what count.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: We see what's happening in the new players. We see what's happening with our primary competitor. We see what we've got to do, and nobody -- let me tell you, nobody wants to be #2 in this company. Nobody.
finding: He uses Airbus and new entrants as a motivational benchmark and frames losing to Airbus as unacceptable.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: we have basically the same advantage with the MAX 8 versus the 320. ... They've got a seat advantage on us at the 9, and -- but we still believe the heart of the market still sits in the 8 size. ... we're thinking through how do we want to address the very top of that market with the MAX.
finding: He conceded Airbus's seat advantage at the top of the narrowbody market and was weighing a larger MAX, while holding that the market's core is the MAX 8 size.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: At the lower end, the airplanes that have been purchased have been CS100. Okay? We aren't competing with those with the MAX. We competed at Delta with used 717s and used Embraers. And then they came in and had to do amazing things and then take an immediate $500 million write-down.
finding: He dismissed Bombardier's CS100 Delta win as bought with loss-making pricing (a $500M write-down), not a product defeat for the MAX.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: They've deemed some things as must wins, we've deemed some things as must wins. And we always balance those with other places where maybe it's not as critical
finding: He picks a portfolio of 'must-win' campaigns to fight hard on price, balanced by restraint elsewhere, and widebody competition is sharper than usual.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: all that is just our efforts to kind of flatten the organization. We're taking management layers out. We're reducing executives, and everything about this is to drive more organizational efficiency and operational efficiency.
finding: He flattened BCA's management, cutting executive layers to reduce cost as competition intensified.

speaker: Raymond L. Conner, Former Vice Chairman
quote: That means you have to share things that you maybe wouldn't have shared before. You have to bring the reality of the marketplace to people sometimes that you are somewhat afraid to do or you're reluctant to do.
finding: He drove a culture change by sharing hard competitive and cost facts with the workforce, which earlier BCA leadership had not done.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: At the last moment, our quality management system caught a defect in the fuselage, 2 defects, and ... We'll recover on that quickly. We can surge, and we will recover for our deliveries at
finding: He presents supplier quality escapes as contained by the QMS and recoverable, a minimising frame for delivery misses.
trigger: Oct 2022 737 fuselage defects cut deliveries to 23
response: promised year-end recovery via surge

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: The low end assumes a lot doesn't happen. Obviously, the commitments we have are actually more towards the normal to the high side of this.
finding: He frames guidance as a range with a conservative floor while signalling confidence toward the upper half.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: On the MAX, we've talked, we continue to work the certification. And we anticipate that will close either later this year or early into 2023. On the MAX 10, we'll continue to work with the FAA, and we anticipate the closure of certification by late '23 or early '24.
finding: He forecast MAX 7 certification by end-2022/early-2023 and MAX 10 by late 2023/early 2024; neither was certified on those dates.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: The 777-9 remains on track and unchanged relative to its certification. We announced that, that first delivery will be in 2025.
finding: He reaffirmed 2025 first delivery for the 777-9; it later slipped to 2026 and then 2027.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: We have a clear path to returning BCA to double-digit margins and a robust ... to get us well into 800 aircraft of output as we think about the 2026 time frame and return us to double-digit margins with free cash flow.
finding: He committed to over 800 annual deliveries and double-digit BCA margins around 2026; the 2024 door-plug crisis and strike pushed this out.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: 4 is what we see right now. ... but 4 is what we're calling right now.
finding: He held the 777/777X combined plan at 4 per month pending certification and the 777X buying cycle he expected in 2024-25.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we made the difficult decision to consolidate the 787 in South Carolina. ... We eliminated that building. We liquidated it.
finding: He used COVID to make structural footprint cuts (consolidating 787 final assembly in South Carolina, eliminating the remote BCA headquarters building).

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: the supply chain really is our limiter on how fast we can take rate up. And we've factored in the performance in this commitment we've provided on the financial guidance.
finding: Deal names the supply chain, not demand, as the binding constraint on post-COVID rate increases and says guidance reflects it.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: So we'll liquidate that inventory largely through 2024, a few that spill into '25.
finding: He set a timeline to clear the 737/787 inventory of parked aircraft by 2024-25.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we carry excess capacity to bail out and rescue distressed suppliers. ... In addition, we've had to use some of the inventory, engines, pulling aircraft that already had engines in inventory to ensure continuity of production, avionics. And we'll do that as a last resort.
finding: He keeps in-house fabrication slack to rescue distressed suppliers and cannibalises inventory aircraft parts only as a last resort.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we've already hired the end employment for the next rate break. ... typically like to bring our resources in about 6 months in advance of break. ... Typically a month to 2 months in advance of a rate break, we posted at the rate job time.
finding: His rate-break playbook hires labour about 6 months ahead and 'posts paper' at the higher rate 1-2 months ahead.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we bake some of that in, in the low side case going forward. That's kind of part of this defining ... When we see that and then we see the supply chain stabilization, we'll break that next rate.
finding: He gates the next 737 rate break on consistent Renton output plus supplier stabilisation, with output variability built into the low case.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: we're going to have a little more buffer stock, when we get through this. I think that's going to be an important insurance policy. We proved the fragility of supply chains with net probably isn't the way we want to run steady-state moving forward.
finding: He plans to move away from lean, just-in-time supply toward more buffer stock as insurance after the COVID fragility.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: But stability and quality will be the key metric we manage the commercial division as we move forward through '22 and throughout the period of guidance we've given you.
finding: His stated management priority post-MAX/COVID is production stability and quality over rate speed.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: But for now, our development pipeline is full. It's absolutely full. ... Like in the past, once we fill these products, we'll continue to improve them.
finding: He signals no new clean-sheet launch while five derivatives are in development, favouring incremental improvement of in-service products.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: what we learned in modifying airplanes is you need to bake a little extra time. Even though you have an industrial plan, you've demonstrated once, there is some variability in that mod sequence. ... cautious rate ramp-ups from where we're running today out into that '25, '26.
finding: He builds schedule margin into inventory rework and keeps rate ramps cautious through 2025-26.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I would submit to you this is the next queen of the skies. ... And then we have the 777-9 and 8, which really stand alone. There is no competition.
finding: He positions the 777X as uncontested in its size class, replacing the 747 and A380.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I'm not going to comment on A350. I'm more focused on my products. ... So I think we'll get more than our fair share. We always have on the wide-body fleet.
finding: He declines to discuss Airbus directly and asserts the 787 will win more than its fair share of widebodies.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: Mike Fleming and a team that led the MAX to recertify on a single management team, we're taking that experience and using it to manage all of our development programs.
finding: He centralised all development programs under the team that recertified the MAX, valuing regulator-relationship continuity.

speaker: Stan Deal, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes
quote: I redeploy here, right, we're revenue occurs. And I've had my leadership deployed out and in the factory. We're getting our teams closer to the factory, closer to the people where the great ideas get unlocked
finding: He moved BCA leadership physically onto the factory floor.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: This outlook continues to assume significant capital expenditures for future products and growth, particularly in St. Louis and Charleston. This ramp-up was seen in our third quarter CapEx spend, which we now expect to be closer to $3 billion for the year.
finding: Even mid-recovery, capex rose toward $3bn for growth in defense (St. Louis) and the 787 (Charleston).

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So next year will be a heavy use year. The year after that will be better in 2027. And then we would expect ourselves to get closer to neutral in 2028. ... So I would expect starting in 2029, neutrality will go to a benefit, positive free cash flow for the program.
finding: He set out a 777X cash path: heavy use in 2026, roughly neutral in 2028, positive from 2029.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: While disappointing, the reset allows us to operate to a higher confidence plan and allows our customers to manage their operations accordingly.
finding: He delivered bad news as a 'reset' to a higher-confidence plan, a kitchen-sink style of owning the slip.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But it's early for me to really make a strong kind of call on that right now. I'm still going through the planning process. ... But as I mentioned, things are trending favorably, and we're bullish on our outlook.
finding: As a new CFO he deferred 2026 numbers to January while signalling optimism.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Finally, on 777X, during the quarter, we recorded a $4.9 billion loss provision, net of a cost-based extension benefit to reset the development and production schedule on the program, with first delivery now expected in 2027 versus the prior expectation of 2026.
finding: In his first call Malave reported the second 777X slip in a year (2026 to 2027) and a $4.9bn charge, the outcome of West's repeated 2026 reaffirmations.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Importantly, we completed the rework on the last of these airplanes and shut down the shadow factory in the third quarter.
finding: The 737 shadow factory closed in 3Q25, about nine months after West's original year-end 2024 target, with the strike as the cause of the delay.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Net-net, even with the higher CapEx, our better-than-expected performance year-to-date supports updating our 2025 outlook to a free cash flow usage of about $2.5 billion, barring the impact of a prolonged government shutdown.
finding: Malave improved the 2025 cash guide from about minus $3bn to about minus $2.5bn, beating West's July figure.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So as we mentioned, we have a higher confidence plan from a schedule and cost perspective on here, so that we've got ourselves protected. ... But this baseline puts us in that position to be able to not only meet it but potentially beat it.
finding: Malave prefers conservative baselines with buffer built in, aiming to beat them rather than stretch.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On production, the factory stabilized at 38 per month in the quarter. Importantly, we jointly agreed with the FAA in October to increase to 42 per month, and the program is now focused on continuing to drive a stable production system as they transition to this new rate.
finding: The 737 rate increase to 42 was agreed jointly with the FAA after stabilizing at 38.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: but I'm confident in the underlying cash generation capability for us to return historical levels that you've seen before. You've got a great backlog, and operational excellence will be the key to unlocking our cash flow potential.
finding: He continued West's thesis that cash can return to historical levels through operational excellence, but gave no new long-term framework.

speaker: Jesus Malave, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It's maintaining the focus on fully restoring the health of our balance sheet. It's enabling and driving the planned improvements of our recovery and ensuring that they are sustainable. And finally, it's keeping an eye on the future while maintaining the focus on the short-term and medium-term recovery.
finding: Malave's stated priorities: balance-sheet repair first, a sustainable recovery second, the future third.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: I would characterize the weight issue we have here as more normal than abnormal... We are paranoid every day about them and trying to attack them and leave no stone unturned at this stage. I would rather be paranoid now than deeply disappointed later.
finding: Paired a reassuring 'normal for the stage' framing of development problems with a claim of daily vigilance.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: The facts are that our business model is not being met... restructure, terminate, affiliate being the obvious options, but continuing to operate as we are now is not an option.
finding: Applied a fast business-case test to an underperforming venture (Connexion) and moved within a quarter to exit it.
trigger: Connexion by Boeing missing its business model
response: Connexion ended (charge announced FQ3 2006)

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: In a perfect world, we would like to be able to produce as many of these things as people have interest in. But of course, we have to balance orders with supply chain, with development considerations, and yes, there is upward pressure on our current production plans.
finding: Even with unprecedented 787 demand he framed rate increases as a balance against supply-chain and development capacity, deferring the call by about a year.
response: study alternatives; final answer within a year

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: Without question, the short-term financial impact of the taxability issue is significant... Accordingly, I feel strongly that the right thing for Boeing to do is not to seek tax deductibility for the settlement charges.
finding: Early in his tenure McNerney deliberately gave up a tax deduction on the government ethics settlement, ranking reputation and visible accountability above near-term earnings.

response: forgo tax deductibility; frame ethics/compliance as competitive advantage

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: I think when the timing is right, in all likelihood, we will. We are just sorting through it right now with a number of customers, but there is clearly demand for that airplane. We just have to fit it into our development plans.
finding: Treated a derivative launch (787-10) as customer-led and gated by space in the development pipeline rather than as an immediate competitive move.
response: defer launch until it fits development plans

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: this will be the most efficiently developed airplane that we have ever done. The strategy of working together with our partners and our suppliers where they are shouldering some of the development work in concert with us is producing a cash model for this airplane
finding: Championed the 787 risk-sharing outsourcing model mainly for its cash efficiency for Boeing.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: But I think what this company does are things that no other company does and as a result, we can push the envelope a little bit. We have to be more careful, not only in execution, but on things we choose to do.
finding: Accepted envelope-pushing programs as part of Boeing's identity but signalled more selectivity about which risks to take on.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: I will say that it seems they are trying to cover two of our airplane families with one airplane, which is a tough putt.
finding: Dismissed the revamped A350 as an over-ambitious single airplane stretched against both the 787 and 777 families.
response: no change to Boeing plans

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: will they aggressively price old technology to bridge some customers? I would be tempted to do that, and that is the A330 story.
finding: Expected Airbus to discount the legacy A330 to bridge customers until its new product arrived, and treated such pricing as rational rival behaviour.
trigger: A350 redesign leaving Airbus with a 2-3 year gap

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: In August, our Board approved a new $3-billion share repurchase program, an important element of our balanced cash deployment strategy. With this strategy, we continue to deliver value to customers and to shareholders by investing in our growth and returning capital to investors.
finding: Pursued a 'balanced' cash deployment: funding growth programs while steadily returning capital through buybacks and dividends.
response: $3B buyback authorised

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: The R&D I would characterize as a conservative number, one that anticipates contingency actions that could happen. We'll be ready for them if they happen. Could there be an upside? Perhaps, but I think planning on an upside is not the way to run a business.
finding: Guided conservatively, building contingencies into forecasts and refusing to plan on upside.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: Just to give you some context, we have got eight contingency plans that we're looking at. We've funded one right now... We know how to build this airplane. This plane will be done on time and will be done within contractual commitments.
finding: Backed a flat on-time 787 commitment with a portfolio of pre-funded contingency plans; the schedule still slipped a year later.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: That's the business model we run under. I mean when we talk about growth in productivity simultaneously, we mean it. The reason we drive productivity so hard in the Company is to make sure we have resources available to properly fund these huge opportunities we've got.
finding: His core operating model was 'growth and productivity' together: productivity pays for development programs and absorbs shocks.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: this is a derivative program, and the amount of money we're spending on this reflects that... So as we adjust and tweak to meet specific market requirements, we have to keep the context that it is not a huge development program for us.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: even notwithstanding some upward pressure on research and development here in the short and medium term, we are well within the business case. Our internal targets are significantly within the business case because that's the way we like to run our business.
finding: Ran programs to internal targets set well inside the external business case, so cost overruns could be absorbed without changing the decision.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: Call that as we saw it, did not try to bury the issues, tried to get them out and deal with them, and I think we've worked through a lot of that and you have seen the results of some of that, which haven't always been pretty.
finding: Presented early-tenure charges as the result of candidly surfacing problems instead of burying them.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: As you know, we are targeting a first flight in late August, which will kick off our flight test program. We will remain on-track for first delivery to ANA in May of 2008.
finding: Reaffirmed the original 787 dates three months before rollout; both were missed.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: In terms of the triple, I think we need to see what the A350 is or isn't before we can make a judgment on whether a competitive response is needed... I am focused on making sure that everybody is ready to move as the market needs it.
finding: Waited for the rival product to be defined before committing to a 777 response, keeping readiness rather than acting early.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: the best customer service is to deliver on your promises. And so to raise rates and then later not be able to deliver because the supply chain was not with you and the planning was not done properly is a lesson that this industry teaches itself every decade or so
finding: Resisted pressure to raise production rates faster than the supply chain could support, citing past industry rate breaks.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: Meeting the financial commitments we make to you is as important as meeting the performance commitments we make to our customers. We are determined to deliver on both.
finding: Explicitly put investor financial commitments on a par with customer commitments.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: every dollar of improvement that we get may not flow to the bottom line because we have customers that need to be productive, and we have competitors that aren't going to sit still and let us take easily as much of the market forever as we are taking now.
finding: Expected Airbus to fight back on share and was willing to give up some productivity gains in price.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: I think there is no doubt that the Chinese will be someday in the commercial airplane business... I am one of these people who believes that partnering with people who are potentially competitors is not necessarily a bad thing.
finding: Expected a Chinese narrowbody competitor within 10-20 years and favoured partnering with that potential rival.

response: compete and partner locally

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: I think though we are emerging from era of management turmoil, some uncertainty with regard to priorities and I thought, just to use a term, some of the software the company needed addressing in terms of leadership development, management needed to be infused with a little more accountability in some cases.
finding: Saw his early mandate as fixing leadership 'software': clearer priorities, leadership development and more accountability, not strategy.
trigger: Question on what he changed since 2005

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: our primary strategy is organic growth, so where we can support that through selected M&A, we will consider looking at it. On the other hand, I don't think it is all that bad to just grow a little cash balance either. In case something does go really, really bad, we would be able to deal with it.
finding: Ranked organic growth first, selective M&A second, and valued a cash cushion against downside alongside buybacks while the stock was 'good value'.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: First of all, I am confident we are beyond what I will call the invention activities. We have proven the airplane's technologies, especially its large composite sections and its major systems. It took longer and cost more than planned, but we are confident we know how to build this airplane.
finding: Admitted overruns but declared the technical risk retired; three months later the 787 schedule broke on assembly and supply-chain problems.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: We feel that we can still deliver the plane on time in May of '08, even if we pushed a little bit beyond that but that is not the plan. The plan is to fly it by the end of September.

quote: I think in our contingency planning we have 20% fewer flight test hours in the plan than we did, for example, on the 777... When you add it all up, it is aggressive but it hangs together, so off we go. We think we can do it.

quote: the new plan reinserts normal margins in the schedule for dealing with issues we might uncover in our remaining ground or flight testing. finding: His recovery playbook was to put schedule margin back and send Boeing staff into supplier plants.

quote: No, we do not want work stoppages, okay. I understand why you make that comment, but the disruption for our customers and the pain we would cause them would be far worse than any slight sorting out of a supply chain issue.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: In making the decision to bring in Pat Shanahan to take over the leadership for the 787, we recognized the exceptional job Mike Bair and the team had done... We also recognized that we're at a stage where a different set of strengths is needed to bring it all home.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Chairman, President and CEO
quote: we also further enhanced the value we provide to shareholders by increasing our dividend 14% and authorizing a new $7 billion share repurchase program. We see more potential to return capital through share repurchase and dividends as our financial performance gets even stronger.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman

finding: He saw the 777 segment as largely uncontested and intended to exploit that in pricing and bundled orders.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman
quote: I'll just leave the statement highly confident on the 80% and realize that there is cash strength that could lead people to conclude there's opportunity beyond that.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman

finding: His guidance style was deliberately prudent, with buffers for lumpy cash, and he rejected the 'sandbagging' label.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman
quote: I'm the one who began the inning vocabulary.
finding: He owned the 'innings' metaphor for multi-year initiatives, a signature phrase.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman
quote: So we're not going to eat our seed corn, but we're going to keep the margins at that low-double-digit place it's been.
finding: In flat defense markets he put margins first while protecting R&D.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman
quote: The -- no business case would close today as we look at it, which doesn't mean pretty far into the future it might not. But right now, it doesn't.
finding: His launch test for a middle-of-market airplane was a closed business case, and he said none closed in 2015.

speaker: W. James McNerney, Former Executive Chairman
quote: we're very cognizant of another 787. We don't want that in terms of the risk profile. We love the airplane. And customers like it. But the financial characteristics were not fun.
