speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Yes, I want to have a good feeling internally by the end of the year as to what I want that. We've got a process underway where we do our long-range planning, which will facilitate that.
finding: He set himself a deadline to finish the portfolio review by the end of 2024 and met it.

numbers.outcome: Jan 2025: 'we've been through the detailed portfolio review... and that's complete'; Apr 2025 Jeppesen divestiture announced

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I've met with the union leadership the first week on the job and let them know that I was committed to resetting the relationship. And I remain committed to getting the team back and improving our relationships so we don't become so disconnected in the future.
finding: In the 2024 IAM strike he went to union leaders personally at once and framed the problem as a broken relationship, not only a contract dispute.
response: Personal outreach to union leadership in first week; improved offer

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I think that we're better off being -- doing less and doing it better than doing more and not doing it well. So we're in the process of taking an evaluation of the portfolio.
finding: His instinct is to narrow scope to execute well. Very early in the job he started a portfolio review with this filter.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Our risk management -- this is the thing that I think is so important is that we're not admiring these risks, but we're acting on them. ... I don't think we've been doing enough work with our customers to figure out how to derisk these things before it turns into an EAC overrun.
finding: He wants risks dealt with early and actively, including renegotiating with customers, rather than carried until they become charges. 'Not admiring these risks' is a signature phrase.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: It is so much more important that we do this right than fast coming out of the chute.
finding: Faced with pressure to restart after the strike, he explicitly put doing it right ahead of speed and would not give a restart month.
trigger: Analyst asked for the month production would resume after the strike

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Look, as I've commented, we're inefficient. And one of the things I've heard from a lot of employees is there's just too much overhead. It slows them down in being able to get their work done. So we're going to really focus this workforce reduction in streamlining those overhead activities, consolidating things that can be consolidated.
finding: He aimed the roughly 10% workforce cut at overhead and layers of management, explicitly sparing production and engineering, and justified it with what employees told him.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Now I think in some cases, we've kept people hot, as I've said, either because we felt that they were behind or there was too much risk associated with turning them down.
finding: During the strike he kept funding suppliers that were behind or fragile ('kept people hot') rather than idling them, trading cash for restart readiness. He had done the same at Collins in 2019.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So my mission here is pretty straightforward, turn this big ship in the right direction and restore Boeing to the leadership position that we all know and want.
finding: On his first call he framed his job as a turnaround ('turn this big ship'), a metaphor he kept using in later quarters.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: First, we need a fundamental culture change in the company; second, we must stabilize the business; third, we need to improve our execution discipline on new platform commitments across the company; and fourth, while doing the first 3, we must build a new future for Boeing.
finding: He set a four-part, ordered agenda (culture, stability, execution on development programs, future) and used it to structure every later earnings call. A new airplane comes explicitly after the first three.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: But it's clear, I want to be the leader in the aerospace and defense market. I want to be setting the standard for the products that we deliver. I want our customers doing our marketing for us, not us doing our marketing.
finding: He defines success as product and execution leadership that customers can see, rather than marketing or chasing new markets. He says the demand is already in the backlog.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Boeing's an airplane company. And at the right time in the future, we need to develop a new airplane but we have a lot of work to do before them. ... restoring the balance sheet so that we do have a path to the next commercial aircraft.
finding: He said a new airplane will come but made it depend on a stable business, fixed development programs, a pruned portfolio and a repaired balance sheet.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Hey, look, there's an incoming on the 767 freighter. It's coming soon. Let's make the decision now and get that distraction out of the way. ... But let's declutter our minds with some of this stuff and get our resources really focused on what's going to make a difference for us going forward.
finding: He ended the 767 freighter quickly once its end was in sight, rather than prolonging it. He prefers to remove distractions decisively and focus resources.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: But we're also, I will tell you, really focusing on our bid and proposal activity, putting discipline around that to make sure that we absolutely understand the risks that we're taking on as we enter into new contracts as well. So burn down the tough ones, get better execution on the future, and I think the opportunities are there.
finding: He tightened risk discipline at the bid stage for new contracts: finish the legacy problem programs and avoid taking on new ones.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And so I think the first one's probably going to be the hardest going beyond rate 38. And so we just can't be overly aggressive in how we're forecasting that because anything in aerospace, the first time you do it, it's hard.
finding: He deliberately builds schedule conservatism into forecasts for first-of-a-kind steps, such as the first FAA-approved rate break above 38.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I don't think we can just -- even if we wanted to, I don't think we can walk away from these contracts. These are our core customers that need this capability. ... we do have to get in a position where we've got a portfolio much more balanced with less risky programs and more profitable programs.
finding: He ruled out walking away from loss-making fixed-price defense contracts because of the customer relationship, and aimed instead to rebalance the portfolio toward lower-risk work over time.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I know culture change starts at the top. Our leaders from me on down need to be closely integrated with our business and the people who are doing the design and production of our products. We need to be on the factory floors, in the back shops and in our engineering labs.
finding: He made leaders' closeness to the factory and the labs his main lever for culture, aiming to stop problems 'festering' far from management.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Well, let me just say that that's not my focus right now. They're doing really well. Chris Raymond and his team are executing. And the one thing I want to do right now is just help them make sure they get all the support from the corporation they need to continue to execute.
finding: He leaves units that perform well (Global Services) to their leaders and spends CEO attention on the problem areas.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: This is not going to be a major restructuring of the Boeing Company. The core business that you see us in and we're going to continue to be in those core areas. ... But I think if I give you any guidance, think of it as more pruning the portfolio, not cutting down the tree.
finding: He limited the scope of the portfolio action to small divestitures and stopping work at the edges, not breaking up the company. 'Pruning, not cutting down the tree' is a signature phrase.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: While the charges for the quarter in BDS are disappointing, I have had the opportunity to complete deep-dive EAC reviews on all the troubled programs. We are very focused on creating stability within the EACs, so we stop this quarterly drumbeat of cost growth.
finding: After his own deep-dive reviews he took large defense charges in Q4 2024. The stated aim was to end the 'quarterly drumbeat' of charges by booking realistic estimates once.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So we're in really, really good shape on fuselages with Spirit, which sets up a very successful integration. ... And I think that sets us up well for the upcoming integration, which will happen sometime still we're projecting middle of the year.
finding: He projected the Spirit AeroSystems close for mid-2025. It slipped: by Oct 2025 U.S. approval was still pending.

numbers.outcome: Oct 2025: EU approval received, 'still waiting for the U.S. approval with Spirit'

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I do want to get through the rate 38 approval and move to that next rate of 42 -- get through the approval this year and get to that 42% sometime towards the end of the year.
finding: He gave a soft target (FAA approval for 737 rate 42 toward the end of 2025) and met it: the FAA agreed in Oct 2025 and the line was loading at 42.

numbers.outcome: Oct 2025: 'we jointly agreed with the FAA to increase 737 production to 42'; exiting 2025 at 42

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So as you know, we came out of the strike and didn't actually jump right on building aircraft. We spent time training the workforce, getting them all up to speed, but also really, as I said, balancing the line, which is really important, starting the line up in a stable manner. And it already is paying dividends.
finding: After the strike he restarted deliberately (retraining, rebalancing the line) before building, and later pointed to the stable ramp as proof the approach worked.
response: Methodical restart: retraining, line rebalancing, then ramp

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We won't request one if we don't see these KPIs performing the way that we want to. And so I think we've got a disciplined approach. ... I'm pleased that it's pretty well grounded in facts and data. So there's no subjectivity here as far as what it's going to take.
finding: He ties rate decisions to six KPIs agreed with the FAA, each with control limits. Data, not management judgement or the calendar, gates each production rate increase.

numbers.KPI_list: notice of escape, part shortages, employee proficiency, rework, travelled work, ticketing

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: because we've forecasted rates that the supply chain has built to and then we haven't met those rates. So I want to make sure that supply chain isn't making independent decisions on readiness for these out-year production rates and continuing to invest in the capacity that they need to supply us.
finding: He admitted Boeing's missed rate forecasts had damaged supplier trust. He started talking with suppliers at CEO level to stop them hedging on capacity.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So it's an important technology development program. It's very challenging. It's taking some dedicated resources that I think are learning new things and exploring new technologies for us. And then we'll look at what comes out of that and how that factors into our next airplane.
finding: He keeps funding the X-66 transonic truss-braced wing demonstrator, partly with NASA money, as an option for the next airplane, without committing to the configuration.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We've been burned on that on the tanker program. And clearly, that's been a challenge for us on T-7A. So we've taken our medicine. We're not going to do that anymore.
finding: He drew a firm line: no more fixed-price development bundled with fixed-price production options without fixed-price supplier contracts behind them. This rules out a class of risky bids.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: by concurrency, what I mean is we're still -- we've got -- we're building production airplanes while we're testing and certifying the design. And that's a disaster because every time you come up with a change that comes out of that, you've got to go ripple that change back through the production process
finding: He sees overlap between development and production (concurrency) as a major schedule and cost risk, and will trade revenue timing (more test aircraft) to remove it.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: making sure they understand our overall market demand as well as the aftermarket demand for the engines as well because they've got a big challenge with supporting our rate increases, our competitor rate increases and managing the aftermarket. And I work very closely with Larry and his team to make sure we stay aligned.
finding: He sees the engine maker (GE/CFM) as a shared constraint: it must split capacity between Boeing, Airbus and spares. He manages it personally at CEO level.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Leadership promotions will be grounded not only in what we get done, but how we get things done. We're going to help focus the teams on what it takes to make Boeing successful and promote a culture of unity and accountability by implementing a single enterprise score for all of our annual incentive plans.
finding: He tied promotion and pay to behaviour and to a single enterprise-wide score, replacing incentives by business unit to force cooperation.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Well, you can never say, until the programs are done, you can never say there's no risk left in these programs. Unfortunately, they are fixed price and they are what they are. Having said that, the fourth quarter charges, I clearly wanted to be in a position to where we have stability through 2025.
finding: He sized the Q4 2024 defense charges to deliver stable cost estimates (EACs) through 2025, with caveats. Through Q3 2025 he delivered it.

numbers.outcome: Q1 2025 EACs held; Q2 2025 'held our EACs for the second consecutive quarter'; Q3 2025 'again demonstrated stability on our EACs'

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Well, fundamentally, I don't see anything that doesn't get us back to those profitability numbers. Obviously, we got to get back to them before we can start talking about improving them, right?
finding: He signalled that BCA could return to its 2018-19 margins (low-to-mid teens) but gave no date, and would not talk about exceeding them yet.
trigger: Analyst cited BCA low-to-mid-teens program margins in 2018-19

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I've been reluctant to put out and I haven't put out any guidance yet. I want to get to stability. ... Let's get to positive by the end of the year. ... The question to me is not if, it's when do we get to that kind of level of cash flow? And I'm not ready to answer that yet.
finding: He gave one near-term cash milestone (positive free cash flow by end-2025) and withheld long-term guidance. Boeing turned FCF-positive in Q3 2025, ahead of that milestone.

numbers.commitment: positive free cash flow by end-2025
numbers.outcome: Q3 2025 operations generated positive FCF 'for the first time since 2023'

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And Elon Musk is actually helping us a lot in working through the requirements on VC-25 to try to help us get the things that are non-value-added constraints out of the way ... So I'm embracing that, working with the DOGE team to help us improve the delivery.
finding: He embraced intervention by the White House and DOGE on Air Force One requirements and framed faster delivery as reducing the risk of cost overruns on a fixed-price program.
trigger: President's public displeasure with VC-25B delivery timing

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: But I will tell you, there's great operational leverage in the ramp back up. ... there's a lot of productivity opportunities in the organization. I'm not really attacking that right now because I want to get stable, I want to get ramped back up. I don't want to get things confused.
finding: He sequences initiatives deliberately: stability and ramp first, lean and productivity drives only after cash turns positive, so as not to confuse the organisation.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I'll just say generically, we'd want to see 2 to 3 months of stability at a rate. ... I will tell you, we won't go and ask for a rate increase if we're not ready for a rate increase.
finding: He gave a working threshold: two to three months of stable KPIs at a rate before asking the FAA for the next rate.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I think one of the smartest things that we did in concert with Spirit was we stopped bringing fuselages into Renton that had known defects in them. ... So we pushed all that back to Spirit and said, no, we're not going to deliver any of those to Renton.
finding: He stopped accepting defective fuselages and pushed the fixes back to the source supplier, ending traveled defects at final assembly.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So we've got to recover that trust; and it's easy to lose, and it takes a long time to rebuild. So we just got to get at that every transaction that we have with our customers' needs to be a positive trust-building transaction.
finding: He made rebuilding customer trust, one transaction at a time, an explicit priority, accepting that recovery is slow.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Now that creates some challenges for our customers because it's fewer airplanes than if we went faster. But I think it's much more important that we'd be deliberate here and do it the right way than to try to go fast and let our production system get instable again.
finding: He openly accepted fewer near-term 787 deliveries, and unhappy customers, as the price of production stability. He held the rate at 5 until one KPI turned green.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I made a comment that we put together our recovery plan, assuming that we'd have some hiccups in the supply chain. And so we weren't leaning out over our skis so that we don't have any room to manage some of these types of things.
finding: He builds headroom into plans on purpose so shocks (here a supplier fire) can be absorbed without resetting guidance. 'Not leaning out over our skis' is a signature phrase.
trigger: Fire at a Precision Castparts/PCB supplier factory, Feb 2025

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So I know from the outside in of some of the challenges that we have. And I think it's refreshing I can come in and give a little bit of an outside critical perspective to the team that sometimes is insular and can't see some of these things from the inside out.
finding: He uses his supplier background as an outside critic of an organisation he calls insular, and says so openly.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I'm trying to do is be very careful when I ask how we're doing, I don't ask the question of how many do we deliver, how many are we going to deliver or how do our KPIs look, because I do believe the KPIs are what's key to allow us to unleash the production ramp-up.
finding: He says he consciously frames his questions to managers around stability KPIs rather than delivery counts, to avoid signalling pressure to push volume.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And obviously, our goal here is to get our defense business back up to a high single-digit kind of performing business. And there's no reason I see that we can't do that.
finding: He set an undated target of high single-digit BDS margins and repeated it through 2025.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: we have many customers who want near-term deliveries, so we plan to redirect the supply to the stable demand. And we're not going to continue to build aircraft for customers who will not take them. We bounded our exposure
finding: When Chinese airlines refused deliveries over tariffs, he quickly capped exposure (about 50 aircraft) and moved delivery slots to other customers rather than build for unwilling buyers. China reversed course within weeks.
trigger: China retaliatory tariffs; Chinese customers declined deliveries (Apr 2025)
response: Bounded exposure, remarketing of built aircraft, reassigning 9 unbuilt positions

numbers.outcome: May 2025: China reversed; deliveries to resume following month

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And if it induces safety risk like we saw with the door blow out, we're not going to move the airplane. ... we had implemented that process on 800 airplane moves, and we had stopped the airplanes 200 of those 800 times.
finding: In response to the 2024 door-plug lesson he made 'travel-ready' a gate. Planes with unfinished work posing a safety risk do not move, and a quarter of moves were stopped, at a cost in flow.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And then our first rate increase will be from 38 to 42, and then we'll do 5 per month increments after that. So 42 to 47, 47 to 52. Those rate increases would be no earlier than probably 6 months in between. But again, it depends on each one will require that we have stable KPIs.
finding: He set a 737 ramp rule: steps of five per month, at least six months apart, each gated by KPIs. This is a clear rate-change threshold for the game.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: The thing I'm really trying to make sure we're focused on is making sure that an argument over a 10% tariff, who's going to pay doesn't turn into a continuity of supply issue. ... and then we'll work through the financial implications.
finding: Under tariff shocks he puts continuity of supply ahead of short-term cost recovery and settles who pays later.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We invested in this area more than any investment we've ever made in our defense business and that investment paid off. We had a -- we have a superior product, very mature and where we are in terms of the design of the product.
finding: He presented the F-47 win as a reward for keeping a large, long-horizon competitive investment going during the crisis. Strategic franchise bets were protected.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: let me just clarify ... at the end of the year, I would expect we'd be doing the milestone review from 42 to 47, so that we can move with that, so we won't be outputting at 47, to be clear.
finding: When his answer sounded more aggressive than intended, he corrected it in the same session to keep expectations conservative.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: On a price development program, the risk is not behind you until you're done and we still have a lot of work to do. ... I don't think one quarter is a good quarter. I think we're doing a better job of baseline management. But again, we're not done until we're done on these projects.
finding: He refuses to declare victory on one good quarter. 'Not done until we're done' is a repeated hedge against overpromising.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: There's still risk that we have to manage. I don't want to imply that we're done here. Restoring the company and stabilizing the company is our first step. We're not through that yet. I'll maybe claim victory on that when we get to a positive cash flow and we're through our first rate increase and we've got the certifications complete.
finding: He publicly set his own success criteria (positive cash, first rate increase, certifications) and refused to claim stabilisation before all three were met.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I'll just tell you, it's going to follow the performance of the production. As I said before, the financials will follow our production performance. So the faster we ramp up, the better our cash performance will be.
finding: 'The financials will follow' is his signature line: he points investors to production performance instead of financial targets.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So we're pretty confident in our ability to move from 38 to 42. ... So the next one would be to 47. I would not expect those to be any earlier than 6 months apart. And so that could get us to where we'd like to get to 47 here by the end of the calendar year.
finding: He floated a 42-at-midyear, 47-by-year-end path, then clarified it. The 42 approval actually came in Oct 2025, about a quarter later than this implied.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So both the 737-7 and 737-10 are slated to complete the certification this year. And the critical path right now for us is the anti-icing design for the inlet.
finding: He reaffirmed certification of the 737-7/-10 in 2025. Two months later it slipped to 2026 because the engine anti-ice design was not closed.

numbers.outcome: Jul 2025: 'we now are expecting certification in 2026'

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So I'm hopeful that we'll get through the certification flight tests by the end of the year. We may still be doing some ETOPS testing going into next year. But no real change to our forecast of getting that certification done so that we can start deliveries next year.
finding: He reaffirmed first 777-9 deliveries in 2026 (as in Feb 2025). In Oct 2025 he moved them to 2027 with a $4.9B charge.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So in some cases, going slow and deliver has allowed us to actually go faster. So we're going to keep disciplined here and we'll move to the next rate when the indicators say we're ready to go there.
finding: He treats the gains from the deliberate ramp (output above his own expectations) as proof of 'slow is fast' and stays with gating by indicators.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: What we're going to do with that fourth line is primarily focus it on the Dash 10 variant of the 737. ... It has the most complexity, meaning it will probably flow through the factory at a slower rate. And that will allow us to keep the Renton -- the 3 lines in Renton flowing much more efficiently.
finding: He set aside capacity (a fourth 737 line in Everett) to isolate the most complex derivative, protecting flow on the main lines rather than mixing variants.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Backlog is not our challenge. We have a very, very strong backlog. Our challenge is ramping up production and delivering on that backlog and making sure that we have slots available for the customers who want the aircraft.
finding: He sees Boeing's binding constraint as supply and execution, not demand. That pushes priority to production rather than sales campaigns or new products.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We just got to be extremely careful as we do these efficiency initiatives that we don't take away value, particularly if it's value to the safety or quality of the product. ... I think we know cutting corners can't be an answer for our recovery. We've got to do this right.
finding: He ranks safety and quality above cost efficiency and limits productivity drives to what does not harm the product.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I think my energy in the next year is going to be focused on probably less on the production ramp-up and more on getting through the certification and the development programs and getting those things behind us.
finding: By mid-2025 he moved his personal focus from the production ramp, now delegated to BCA, to certification and development programs.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: One is, when is the market ready? And two, when are we ready, both financially and from a capacity perspective? And third is, when is the technology ready? And I would say the answer is not now on all 3 of those work streams. ... We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready.
finding: He launches a new airplane only when three conditions meet: market readiness, Boeing's financial and capacity readiness, and technology (especially engines). In 2025 all three were 'not now'.
trigger: Analyst asked about timing of the next new airplane

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Having said that, if there are any delays in getting the -- through the certification, which we're not anticipating right now, we will just continue to build the Dash 8. So I don't think it's like a production output concern.
finding: He hedges derivative certification risk by keeping the certified MAX 8 as a production fallback, so delays in derivatives do not hit output or cash.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: If you talk to our airline customers today, I think universally, they would say, we still have work to do and the durability of the existing newer engines that are there. And we'd like to make sure that we don't see the type of durability issues in the future.
finding: He sees the durability problems of current new-generation engines (GTF/LEAP) as a reason not to rush a new airplane on the next engine generation.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Work on the solution is taking longer than expected, and we now are expecting certification in 2026. As we previously said, we don't expect a material impact to our production plans, and we're prepared to build other 737 models for our customers.
finding: He gives bad news briefly and plainly in prepared remarks, and pairs it at once with the mitigation already in place (build other 737 models).
response: Certification moved to 2026; production shifted to other MAX models

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: My role here is just to help everybody get organized and headed in the right direction. It's turning a big ship around. I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned. We still have a lot of work to do.
finding: His assessments are measured ('turning, not turned'), and he describes his role as organising others rather than as personal heroics.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Noah, look, I see nothing structural that says we can't get back -- get to that $10 billion. So I think you framed it perfectly. It's not if, but when. And I'm not ready yet to say when.
finding: By mid-2025 he endorsed the $10B FCF ambition in principle ('not if, but when') but still gave no date. He moved from withholding in Oct 2024 to a conditional endorsement.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So the order of magnitude of this is much, much less than what we saw last fall. That was roughly 30,000 machinists. So we'll manage through this. I wouldn't worry too much about the implications of the strike.
finding: He played down the 2025 St. Louis IAM strike (about 3,200 workers) as manageable and relied on contingency staffing. This contrasts with the personal outreach he made in the far larger 2024 strike.
response: Contingency plan; maintained JDAM output

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I don't think the market is ready yet for a new airplane. When are we ready and this whole discussion around turning the company around and generating cash flow is really important to when we're ready to launch it ... we'll do that when those 3 work streams all kind of converge. That's not today and probably not tomorrow.
finding: He repeated that a launch depends on market, cash/turnaround and technology meeting, and pushed timing beyond the near term.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So these recent big wins we have, the development parts of those programs have all been cost plus. So we're not making the errors of the past and signing up for fixed price development, high-risk programs. So we do have this pig in the python that we've just got to push through relative to these big development programs.
finding: He enforces a firm rule against fixed-price development on new defense wins (F-47 and others are cost-plus) while working through the inherited fixed-price backlog.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Far and away, our priority is debt. Through this crisis we've been through, we've taken on way too much debt. And so as we come back and we start generating cash, we want to be solidly investment grade. And we need to be there for the next-generation airplane as we start to think about that.
finding: He ranks cutting debt to a solid investment grade first for returning cash, ahead of shareholder returns. He links it directly to funding a future clean-sheet airplane.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: But we still don't have authorization from the FAA for a good portion of the certification program. So we're working through that right now with the FAA, but we're clearly behind our plan in getting the certification done.
finding: He warned of the 777X slip a quarter before taking the charge, giving investors early warning rather than a surprise.
response: Oct 2025: 777-9 first delivery reset to 2027 with $4.9B charge

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We're going to go to 8, and we're planning to do that in the near future. And then from 8, we'll go to 10 and we're hopeful to be at 10 next year. ... There's demand to support teens kind of production rate.
finding: He set a 787 rate path of 7 to 8 (late 2025) to 10 (2026), with demand for rates in the teens once the Charleston expansion is ready (about 2028).

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Pricing, I would say, is almost independent of the trade demand activity right now. We've been in this, a supply-constrained environment for quite a while. We do have inflationary pressure coming from the supply chain. And certainly, we're taking that into account in how we're pricing the new product.
finding: He uses the sold-out, supply-constrained market to firm up pricing on new orders and pass on supplier inflation, helped by customers moving to larger variants.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Thinking about the certification process, it's way too slow. We've got to work with the FAA in swinging the pendulum back and making that process that will work. I can't imagine that we can do a new airplane without having that process refined.
finding: He makes a faster, reformed FAA certification process a precondition for launching a new airplane, and moved his own focus there.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: However, I've said this all along, and it's super important is we got to do this right, and we are not going to push. If we're not ready, we'll wait a month. A month will not matter in the big scheme of things and losing stability will matter.
finding: His trade-off is explicit and lopsided: a month's delay is cheap and lost stability is costly, so he will not push a rate increase early.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Hey, we almost -- we are almost at parity on deliveries with Airbus this last month. So it's like we're getting there.
finding: He uses monthly delivery parity with Airbus as a scorecard for the recovery, without claiming to lead.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So we put Steve in that role full-time permanently here recently, but he actually has been acting in that role since last fall and doing a fantastic job.
finding: He tests leaders in acting roles for about a year before making them permanent, here promoting the interim defense CEO from within.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: I think we got too far away. We got distant. I moved to Seattle. My office is right on the Seattle Delivery Center. I can -- every morning and I do every morning, look out and see what airplanes are where and are they moving? And if not, why?
finding: He moved the CEO's working base next to the factory and delivery centre and checks aircraft flow daily himself.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We also immediately changed our incentive program to a One Boeing incentive program. Prior, we had -- each business unit had a separate incentive. In some cases that caused people not to work together very well. They worked for their own success and not for the overall success of the Boeing.
finding: He quickly replaced incentives by business unit with one enterprise metric to break silos between units.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: If you talk to our DoD customers, many of them will say, hey, this is a different Boeing showing up. A little bit of the arrogance knocking it down. A little bit of humility. Get up, let our technical people do the talking and not forcing things.
finding: He wants Boeing to show customers humility instead of arrogance, and to let engineers, not salesmanship, carry customer relationships.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: It's something that I've asked Jay Malave, who's our new CFO, to spend some time as we come through this quarter, really looking at the schedule slip and understanding what the implications are
finding: He gave the new CFO the job of re-baselining the 777X schedule and its financial impact, using the CFO as an independent check on program estimates.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So a major expansion of the Charleston facility, and it's all around getting to rates higher than 10%. We think that the market demand will allow us to get to rates in the teens, and that's what we're focused on, putting the capital in place, getting the facilities in place.
finding: Even while short of cash, he committed growth capex to double the 787 footprint in Charleston for rates in the teens, ahead of need, around 2028.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And the philosophy I want here is, I don't want this to be a continuous quarterly issue for us to make sure we have a solid financial estimate here, that we have a high level of confidence that we can get this certification work done.
finding: His stated philosophy for bad news is one conservative reset rather than a series of small revisions.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: We very much underestimated how much work it was going to take for us to get the TIA approvals and for the FAA to have the opportunity to review all the data submissions that are required. So we've stepped back and we've rebaselined this program to incorporate those learnings
finding: He admits plainly that the earlier 777X plan was unrealistic and owns the underestimate rather than blaming outsiders.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: In St. Louis, we are executing our contingency plan, as our IAM-represented workforce remains on strike. ... We are building JDAMs without IAM workforce at about the same production rate as before the work stoppage
finding: When the tentative St. Louis deal failed, he kept defense output going through contingency staffing rather than signal urgency to settle.
trigger: St. Louis IAM strike continued after tentative agreement (Sep 2025)

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: This is obviously a disappointment, but we just need more time to complete the certification process. With this charge, we now have a higher confidence that we'll complete the certification within the financial estimate.
finding: On the 777X slip he took a single large charge ($4.9B, first delivery 2027) sized to give 'higher confidence', a reset meant to end repeated charges.
response: Rebaselined schedule; $4.9B non-cash charge

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: And I will just reiterate what I said when we started this campaign here a year ago is it's way more impactful for us to move when we're not ready than to hold off and wait till we're ready. ... I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early in this process.
finding: A year in, he restated the same rule on rate decisions unchanged: late beats early. This shows his decision style stayed consistent.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: So I'm certainly not throwing the FAA under the bus with this. This is a learning collectively for the both of us in terms of what it takes to get through the new process.
finding: He avoids blaming the regulator in public and treats the FAA as a partner in fixing the process. This protects a relationship he depends on for rate and certification approvals.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: Also in the quarter, the FAA announced it will allow delegation to Boeing to issue airworthiness certificates for some 737 MAX and 787 airplanes. ... earning limited delegation authority is a responsibility we take very seriously.
finding: He presents regaining partial FAA delegation as trust earned back from the regulator and uses humble language about it.

speaker: Robert K. Ortberg, President, CEO & Director
quote: we have to watch the continued demand on the engines in both the forward fit and the aftermarket and the durability upgrades that are going on in the market. So that'll be an area that we'll continue to work with GE and CFM on.
finding: He sees engine supply (GE/CFM) as a standing constraint on the ramp, because new-build engines compete with durability fixes and spares.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, VP & CFO of Boeing Global Services
quote: We see about $70 million of expense on every 25 basis points around the discount rate sensitivity.
finding: She gave a precise pension sensitivity and flagged a 2013 headwind early, a quantified disclosure style.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: And finally, disciplined profitable growth. This is all about optimizing working capital and being very deliberate and intentional about where and how we expand our capability and capacity where we can leverage and increase our IP and drive value.
finding: She frames growth as disciplined, working-capital-aware and limited to areas where Boeing's IP adds value.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: Inclusive of that is our 2018 acquisition of KLX, where we have successfully integrated that business and captured both our top line and bottom line synergies.
finding: She points to the KLX acquisition integration and synergy capture as a delivered M&A outcome.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: We've invested significantly in driving capacity to meet our customer needs. In fact, in just the last couple of years, we've almost doubled our Boeing converted freighter capacity
finding: She invests in capacity where demand is visible (doubling converted-freighter lines).

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: We are being very thoughtful at our capital deployment, where we invest where we can leverage and grow our IP to deliver value and creating different business models within the industry to partner and collaborate where we can't.
finding: Her capital rule: invest directly where Boeing can leverage its IP, partner where it cannot.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: First and foremost is on-time predictable delivery, key to everything we do in meeting our customer commitments.
finding: As BGS CEO she ranks predictable on-time delivery first.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: Emerging from the pandemic with a robust portfolio, with a right-sized cost to serve and a disciplined investment gives us confidence in meeting the financial objectives Brian laid out earlier, continuing to deliver profitable growth and strong cash conversion.
finding: She ties confidence in targets to a cost-cut base and emphasises cash conversion alongside growth.

speaker: Stephanie Pope, Executive VP and President & CEO of Boeing Global Services
quote: We also look for opportunities where we can invest and needs for our customer as well as expand our IP. This is illustrated in our comprehensive cabin offering that we've been developing in partnership with our JV at Adient Aerospace as well as our acquisition of EnCore.
finding: She uses JVs (Adient Aerospace) and bolt-on acquisitions (EnCore) to build IP-based service offerings.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Well as I said, I think as we execute '12, we'll be looking a lot harder and ramping up our deployment strategies '13 and beyond.
finding: Defers large shareholder distributions until operational execution on the 787/747-8 ramp has generated the cash; deployment follows delivery, not the reverse.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: We anticipate the deferred production cost to peak at slightly over $20 billion and then decline after the program achieves the planned production rate of 10 per month and stabilizes at that level.
finding: In his first call as CFO he sets a dated, numeric anchor for the 787 deferred-production balance tied to reaching and stabilising rate 10, the metric he then repeats every quarter.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: Once we've demonstrated our ability to successfully execute the planned rate increases, we will consider rates above 10 per month.
finding: Rate policy is demonstrate-then-step: no commitment to rates beyond 10/month until the planned ramp is proven in the factory.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: All of these and other opportunities are being actively addressed, as improving our profitability on the 787 program continues to be a top priority for us.
finding: From day one he ranks 787 unit profitability (purchasing leverage, lean, design for producibility, rate) as a top financial priority.

speaker: Greg Smith, CFO
quote: it's a competitive environment we're dealing with on the 737, but we're facing into that. We're looking at obviously cost reductions going forward.
finding: Frames competitive pricing pressure on the 737 (the A320neo/MAX launch period) as something to absorb through cost reduction rather than a reason to change the plan.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So as those mature -- and some of those, obviously, won't all come to fruition, but the ones that do mature, then we'll put them in the booking rate.
finding: Conservative accounting discipline: cost-reduction projects only enter program margins once they are proven, signalling a bias to under-promise.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And then we do have some provisioning for just risks and uncertainties that are just tied to -- in fact, we got to make another rate break ... Now if we execute through that, that'll certainly give us more confidence, and we'll come back to you.
finding: Builds explicit contingency into guidance for rate breaks and releases it only after execution is demonstrated; guidance rises in steps after proof.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: from the first airplane that was delivered, say, to like line 60, we're seeing about a 40% to 50% reduction in unit costs. And that's truly coming down that learning curve.
finding: Uses the 787 unit-cost learning curve as the proof point for the program's eventual profitability, a claim he repeats through 2012.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're tracking airplane by airplane versus what we would consider our target and budget. We're looking at out-of-position items on every airplane, shortages, condition of assembly, quality, flow time, how many hours we're burning per job versus what we budgeted.
finding: A metrics-first CFO: rate-break and margin confidence is derived from granular tail-by-tail production health data rather than top-down assertion.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: what capabilities are you trying to add to the portfolio, what's that market look like. And at the end of the day, how much value you're going to bring back to the Boeing Company. So this is obviously -- you've seen how we've done this, it's been very methodical.
finding: M&A test is capability, market and value returned; describes the approach as methodical and disciplined rather than transformational.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: The third key indicator, obviously, is deferred production. So as you watch us disclose that on a quarterly basis, it truly will give you a sense of how we're performing on the program
finding: Tells investors exactly which observable metrics (monthly deliveries, rate breaks, deferred production) to hold Boeing to, a transparent scorecard style of guidance.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: the percentage of those blocks that are sold, which is one of the indicators that we utilize before we make a rate or make a block extension.
finding: Rate and accounting-block decisions are gated on the sold position of the backlog, a demand-proof test.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So I think we're going to be relentlessly focused on this, and so we don't have a number as far as a target. But we certainly would like to get it into the double digits sooner rather than later.
finding: Aspires to double-digit BCA margins and '777-like' widebody economics on the 787 but refuses to set a numeric target date.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think the key differentiator, as you described, is if and when we do a 777X or a 787-10, that'll be a differentiator, obviously, in that trajectory. But as you know, we haven't decided that yet.
finding: Views the next widebody derivatives (777X, 787-10) as the swing factor in R&D, and keeps them explicitly undecided in 2012.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But the bottom line is where we would like to run the bottom line, assuming for the worst, and manage the business efficiently and effectively in that regard.
finding: On sequestration he plans for the downside case and manages cost to it (market-based affordability) rather than betting on a benign outcome.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But as we have always kind of focused on a disciplined approach to funding our pension plan, we're going to continue that. But it certainly does give you some flexibility in the years to come. But I don't see our plan on how we will fund that changing going forward.
finding: Does not use legislated pension-funding relief to free cash; keeps discretionary pension funding as a standing use of cash.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But expect to kind of restart share repurchase, in particular, in the 2013 timeframe and then, of course, pay down our debt.
finding: Dated commitment to restart buybacks in 2013; delivered in December 2012 with a $1.5-2bn 2013 repurchase plan and a 10% dividend raise.
response: Dec 2012: dividend +10%, buyback resumption announced

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Just as an example, I just walked line 70, and we're looking at about 160 open jobs, so much, much improvement. We're cycling landing gear where we should be cycling landing gear.
finding: Hands-on CFO who walks the 787 line and argues from traveled-work and shortage data to support confidence in the production system.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So I think we got it well understood, and we're going after it. So I'm not, I don't think, as concerned about it as some of the folks that I've seen publish on this topic are.
finding: Pushes back on analyst fears of MAX introductory-pricing margin damage, claiming it is already provisioned in guidance.
trigger: Analyst concern on 737 MAX launch pricing

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well I think as we've retired risk, you've seen us retire risk, as we've kind of gone through this year, certainly set this up well for 2013.
finding: Describes guidance raises as 'retiring risk' quarter by quarter, his standard framing for stepwise upward revisions.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, Cai, if we can get more out, we will. But that's our current plan, to execute within that range.
finding: Resists pressure to raise 787 delivery targets beyond plan; prefers to beat a range than to stretch it publicly.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And as we think through cash deployment, we'll certainly consider it but as I said, first and foremost is ERISA funding and returning cash to shareholders.
finding: Ranks ERISA funding and shareholder returns first in cash deployment, ahead of incremental discretionary pension contributions.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But I can tell you, R&D is managed at a very detailed level and decision by decision, business case by business case we're allocating dollars in.
finding: R&D is allocated program by program on business-case returns, with corporate-level oversight; next-widebody decisions (787-10, 777X) still pending.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But the overall objective, obviously, in this case would be providing further transparency for the investor base into the core operation. How is the core operation performing on a year-to-year basis and providing more visibility into that.
finding: Initiates the move to non-GAAP 'core' earnings that strip pension volatility, framing it as transparency; implemented with 2013 guidance.
response: Jan 2013: core EPS introduced

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, I mean, I don't see that. I see that we've got 4,100 airplanes in backlog that people want, and that's what I see. I don't see pressure on lease rates on our products.
finding: Flatly rejects the 'aerospace bubble' narrative when challenged, anchoring on the backlog.
trigger: Analyst concern about lease rates and bubble

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But we put a cash deployment, I'll say, discipline in place in 2008 that is pretty robust, and it continues today. So we have cash calls twice a week with our businesses, really getting into the details of what's driving the cash
finding: Runs cash through a high-frequency centralised operating rhythm (twice-weekly cash calls with the businesses).

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So I guess I'm more operational approach in visibility, but I think it's the right one considering where we need to go and where we want to go going forward.
finding: Self-describes as an operationally oriented CFO who interrogates rate confidence and profitability capture, not only financial reporting.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we go through that discipline process before we'll make the final decision to make the rate break. So if there's metrics that are outside the control limits, there'll be a pause, and you've seen us do this before. But it is absolutely the right thing to do
finding: Explicit rule for rate decisions: break rate only when production metrics are inside control limits; otherwise pause, which he endorses as correct.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Like I said, I wouldn't tell you the chart's all green, certainly. But we know where the hot points are, and we got teams deployed on it.
finding: Treats rate readiness as a weekly metric with explicit red/green tracking and pre-deployed teams to known supplier hot spots.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I mean, they are an extension of our factories, and we've got a lot of experience and a lot of knowledge doing this, in some cases, more than the supply chain.
finding: Sees suppliers as an extension of Boeing's factories and is willing to deploy Boeing resources into sub-tier suppliers to remove bottlenecks before rate breaks.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It's all about balance, right? It's all about balancing that short-term, long-term demand with your production system. So stability in the production system is key.
finding: Production rate philosophy prioritises stability over chasing short-term demand, citing Boeing's holding rate through 2008-09.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Certainly, we were in a development phase. Recently now, we're in the production phase. It's all about delivery. It's affordability at BDS. So you shift accordingly. And cash deployment, obviously, was not something we were talking about going through development. Now we are.
finding: States explicitly that priorities shift with the program cycle: development era to production/delivery and cash deployment era by late 2012.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So when you look at an 87 and look at how much more efficient that is to the customer, you can close a business case when you're 20-plus percent more efficient. And I think that's driving a lot of the replacement
finding: Believes replacement demand (half the backlog) is driven by step-change efficiency; a 20%+ efficiency gain is what closes an airline business case.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: What we've been trying to do is manage the bottom line assuming a sequestration environment, and I think we're starting to see that effort pay off on the top line. ... If sequestration doesn't happen, I think we'll still be better off as a result of it.
finding: Prefers to plan to the adverse case early ('no-regret' cost actions) rather than wait for clarity.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: in December we increased our dividend 10% and announced our plan to ... resume share repurchase in 2013. We expect to spend about $1.5 billion to $2 billion on repurchases in 2013.
finding: Follows through on the mid-2012 commitment to restart buybacks in 2013, sized modestly while the 787 is still consuming cash.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: This includes greater than 60 deliveries for the 787, which takes into account our planned increase in build rate and additional production flow time provided throughout our factory and across our supply chain that will minimize disruption as we introduce the new 787-9.
finding: Sets a conservative 787 delivery floor for 2013 that builds in extra flow time for the -9 introduction, accepting fewer deliveries for stability.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Looking forward as I've said before, right now the plan is to have them complete by 2015, all airplanes out of EMC.
finding: Dated commitment for clearing all early 787s through the Everett modification center by 2015.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: In addition, our guidance assumes no significant financial impact resulting from the FAA directive on the 787 program. If this assumption changes after we have gained greater fidelity, we will let you know.
finding: During the 787 battery grounding he holds guidance unchanged and conditions any change on getting greater fidelity, rather than pre-emptively provisioning.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we've got a -- I think, a very good plan in place based on facts and data of how we've performed prior along with some productivity improvements.
finding: Bases derivative ramp plans (787-9) on historical analogues such as 777 derivative introductions, i.e. data from past performance plus modest improvement.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We haven't talked specific on the numbers, but it's minor in comparison to the overall results. And again, we were able to absorb that by reallocating resources and expertise onto this.
finding: Declines to quantify a crisis cost, characterising it as minor and absorbed; when pressed again his answer is a flat 'No.'
trigger: Analyst request for battery cost figure

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But as we peak, and then that's when it will start to become positive on a unit cost basis, again, as it stabilizes. And that's usually about 1 year, 1.5 years once we hit 10. That's the plan right now.
finding: Forecasts 787 unit-cost breakeven roughly 1-1.5 years after reaching rate 10 (about 2015), with deferred production peaking just over $20bn.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And timing of the 787 events limited our ability to repurchase shares in the first quarter. However, we expect to begin our repurchase plan in the second quarter and remain committed to our $1.5 billion to $2 billion of share repurchase planned for 2013.
finding: Paused buybacks during the 787 grounding but kept the annual commitment intact, signalling the crisis does not change capital-return policy.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, we managed to absorb this. So it was really a matter of priorities. I mean, we re-shifted our priorities and our people onto this effort from other efforts, and this was a One Boeing effort.
finding: Handled the 787 battery cost by absorbing it within existing spending (reallocating engineers) and holding full-year guidance.
response: Absorbed costs; guidance held

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, I think once we get to 10 and stabilize and feel good about where we are and all the operational metrics are in the -- all within the right bandwidth, that's the timeframe where we'd be making a decision
finding: 787 rate-above-10 decision is explicitly deferred until rate 10 is stable and metrics are within bandwidth, with capital and demand also weighed.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: as you phase out NG, ramping up MAX at the same time, so there's some capital that we've invested there to really do that seamlessly and have the MAX running down, being proved out on a -- on 1 line as the NG line continues to be at peak rate
finding: Prefers a de-risked, capital-backed parallel-line transition from NG to MAX that protects peak NG output while the MAX is proved out.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Our target going forward is a payout of approximately 80% of our free cash flow in the form of dividend and share repurchase.
finding: Sets an explicit shareholder-return policy of roughly 80% of free cash flow via dividends and buybacks, with 2013 buybacks of $1.5-2bn as a 'first step'.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: From a dividend perspective, payouts will be indicative of our financial strength and stability. And we continue to expect dividends to increase in line with our core earnings growth.
finding: Dividend policy: grow in line with core earnings as a signal of financial strength.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, as I said, the $1.5 billion to $2 billion is a start. So we're continuing to monitor that, at the same time, monitoring our success in our production rate increases
finding: Declines to front-load buybacks despite cash on hand; increases are paced to demonstrated rate execution.
trigger: Analyst suggestion to front-end the buyback

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, as Jim discussed, we kicked this off in September last year and we issued double digit targets for the supply chain varying by supplier, by program.
finding: Partnering for Success: imposes double-digit cost-reduction targets on suppliers, program by program, as a core earnings lever.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And we're continuing to use a disciplined gated development process to retire risk early, drive first time quality and affordability and tightly manage work and schedule.
finding: Development programs are run through gated reviews designed to retire risk early, a direct reaction to 787 development overruns.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It would be trade off component by component, but also stepping back and looking at our long term objectives and strategy about what do we want to do versus what we think should be in the supply chain.
finding: Open to vertical integration (bringing work back in-house) as leverage on suppliers, decided component by component on investment, risk and competitiveness.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: maximizing the reuse of hard fought technology investments and lessons learned to reduce development risk, at the same time minimize the volatility we've historically seen in research and development
finding: After the 787, prefers new-product development that reuses proven technology (derivatives) to cut development risk and smooth R&D spend.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It's not an initiative, and this is how we run the company, how we issue the target, how we monitor performance.
finding: Describes cost and productivity targeting (market-based affordability) as the permanent management system rather than a campaign.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: With regards to deferred production balances going forward, we're still comfortable with that peaking at slightly over $20 billion. And again, think of that as we reach 10 a month and stabilize at that level, that's when we'll see that turn
finding: As late as July 2013 he reaffirms the 'slightly over $20bn' 787 deferred peak (turn in early-mid 2015); three months later it is reset to ~$25bn.
response: Oct 2013: peak reset to ~$25bn with rate 12/14 plan

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: this quarter metric at a summary level is no longer a good reflection of the overall program performance.
finding: Retires the per-unit deferred metric he had told investors to watch, replacing it with operational indicators once it stopped flattering the program.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We now anticipate deferred production to peak at approximately $25 billion by 2014 and then moderate at that level before beginning to decline shortly after we complete the transition to 12 per month.
finding: Resets the 787 deferred-production peak from 'slightly over $20bn' to ~$25bn, attributing it to 787-10 launch and higher-rate investments rather than performance slippage.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: bringing year-to-date repurchases to $1.8 billion and we now expect 2013 share repurchase will exceed $2 billion.
finding: Over-delivers on the $1.5-2bn 2013 buyback commitment despite pausing during the battery grounding; full year ended at $2.8bn.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Program margins now include investments to support the -10 introduction and production rates of 12 per month in 2016 and then 14 per month before the end of the decade.
finding: Commits to aggressive 787 rate growth (12/month in 2016, 14 by decade end) on the back of 787-10 orders, and books those investments into program margins.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But as we're looking at rate going to 12, we're obviously making investments to 14 at the same time. So we're trying to be as -- be very efficient with our resources
finding: Willing to invest ahead of demand for the next rate step (14) while still ramping to 10 and 12, given backlog depth.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: In December, we announced the next steps in our balanced cash deployment strategy, with the new $10 billion repurchase authorization adding to the $800 million left in the prior authorization at year end. We anticipate completing the repurchase authorization over the next 2 to 3 years.
finding: Once the 787 ramp and battery risk eased, escalates sharply to a $10bn buyback over 2-3 years and a 50% dividend increase.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So as I think I said before, plus or minus 80%, it's going to vary from year to year, but I expect us to be north of that in 2014. So we're committed to doing that.
finding: Signals above-target payout in 2014, i.e. willingness to return more than 80% of FCF when confidence is high.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Team's very focused on cash management, as you've seen over the last couple of years in how we have executed on meeting our objectives and, quite frankly, exceeding them a couple of years in a row.
finding: Positions his record as beat-and-raise on cash (2012, 2013), explicitly using it to support confidence in the 2014 guide.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So to address this, we have applied additional resources. We know how to do this, and we'll get those jobs back to what we view as a more acceptable level. So we've got mitigation plans.
finding: Addresses 787-9 midbody jobs-behind-schedule in Charleston by surging resources and asserting competence, framing it as normal for an unprecedented widebody rate.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: the unprecedented 10-year agreement further de-risks the business and 777X production, providing a stable foundation for productivity improvements and employment of our highly skilled workforce as we strive the remain competitive.
finding: Values the IAM 10-year extension (DB-to-DC transition) primarily as labour-risk removal for the 777X and as cost competitiveness.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: On MHI, we're essentially through all the MHI rework. As of last night, we have 3 airplanes left to go. And again, the team's executed that flawlessly, and met all the requirements there. So I'd say that's behind us at this point.
finding: Closes out supplier quality issues with a precise count and declares them 'behind us', paired with no change to delivery guidance.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we believe these pension changes and long-term labor agreements further de-risk our business and will improve the company's long-term competitiveness and further drive value for all of our stakeholders going forward.
finding: Moving 100,000+ employees from DB to DC pensions is framed as de-risking and competitiveness; accepts one-time GAAP charges to do it.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And the 37 is a great example, right? 8,000 airplanes, best-selling aircraft ever, and we're still able to capture additional productivity gains there.
finding: Believes mature programs still yield productivity, so margin expansion can come from cost rather than price.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: you're going to see more people converting from -8s to -9s, and potentially -9s to -10s, just because it fulfills their mission more efficiently.
finding: Expects customers to up-gauge within the 787 family over time, supporting the derivative strategy.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Clearly, we're returning more than that. And if we have an opportunity to do that, we will do so. With this authorization put in place, it gives us that opportunity. I think you saw, in the first quarter, where we, I'll say, took advantage of our stock price
finding: Becomes opportunistic on buybacks once the authorization is in place, returning more than the ~80% FCF guide and buying on price weakness.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Now I will also tell you that we're making decisions day in and day out on that program that, in some cases, have impacted deferred near term but benefit the program long term.
finding: Accepts worse near-term reported metrics (787 deferred) for long-run program economics, e.g. pulling -9 inventory ahead to de-risk the ramp.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Really focused on de-risking the business, driving growth and productivity, and increasing long-term shareholder value.
finding: By 2014 his priority set is de-risking (pension, labour, 787) then growth/productivity then shareholder value.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: The -8, the -10, the 737 MAX and the 777X are all examples of how we are working to break the historical cost curve in the design and the development.
finding: Favours derivative programs (787-9/-10, 737 MAX, 777X) and a centralised development organisation as the way to break the historical development-cost curve.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So the more success that we can have on the Partnering for Success will help margins. At the same time, we're in a competitive environment, face any pricing pressure, which is certainly how we utilized it on the transition on the 737.
finding: Uses supplier cost-downs as ammunition against competitive price pressure, as on the NG-to-MAX transition, rather than only as margin upside.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: By no means do I see us oversupplying into this environment.
finding: Rejects the view that the duopoly's rate increases are oversupplying the market, anchoring on replacement demand and fuel economics.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we've established aggressive productivity targets on an annual basis, throughout the enterprise, and hold individual employees personally accountable with our annual performance review process, which ultimately drives employee incentive plans for both union and nonunion employees.
finding: Accountability model: annual productivity targets cascaded to individuals and tied to incentive pay across union and non-union staff.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're comfortable with our approximate $7 billion of cash flow. And if we see that improving through the next quarter, then we'll update our guidance going forward.
finding: Holds conservative cash guidance mid-year and signals upside only after it materialises (2014 ended at ~$8.9bn OCF).

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: This is not new technology or innovation. This is basic kind of blocking and tackling as we work through the redesign on the engineering effort, primarily around the wire harnesses and then the manufacturing labor to work through installing those.
finding: Bad-news style on the tanker: take the charge, then bound the problem as well understood and non-technological, and reaffirm long-term profitability.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we bid the EMD phase of the Tanker program aggressively at 0 margin, with planned profitability generated during the production phase.
finding: Accepts aggressive fixed-price development bids (zero-margin EMD) to win long-term franchises, betting on production-phase profit.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: The risk profile obviously has changed dramatically and the continued focus on execution and repurchasing $5 billion of stock this year, really, again, looking forward, looking at the strength of the backlog
finding: Explicitly links the pace of buybacks to the reduced risk profile and backlog visibility; $5bn repurchased in nine months of 2014.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And again, I wouldn't call it moving investments or moving rate to the right, it's more moving rates up.
finding: Reframes analyst suggestions of rate delays as rate increases (737 investments for 52/month already booked), a positive-spin style on rate news.
