speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: No, we're not, as I've said before, we're not cash-positive yet. We expect to be cash-positive in the 2015 time frame, and that will be a blend obviously of -8 and -9.
finding: Dated commitment that the 787 program turns cash-positive in 2015, reaffirmed in January 2015.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: On the overall deferred, there's really no change. I said it would be approximately $25 billion. We're at $25.2 billion, but again, keep in mind, in the last 2 or 3 quarters, we pulled forward -9 and that wasn't in the original plan.
finding: Claims the reset ~$25bn deferred target is on track while acknowledging unplanned -9 pull-forward; frames overshoot as deliberate risk reduction.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Now once you get to peak rate, I would say that's where you really maximize the cash flow of just the basis of the elements of what's driving the cash flow between progress payments and delivery payments.
finding: Sees peak production rate as the point of maximum cash generation, a reason to push rates higher on both 737 and 787.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we announced in December that our Board of Directors increased the share repurchase authorization to $12 billion and increased the dividend 25%, up 88% in the last 2 years.
finding: After returning $6bn via buybacks in 2014, escalates again to a $12bn authorization and a further 25% dividend increase.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As a result of legislative pension changes, we are now foregoing discretionary pension funding in 2015.
finding: Reverses his 2012 stance that pension-funding relief would not change Boeing's discretionary contributions, redirecting that cash elsewhere.
response: Discretionary pension funding stopped in 2015

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, as you know, Doug, one of the strategies we had in place was to derisk the decade, and we've certainly done that. The risk profile going forward is very different than it was in the past.
finding: Signature phrase 'de-risk the decade': frames 2012-2014 actions (pension, labour, 787 ramp, product decisions) as removing structural risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we now anticipate 787 deferred production to grow at moderate levels for the next several quarters as productivity improvements on both models offset timing of supplier negotiations, further investments to operate -- optimize the production system and our decision to maintain higher employment levels
finding: Second reset of the 787 deferred profile (beyond ~$25bn) explained as deliberate decisions (staffing, supplier timing), while holding cash-positive 2015 and decline after rate 12 in 2016.
response: Deferred kept growing past the $25bn 'peak'

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: On -- as far as labor, we are coming down on unit cost, but we're coming down at a lower rate than what we expected or anticipated.
finding: Concedes that 787 labour unit-cost reduction is slower than planned, while attributing it to choices for stability and reliability.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So again, a near-term sacrifice but much long-term benefit, frankly, for us and our supplier.
finding: Deliberately delays supplier price negotiations until suppliers are down their learning curve, trading near-term deferred growth for better long-term terms.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I know folks are focused on quarterly. You can't really focus on quarterly within our company. I mean, just because of the amount of advances, and the delivery profiles and the milestone payments, and so on, you really kind of got to look at this over an 18- to 24-month period.
finding: Pushes investors to judge cash over 18-24 months, not quarters, which also softens quarterly misses.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But when we make a rate break, we really try to look at that -- at maintaining that rate at a 2 to 3-year period ... very detailed analysis by airline, how many are firm? How many are options? What do we think the probability of those options are?
finding: Rate-increase rule: only break rate if it can be sustained for 2-3 years, based on probability-weighted airline-by-airline demand (firm vs options, growth vs replacement).

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: All tied into the business cases behind each one of those airplanes and something that I personally review on a regular basis. First of all, I approved it, but then, on a regular basis, there's a progress to ensure that we're staying within the budget framework
finding: As CFO he personally approves and tracks program capex against launch business cases, i.e. centralised financial control of investment.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We'll make whatever adjustments we need to make, but we don't see a need to make any of those adjustments at this time.
finding: On the 777-to-777X bridge (sold out 2015-16, half sold 2017) he holds rate and waits for orders rather than cutting early.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we pretty much -- 3% to 4% productivity is what we target everybody, whether you're a function or whether you're a program on an annual basis, and that has gone unchanged. ... Some of that's going to go back in price as it has
finding: Standing annual productivity target of 3-4% for every program and function, part of which is expected to be passed on in pricing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: From a product portfolio point of view, I think you've seen we've made our product portfolio decisions in the commercial side, with a very successful launch of the -10, on the 787 program and the 777X, as well as the 737 MAX, so clearly, the focus now is executing on those development programs
finding: By 2015 views the commercial product decisions as made (MAX, 787-10, 777X) and shifts focus to execution, risk reduction and cash rather than new launches.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And if you look back over time, I know you have Seth, there's really no correlation between oil and demand for airplanes. I think some people forget that when we launched the 787, we were $40 a barrel and you saw the success of that launch.
finding: Dismisses low oil prices as a threat to demand or product business cases, arguing total operating cost and new routes drive replacement.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: this airplane is certainly operating in the marketplace somewhat of its own, so we don't have a great deal of competition.
finding: Sees the 777 as facing little direct competition, which underpins his patience on the 777 production-gap risk before the 777X.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think the de-risking activity has been very prudent. And if we see any issues along the way, we have a plan B or, I'll say, an offramp to continue with the current production system. So I think the risk is very managed.
finding: Accepts new-technology production risk (777 automation) only when proved offline first and with an explicit fallback 'offramp'.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think as far as cash on the balance sheet, looking at the size of the company today kind of high, mid -- high single-digit balance is what I think is probably prudent as we continue to grow through this period
finding: Sets an informal liquidity floor of a high-single-digit billions cash balance, returning the excess.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think our debt levels, of where they are right now, are probably appropriate. And I don't see a need to run out and either pay some of that down, or go out and double down. If -- the business situation or the portfolio is in different case, then we'd feel differently
finding: Neutral on leverage: no debt paydown and no levering up to fund returns while the backlog supports cash generation.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: typically, our progress payments at the commercial side, about 40% of that comes in flow and about 18 to 24 months out from delivery. And then about 60% on delivery.
finding: Cash model for rate increases: about 40% of aircraft cash arrives as progress payments 18-24 months before delivery and 60% at delivery.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're also expanding margins, and again, the long-term objectives of margins to be industry-leading margins in our sector.
finding: By 2015 the stated long-term goal is industry-leading margins, alongside best-in-class cash management.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: but the fact is, it's the objective that's in mind, not to let the margin ride the wave of maybe a lower revenue through that transition but a focus on how do we maintain it back here long before it's happening
finding: Plans product transitions (NG-to-MAX, 777-to-777X) to protect margin through end-of-line pricing by lining up supplier and internal cost actions years ahead.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: While we have a lot of work to do in front of us, we have added the necessary engineering and support staff to complete the program on schedule to meet the customer's commitments.
finding: A year after saying the tanker was 'sufficiently provisioned', a second, larger charge is taken; response is to add staff and hold the schedule commitment.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Now obviously, that is a key franchise for us. So having that short-term transition period is very minimal considering the benefit that program -- both of those programs bring to the bottom line of the Boeing company.
finding: Accepts a 777-to-777X production-transition dip (2018-19) as minor relative to protecting the twin-aisle franchise, offset by 737/787 rate increases.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, we think that the stock is still undervalued. ... So we see -- obviously see a lot of value still left in that stock. That's why we bought back $20 billion in the last 3 years and remained committed to that.
finding: Justifies continued heavy buybacks by asserting undervaluation, while naming investment in 777X, MAX and 787 as first priority.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But again, I think when you step back and look at the overall profile or deferred to date, it's better than what we originally projected.
finding: Claims the 787 deferred profile beat projections, though the balance ($28.3bn) far exceeded his original 'slightly over $20bn' peak; selective baseline framing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Specifically on the 787, we continue to expect the program to be cash positive in the fourth quarter, and we still anticipate the production to decline shortly after we achieve the 12 per month production rate later in 2016.
finding: The 2015 787 cash-positive commitment narrows to Q4 2015, still within the year promised in October 2014.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And we'll likely take another look at the rate here early next year and see where we are on orders and backlog and move forward from there. But right now, the plan is to hold at 1 a month.
finding: On a weak program (747) he supports stepwise rate cuts (1.3 to 1 per month) and reviews again on orders, while seeking cost reductions.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We still see that as a niche market, but an important one ... And if we need to respond with a new airplane in that marketplace, that would be something that would be more towards the middle of the next decade. It's not something that would dramatically affect our R&D profiles over the next 4 to 5 years.
finding: In 2015 treats the middle of the market as a niche served by MAX-9 and 787; any new airplane is mid-2020s and must not disturb the R&D profile.
trigger: Analyst question on a middle-of-the-market airplane

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We expect to complete the $14 billion repurchase authorization over approximately the next 2 to 3 years. Our capital deployment strategy demonstrates the strength of our backlog and the confidence in our business going forward.
finding: Smith framed large, pre-committed buybacks as a signal of confidence in the backlog, setting a multi-year timetable for completing the authorization.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: listen, this is -- there's nothing more to read into this other than smooth transition into the MAX at the 42 a month rate and building those test aircraft.
finding: When analysts probed a gap between 737 production and deliveries, Smith pushed back on any negative reading and framed it as a planned, routine transition.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we continue to anticipate deferred production to decline shortly after we achieve the 12 per month production rate in 2016. No change to this fundamental milestone. We remain on track to achieve the 12 per month 787 delivery rate in mid-'16, with suppliers already operating at that production level.
finding: Smith anchored 787 cash recovery to a dated, repeated milestone (deferred production peaking once rate 12 is reached in 2016) and stressed it was unchanged.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: the bulk of that is 777X, which is actually performing very well to schedule and to cost as we get ready for that entry into service further out in the 2020 time frame.
finding: In early 2016 Smith described the 777X as on schedule and on cost for a 2020 entry into service.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: 57 a month is very healthy for us as we look at that order book and percentage sold out. So we feel very comfortable about going up in that rate over the long term, but we want to do it as we have, very smoothly and very productively
finding: Smith justified the 737 ramp to 57/month by the sold-out order book while insisting each rate break be taken smoothly, accepting near-term delivery dips in the MAX transition.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Yes, I mean, Dominic, the 747 just is not as profitable. I mean, it's that simple. And where the 777 is a pretty significant contributor to us and operates at a higher margin
finding: Smith assessed programs bluntly on margin contribution, explaining why a 747 rate cut forced a charge while a 777 cut did not.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It's a great airplane in a tough cargo market. And we're expecting that to recover, and we've got a perfect asset to align to that recovery.
finding: Even after taking a 747 charge and cutting rate, Smith kept the program alive on the bet that the freighter market would recover.
response: rate cut and $885m charge, keep program for cargo recovery

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, Jon, I would say our accounting is compliant with GAAP. That's first and foremost. And that's what it is. And obviously, Airbus is under a different accounting standard and they're adhering to that one.
finding: Asked during an SEC probe whether program accounting still suited Boeing (versus Airbus's IFRS), Smith gave a short GAAP-compliance answer and moved the discussion to cash.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Certainly, Howard, the balance of the year just got more challenging, and we got a path forward to meet the guide, even taking that into consideration. But we're accelerating our productivity efforts and focusing there to ensure that we do
finding: After a tanker charge, Smith acknowledged the year was harder but held guidance and promised to close the gap with productivity.
response: reaffirm guidance; accelerate productivity

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: it's about the bottom line at the end of the day, no matter what accounting standard you're under. It's about how efficient you are with your cash and then -- and how effective you are with managing that and deploying it.
finding: Smith's core yardstick was cash generation and deployment rather than accounting earnings.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But exchange rates are going to move around over time. We don't rely on exchange rates. But the fact is, they're sometimes where there's an advantage, there's sometimes to a disadvantage, and we have to have the flexibility in our own enterprise to be able to compete, no matter what that exchange rate is
finding: Smith treated a weaker euro (Airbus cost advantage) as a reason to drive internal cost competitiveness rather than a factor to wait out.
trigger: Strong dollar / weak euro favouring Airbus
response: cost-competitiveness push

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're committed to continued share repurchase at similar levels going forward. Given our unprecedented growth in cash flow, dividend expectations around steady share repurchase, we now expect to return approximately 100% of our free cash to shareholders.
finding: Smith committed to return about 100% of free cash flow to shareholders, a high payout policy based on expected cash growth.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So the path to recover 787 deferred production balance of the $29 billion is clearly grounded on existing contracts with customers and suppliers.
finding: Smith defended the $29bn 787 deferred balance as recoverable chiefly through mix, pricing and supplier contracts already signed (about 95%), with productivity the smallest part.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: the PFS effort. It didn't exist 5 years ago, and that's 65% of our cost structure. So we got to go capture it. There's no question about that.
finding: Smith saw supplier cost (Partnering for Success, 65% of cost) as the biggest margin lever, making supplier price-downs central to his plan.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're not satisfied with our current segment margins, and we're focused on achieving the double digit in the near term and then increasing to mid-teen over the long term.
finding: Smith set explicit margin targets (double-digit near term, mid-teens long term) as the central financial objective.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I wouldn't say, price is a significant driver upward or downward as we look forward through there. It's really more about the productivity and getting to rate. And that's really what's going to drive the cash flow; the pricing, not as much.
finding: Outside the 787, Smith expected cash growth to come from rate and cost, not pricing, so production ramps were the main financial lever.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I'd say first and foremost, remain focused on profitably filling the 777 production bridge. As you know, we need 40 to 50 airplanes a year to fill that bridge. We've got 12 so far.
finding: Smith quantified the 777-to-777X production gap and made filling it profitably the top commercial priority.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: when you step back and assess the segment margins, we do see an imbalance between risk and reward, and we want to fix that.
finding: Smith judged that Boeing was taking too much risk for its margins, motivating risk reduction and margin expansion together.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: First and foremost was a disciplined and conservative approach to production rate increases. And again, that's what's taken place, expect more of that going forward, to further reduce risks on the development programs
finding: Smith positioned conservative rate increases and gated development as the main ways to cut earnings volatility.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Core earnings per share was a loss of $0.44, impacted by the previously announced $3.23 of charges and cost reclassification. Notwithstanding these impacts, the core business performance was solid in the quarter.
finding: Smith presented a quarter of large charges by separating them out and stressing that the 'core' was solid.
response: isolate charges; reaffirm revenue, delivery and cash guidance

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And we made the right decision because it was the time to start spending company funds to modify those airplanes and a limited marketplace for them. So we made that decision and re-classed them, and it was absolutely the right thing to do.
finding: Smith defended reclassifying 787 flight-test aircraft costs to R&D as a deliberate clean-up decision, not a forced write-down.
trigger: Limited market for early 787 flight-test aircraft
response: reclassify about $2.8bn to R&D

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we'll match production demand to production at the right time. And it's one element of the portfolio, and I don't want anybody to over-rotate on that element.
finding: On the 777 production bridge, Smith ran scenarios but held the plan and played down the risk to cash, promising to match rate to demand when needed.
response: run scenarios; hold plan; adjust rate when needed

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: When it comes to payables, we have changed our frequency of pay, that we've gone from daily to twice a month. Again, that's in line with industry practices. At the same time, we're looking at terms across all of our contracts
finding: Smith drove working-capital gains partly by slowing supplier payments and renegotiating terms, aiming for top-quartile cash efficiency.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're not at point of making any different rate decisions or assumptions than what we got in place. But as Dennis said, we got work to do to fill out to the 14. ... But if you were to assume holding 12, it pushes that deferred curve out about 6 months.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So first and foremost, our view on cash flow growth is unchanged. We continue to forecast cash flow growth in '17 and in '18 and beyond.
finding: Smith committed early and repeatedly to growing operating cash flow each year from 2017 onward, making cash growth his main public promise.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We don't have all the answers today, but we have some solid plans in place around the attributes or elements that Dennis indicated. Some of those, we're going to be successful on. Some of them, we may not. And we'll, I'll say, retool and look for further opportunities
finding: Smith treated the margin goals as a portfolio of initiatives to be retargeted as they succeed or fail, not as a fixed plan.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: The 737 MAX introduction, I think, is a good example of derisking to ensure that we have long-term profitability over the portfolio. Same thing with the moves we're making on 777 transition to 777X. So trying to be mindful of moderating and derisking, where certainly that's been a challenge of the past.
finding: Smith described choosing derivatives (MAX, 777X) and moderating rates as deliberate risk reduction after past programme problems.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we announced in December that our Board of Directors increased the share repurchase authorization back up to $14 billion and increased the dividend another 30%. We now have increased our dividend per share by more than 190% in 4 years, and over the same period, we have lowered our share count 18%
finding: Smith continued rapid dividend growth and buyback renewals, showing a consistent bias toward shareholder distributions.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Operating cash for 2017 is forecasted to increase by approximately $250 million to $10.75 billion, largely driven by improvement, 787 cash generation, higher 737 production rates and overall disciplined cash management efforts
finding: Smith guided 2017 operating cash flow to $10.75bn on 787 cash improvement and the 737 ramp. He raised it mid-year to $12.25bn and then to $12.5bn, and the year closed at a record $13.3-13.5bn.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: On the Tanker cash, yes, '16, '17 is the primary burn, and then we'll be cash flow positive later in '18.
finding: Smith gave a dated forecast that the KC-46 tanker programme would turn cash positive in late 2018.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're expecting growth in key financial metrics for 2018: growth in revenue; deliveries; BCA and BDS operating margins; core earnings per share; and finally, operating cash flow.
finding: A year ahead, Smith committed to growth in every key 2018 metric.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Obviously, we're assuming at this point that we go to 14. The market supports that, going to 14. But as we -- we don't have to make the formal decision yet. So as we get closer to that, we'll continue to monitor the marketplace, fill in those unsold positions
finding: Smith kept the 787 rate-14 option open, assuming it in the plan while delaying the formal decision until unsold slots filled.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: that's what's going to allow us to win the marketplace, that's what's going to fuel our investments, that's what's going to allow us to return cash to shareholders.
finding: Smith linked productivity directly to three outcomes (competing, investing and returning cash), which was his recurring ranking of priorities.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So you asked what the focus is? Delivering on our backlog. This is very much an execution story. The fundamentals are in place.
finding: Smith described Boeing's equity story as execution on an existing backlog rather than new bets.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But a lot of that, again, from a risk perspective, I'd say, development is behind us. Airplane's flying great.
finding: In early 2017 Smith declared the KC-46 development risk largely retired, yet further tanker cost growth hit in Q1 2017 and after.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Are all the plans, I'll say, completely understood and have high confidence? No. But they're identified. They're identified with a leader. So this is going to be one of those situations where we're just going to keep going at this and chipping away.
finding: Smith ran the margin programme by giving each lever a named owner and chipping away at it iteratively, admitting that confidence in each lever varied.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So at least currently, 37 skyline is not a worry or a concern. Something we stay focused on though, but not a concern. It's taken over 3,000 MAX airplanes that we sold before we even flew the airplane
finding: Smith saw no demand risk to the 737 ramp to 57 per month and put the execution of rate and productivity first.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: a 7% to 9% share, I don't think you'll find anybody in the company that will say that looks right in a $2.5 trillion market where you know the moving pieces inside and out.
finding: Smith argued that Boeing's low share of the aerospace services market justified creating a separate services business to capture aftermarket value.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: How do we minimize the risk? How do we have a gated process in that we don't push risk and then push requirement, things like that?
finding: Smith favoured gated development processes that stop risk and requirements being pushed downstream, a lesson from earlier troubled programs.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: some of those programs don't have a lot of margin. But the business case on those programs over the long term is very strong. And Tanker's a great example. I mean, that's about a 400-airplane marketplace plus, probably over time.
finding: Smith accepted low or negative margins on fixed-price development contracts like the KC-46 because he saw a long-term franchise behind them.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: a very, I'll say, clear understanding of the competitive landscape and no dismissal of it. We're assuming people are going to be successful, and they want share. And we're obviously going to do everything we can to not only maintain share, we want more share.
finding: Smith assumed competitors would succeed and set Boeing's aim at gaining share, not just holding it.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And certainly, tax reform is one of them. We're not competitive globally. We're certainly not competitive, therefore, directly with our competitors on the commercial side day in and day out.
finding: Smith saw the US corporate tax rate as a structural cost disadvantage against foreign commercial rivals and lobbied for tax reform.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So if you look at the low end of the margin guide at BCA, we're trying to take that into consideration as a hold or delay in a 14 a month, so holding at 12.
finding: Smith built a pending rate decision (787 at 14 vs. holding at 12) into the guidance range so either outcome would not force a reset.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Well, roughly, at the total level, it's about 60% to 70% outsourced to in-sourced. ... And if we win every time, then Tier 1, 2, 3, everybody wins as a result of that.
finding: Smith framed supplier cost pressure as shared competitiveness, with most of the airplane outsourced and suppliers expected to help Boeing win.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're on unit 3 in the factory, or at least the data I have off unit 3. And that unit cost is in line with the -9 already, so -- I mean, that kind of level of performance and really going back into the overall strategy on commonality in that design and really leveraging that technology on derivative platforms
finding: Smith pointed to the 787-10's early unit cost as evidence that high-commonality derivatives cut production risk and cost.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: where we're trying to provide even more clarity right down to the -- to all levels of management and all employees, where 50% of our comp now will be free cash, 25% on core EPS, 25% on revenue
finding: Smith described rebasing incentive pay so half was tied to free cash flow, putting cash at the centre of everyone's incentives.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're taking action to further derisk the company by accelerating $3.5 billion of pension funding, which we expect will eliminate nearly all future mandatory pension funding through 2021.
finding: Smith pre-funded the pension with $3.5bn of Boeing shares and spent cash freed up on an equal increase in buybacks, using the balance sheet to remove a risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But I think as far as general capital structure, what you see today is what you should expect to see going forward. And we're very focused on, again, on risk mitigation and top line and bottom line performance.
finding: Smith signalled no change to the capital structure (low net debt, high payout) and presented pension pre-funding as risk reduction made possible by strong performance.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We continue to expect operating cash flow to grow annually through the end of the decade, and we remain committed to returning approximately 100% of free cash flow to investors.
finding: Smith repeated two standing commitments: operating cash flow growing every year through 2020 and about 100% of free cash flow returned. He restated both on every call through late 2018.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: you look at capability, you look at capacity, and then you look at affordability. And all that will be taken into consideration when we look at the NMA with, obviously, a clear eye towards winning in the marketplace
finding: Smith described the NMA business case as a disciplined comparison of options on capability, capacity (existing plants) and affordability.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: piloting projects before fully implementing like automation. Let's walk a little bit before we start running, learn from it, step back and then get running. 737 automation is a great example.
finding: Smith preferred to pilot changes such as automation before scaling them, an incremental, test-first way of taking on operational risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: What we've asked the supply chain to do frankly isn't any different than what standards we're holding ourselves to. ... since we started PFS, there's been significant savings and you've seen the overall margins in this business really haven't been impacted.
finding: Smith defended aggressive supplier cost-down (Partnering for Success) as holding suppliers to Boeing's own standards and argued their margins had not suffered.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we got to have competition in places where we don't have a competition. ... And so with that, we're looking for people that compete in that, and we're making investments in those areas where we can have more competition.
finding: Smith wanted competition among suppliers where only single sources existed and was willing to invest to create alternative sources.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But first and foremost is you've got to be transparent and recognize where you've got challenges ... and be willing to work together and take the help and improve upon it. So that's what a partnership is all about.
finding: Smith expected struggling suppliers (here Spirit AeroSystems) to be open about problems and accept Boeing's help.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: the focus for us again is executing, executing and executing on this backlog. Big focus on productivity across the enterprise, all elements of cost and then cash generation.
finding: Smith summed up his playbook as backlog execution, enterprise-wide cost productivity and cash generation, ahead of new bets.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: In the avionics, it's really, for us, it's around navigation, flight controls, information systems. To your point, it's modest right now at 100 people, it will grow to about 600
finding: Smith backed selective vertical integration in avionics to capture more content and services value over the aircraft life cycle.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: obviously it starts with the customer and the customer's needs and how do you fulfill that need in a manner in the timeframe and a price point that works. And that was the challenge for the team and minimizing the development cost is key part of that
finding: Smith explained the 737-10's market success as a derivative with low development cost, delivered quickly at a price that worked for customers, a cost-first approach to a new model.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We set up -- we invested in a separate line to run the MAX and to prove it out and minimize risk while running at 37 to 42 a month over here on the NG, to not disrupt that, work out any potential issues we had and then we'll merge these lines together and that's a smart investment.
finding: Smith spent capital on parallel production lines to protect output during the MAX transition, accepting cost to cut schedule risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So a lot of people talk about this, "Cycle" that they've been talking to me about the last 6 years, I don't -- we don't see it that way. I mean, there's always going to be ups and downs certainly in the market but there's a lot of fundamental differentiators
finding: Smith rejected the traditional cyclical view of commercial aerospace because of replacement demand, a view consistent with his support for high production rates and payouts.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: One Boeing score. Everybody is on One Boeing score. It's the success of Boeing. It's not the success necessarily of your scorecard
finding: Smith moved executives onto a single enterprise scorecard (revenue, earnings, cash) to reward cross-business decisions over unit results.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: that business as usual isn't going to cut it. It's not going to cut it. It's not going to allow us to win in the marketplace. It's not going to reward the people that are putting their trust in us to have an adequate return on investments.
finding: Smith pushed cultural change through external benchmarks tied to pay and personal accountability.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Longer term, we are aggressively driving productivity through the business to maximize profitability as we strive to continue to improve cash generation and to achieve mid-teen operating margins by the end of the decade.
finding: Smith put a date (end of the decade) on the mid-teens segment-margin aspiration, turning a goal into a dated commitment.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We look at it as a payout ratio, earnings payout to cash flow, our dividend yield. And it's all about back to competing to win. So we want to be competitive.
finding: Smith set the dividend against payout and yield benchmarks to stay competitive for investors.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think the risk profile you see today versus what you saw 5, 6 years ago, significant difference. Not to say there's no risk in the business, but I think it's much more understood, nowhere near the level it was.
finding: In late 2017 Smith said the derisking agenda (labor deals, pension cap, limits on concurrent development) had sharply cut enterprise risk, and he called the remaining risk 'much more understood'.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: That efficiency and that decision-making and discipline around supply and demand, same application when we were looking at going and firming up going to 14, which includes the entire supply chain, our own efficiency, what capital we need, when and then, ultimately, the marketplace, right?
finding: Smith described the 787 rate-14 decision as a checklist of supply-chain readiness, internal efficiency, capital need and demand, all of which had to line up before committing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: making it real for people that are on the 737 line and talking about flow days and equating those to dollars, that take a day of flow out, that equals $50 million. That makes it real for people, and we're incentivized that way.
finding: Smith turned factory flow time into dollars to push cash discipline down to the shop floor.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're in discussions with over 50 customers on exactly where this would fit in their fleet, what would it do, what do they need, when do they need it and then can we make the business case all come together and be efficient and can we ensure that we've got an R&D profile that we don't have any concurrent risk
finding: Smith made the NMA launch conditional on a closed business case, a price-cost fit and no overlapping R&D risk, for an entry into service around 2024-25.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: getting more and more visibility and ensuring we understand what the risks are and how do we mitigate them ... And any time we have an opportunity to build some buffer, we'll build buffer in there.
finding: On the 777X, Smith favoured building schedule buffer and reusing proven 787 wing technology ('no new invention') to cut development risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: in December last year, we reinforced our commitment to returning value to shareholders as our Board of Directors authorized the new $18 billion share repurchase program and a 20% increase to our quarterly dividend.
finding: Smith scaled up shareholder returns again ($18bn buyback, +20% dividend) at the 2017 peak, staying committed to about 100% free-cash-flow payout.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Tax reform certainly provides a stronger foundation for us to make additional investments in our business, such as R&D. Our funding will continue to be focused on core programs; key future franchises; productivity enablers such as automation
finding: Smith put part of the US tax-reform windfall into R&D and capex while keeping R&D roughly stable as a share of revenue.
response: modest uplift in R&D and capex

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Operating cash flow for 2018 is forecasted to increase by $1.7 billion to be approximately $15 billion, largely driven by the following: improving 787 cash generation, higher 737 production and improved Tanker profile
finding: Smith guided 2018 operating cash flow to about $15bn, relying on the 787, the 737 ramp and the tanker turning around.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: While our organic investment remains the primary engine for our growth, we continue to look for opportunities to partner with other industry players in investments that accelerate our life cycle value strategy and vertical content, as we demonstrated by the joint -- recent joint venture with Adient for seats
finding: Smith used joint ventures (e.g. Adient seats) alongside organic investment to add vertical content and life-cycle services revenue.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Organic is the -- is certainly a key part of that, and then complementary inorganic. But again, it's got to all make sense. ... able to deliver, we think, better value to the customer. It's got to meet our financial hurdles as well and complexity of integration and so on.
finding: Smith required services acquisitions to clear financial hurdles and integration-complexity tests, treating them as supplements to organic growth.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Obviously, what we've been focused on is competing to win. Competing to win, that is the ultimate job security.
finding: Smith's signature 'competing to win' framing justified headcount attrition and cost cuts in the name of competitiveness.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: everything has got to work. Got to work for the customer. The price needs to be the right price. The value proposition and the, ultimately, the cost and the nonrecurring and the recurring all need to come together and meet the requirements that we put in place. And if they do, we'll make a decision at that point.
finding: Smith set strict go/no-go conditions for the NMA (price, value, recurring and non-recurring cost) and kept 'no' as a real option.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So there's a number of, I'll say, big pieces in here, Cai, that we're focused on, engine certainly being one of them.
finding: Smith named the engine as a key open item in the NMA business case, alongside producibility and recurring and non-recurring risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Having said that, Cai, look, if we can't find an agreement that works, then we'll move forward. It's not a have to, but it would be certainly a nice to have, and we think a very complementary combination of portfolios.
finding: Smith treated the Embraer combination as attractive but optional, and was willing to walk away if the structure did not work.
response: pursue Embraer combination as optional

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Remember, we set up a lot of labs, just lessons learned, a lot of labs and investments upfront to derisk the production system. ... But again, we made a lot of those investments purposefully to try to bring the risk profile and allow the introduction of the X to be smooth.
finding: Smith described spending up front on labs and production tooling for the 777X to reduce industrialisation risk, applying 787 and MAX lessons.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As we talked about many times, we've got an incredible product offering when it comes to freight, and there's no one else that can match that product offering.
finding: Smith saw Boeing's freighter line-up (747, 777, 767) as unmatched by any competitor and expected recovering cargo demand to favour Boeing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I had a cost of finance for the entire company target that is global industrial champion. So my job is to meet that target. That's my piece beyond the other pieces, to meet that target, my piece of that mid-teen margin.
finding: Smith held himself to the same benchmarked cost target as the businesses, with every leadership-team member reviewed monthly and quarterly on their share of the mid-teens goal.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And look, if we see more opportunities with regards to R&D spending, we'll certainly capture them. And we're as focused on that level of spending as we are of any level of spending in the company.
finding: Smith treated R&D as a cost to be squeezed for efficiency like any other spending, not as untouchable.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: and that's why I keep kind of bringing it back to cash flow. Look at the overall cash flow of the program, and that ties directly to the productivity, ties directly to the mix and the step-down in the supply chain
finding: When 787 accounting metrics were noisy, Smith steered analysts back to program cash flow as the true measure.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: The rest of the full year guidance, including EPS, cash flow and aircraft deliveries, remain unchanged. And by holding EPS and cash flow guidance, we are absorbing the impact of the Tanker cost growth and Spirit litigation charge, offsetting that with performance.
finding: Smith's usual way of handling bad news was to absorb charges (tanker, Spirit) within unchanged guidance rather than reset expectations.
trigger: KC-46 cost growth and Spirit litigation write-off, Q2 2018
response: hold EPS and cash guidance; offset with performance

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Tanker is going to continue to improve the cash profile going forward as we make more progress and then reach the milestones that Dennis articulated and the first delivery there being in October.
finding: Smith's date for first KC-46 delivery kept moving: in February 2017 he expected deliveries to 'start late this year, early next year', in February 2018 he called 2018 'the delivery year', and by July 2018 he gave October 2018.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: First priority, organic. That's the investments we've been making over the last 10-plus years, and then the partnerships potentially or inorganic.
finding: Smith ranked organic investment first and partnerships and M&A second; KLX was a bolt-on and Embraer a broader strategic combination.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Yes, you'll definitely see more backloaded in Q4 on those deliveries, and we've got a recovery plan in place for them. And for us now, it's about executing to that recovery plan. But I don't want to make it more complicated than what it is. It's work.
finding: Smith played down the 737 supply-chain disruption as ordinary work to be cleared with a recovery plan.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We don't exclude tanker. So I appreciate the you are, but we don't exclude tanker. It's part of our portfolio and it's our job to perform on that program just like every other.
finding: Smith refused to let analysts strip out recurring KC-46 charges and took ownership of the program's losses.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We've seen constraints with what we talked about, with our fuselages in Spirit as well as with CFM. ... But days matter. When you're at 52 a month, a day matters. You don't have a lot of margin for error there.
finding: During the 2018 737 rate-52 disruption, Smith acknowledged Spirit fuselage and CFM engine constraints and stressed how fragile high-rate production is.
trigger: Spirit fuselage and CFM LEAP delays at 737 rate 52 (2018)
response: surge resources into Spirit and Renton; backload Q4 deliveries

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We've increased production rates about 20x since 2010 very flawlessly. And I would say that has not happened by mistake. There's a lot of hard work and effort and a very gated process that we go through internally.
finding: Smith described a formal, gated rate-readiness process that checks market durability, supplier capital, tooling, people and lead times before each rate break.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I would say that we've thought about this a lot over a number of years and it just wasn't the right time, considering things were either taking place in the market or taking place within the company. And we thought that last year was the right time to do that.
finding: Smith described waiting years for the right moment before making a structural move (creating Boeing Global Services).

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: 2020 is the focus area right now to fill that bridge, and we've got a very good active list of campaigns in place to do that. But from a risk perspective, certainly, as I sat here a year ago or prior, that risk profile has definitely changed.
finding: By 2018 Smith judged the 777 bridge risk largely retired (helped by freight demand) and moved attention to 777X orders.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: there's a need or desire to have it into the marketplace in 2025, but we're also going through a very disciplined gated process to ensure the business case is very solid, to ensure that we're transferring technology. No big leaps here. It's really leveraging that $60 billion of investment
finding: Smith framed the NMA as a technology-transfer aircraft with no big leaps and non-recurring cost held down, and put business-case discipline ahead of the 2025 date.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: fundamentally, it's a product line that fits between the high end of the 37 and low end of the 87. ... But you're right, when we see it about 4,000 to 5,000 and it really kind of fits between those 2 product lines.
finding: Smith sized the middle-of-market gap at 4,000-5,000 aircraft between the 737 and 787, plus new routes.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Do you buy it? Do you partner it? Do you develop it? Everything's open for discussion. And so what's the most efficient way to do that and also with a keen eye on risk.
finding: After the 787 outsourcing problems, Smith reconsidered which critical content and IP Boeing should control, choosing make, buy or partner case by case.
response: reassess vertical capability and IP control

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It's also unique that it's a company that we've been collaborating with for over 30 years. So we know each other very well, which is, I think again, highly unusual when you think about M&A.
finding: Smith justified the Embraer deal by complementary products, shared capabilities and a 30-year working relationship that lowered integration risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So it can't just be one-dimensional. Everything needs to work. And if it doesn't work, you shouldn't go up in rate, obviously. ... But if your supply chain or yourself can't meet that demand, there's no upside for you or your customer or your supplier to put yourself into that risk profile that really is not necessary.
finding: Smith's stated rule was that demand alone does not justify a rate increase; Boeing and supply-chain readiness must also be in place.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: doesn't mean you don't take risk, but how do you make sure you don't have concurrent risk on top of risk and how you're thinking about the risk mitigation plans putting in place
finding: Smith accepted risk but not stacked, concurrent risk, which was his main test for adding programs or rate changes.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: NPV, return on invested capital, I'd say a very traditional way to look at a business case. But as Dennis said, not just looking at the contract quantity but looking at the broader market opportunities and what it would take to win, and obviously stressing that
finding: Smith judged program bids on NPV and ROIC over the whole addressable market, stress-tested, rather than on the first contract alone.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As far as kind of broader, I'll say, kind of at a high level, R&D spend to revenue, still kind of that 3.8%, 3.9% is still what we see going forward, taking all of what we talked about into consideration.
finding: Smith anchored R&D at about 3.8-3.9% of revenue, a stable envelope inside which programs like the 777X and NMA had to fit.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And we continue to anticipate completing the remaining $9.6 billion of repurchase authorization over the next 12 to 18 months.
finding: In October 2018 Smith committed to finishing the remaining $9.6bn buyback within 12-18 months, keeping a steady repurchase pace.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: there's a lot of things that we're doing on these programs that Dennis indicated that we're looking at about how does that make us more efficient and more productive on the NMA and how does it derisk the NMA business case.
finding: Smith treated defense development programs as a proving ground for NMA methods (model-based engineering, staff rotation) to derisk its business case.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: our T-X and MQ-25 investments are based on deliberate and intentional decisions to create long-term, valuable products and services franchises. In selective key market opportunities such as these, we are taking into account the considerable market potential in our business cases and not just the initial order quantity
finding: Smith backed winning fixed-price defense franchises (T-X, MQ-25) with bids that required up-front loss charges, valuing the full market rather than the initial contract.
response: aggressive bids; take charges at award

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we've been very committed on our cash deployment and very consistent to what we said. ... And so back to kind of track record of consistency, doing what we said we're going to do and that's going to apply going forward.
finding: Smith's closing message in late 2018 rested on a track record of consistency: organic investment first, about 100% of free cash flow returned, and 'doing what we said we're going to do'.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: 777 will be -- X will be a more use of cash because you're right, we're building a static aircraft, we're building those early test aircraft and we're going through that phase, getting ready for 2020 entry into service
finding: In November 2018 Smith still planned for a 2020 777X entry into service, the same date he gave in January 2016, and kept 777X inventory build inside the cash-growth outlook.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: when you look at a 2025 EIS, you're in that 2019 time frame where we would have to make a decision.
finding: Smith tied the NMA decision to 2019 for a 2025 entry into service; in February 2018 he had said key decisions were due 'in the next year or so', so the decision kept moving out.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: but it's selective. It's not going to be the approach to everything. But in those particular cases, we felt that was the right thing to do, and it lined right up also to our capital deployment strategy and priorities, and that is organic investment.
finding: Smith limited the aggressive-bid, invest-ahead approach to selected strategic franchises rather than making it a general policy.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we got to get the supply chain on all elements fully healthy at 52, producing at a reliable, I'll say, consistency at 52. That will give us our confidence to continue that rate up to 57.
finding: Smith made the next 737 rate break (57) conditional on proven, stable rate-52 production across the supply chain, despite market pressure to go higher.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're seeing very predictable delivery, schedule associated with our load dates. GE is on a path on the recovery. We're still not fully recovered and don't expect to till the end of the year.
finding: Smith reported Spirit back on schedule but GE/CFM engines still not recovered, and planned back-loaded Q4 deliveries.
response: recovery plan; back-loaded Nov-Dec deliveries

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Where's the growth? What region of the world? What airline? What's their financial condition? How much of those do we think will be paid in cash? What's the status around financing?
finding: Smith vetted demand behind each rate break airline by airline, including customer credit and financing, before committing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As you said, we are in an oversold position because of the way we make those rate increases, and we assume that we will have movement and then try to find that, I'll say, kind of optimum place to -- and production meeting market demands.
finding: Smith deliberately kept the production skyline oversold to absorb customer deferrals.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we made investments. We made investments in technology and manufacturing, but ultimately, to get to 2 products, flying and running test flights before we even put the bid in. So certainly what's the risk in that? If we would have lost, we would have had 2 small fighter aircraft.
finding: Smith accepted spending company money on flying prototypes before a competition, treating the downside as limited and the derisking as worth it.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we've got a regular update, the team does with Dennis and I once a month where we go through NMA, and NMA business case and stress-test the business case
finding: Smith and CEO Muilenburg jointly ran a monthly stress-test review of the NMA business case, so the launch decision sat with the CEO and CFO together.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We remain focused and on track with our balanced cash deployment strategy. In 2018, we invested $5 billion in R&D and CapEx, repurchased $9 billion of Boeing stock and paid $3.9 billion in dividends, reflecting a 20% increase in dividend per share from last year.
finding: Before the MAX crisis Smith ran a 'balanced cash deployment' that returned about 2.6x as much cash to shareholders (buybacks plus dividends) as Boeing spent on R&D and capex.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Operating cash flow for 2019 is forecasted to increase by $2 billion to be between $17 billion and $17.5 billion.
finding: Smith's last pre-grounding guidance promised growing cash flow; the MAX grounding six weeks later voided it, and he later reported 2019 operating cash flow of negative $2.4 billion.
trigger: Ethiopian Airlines crash and MAX grounding (March 2019)
response: Guidance withdrawn April 2019; FY2019 OCF reported as -$2.4bn on 2020-01-29

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: our key focus areas are continuing to manage the 737 recovery progress within our factory and throughout our supply chain, including assuring rate readiness for a smooth transition to 57 a month.
finding: Smith committed to taking the 737 to 57 a month in 2019. The grounding cut the rate to 42 in April 2019 and production was suspended in January 2020, so the rate was never reached.
response: Rate cut to 42 (Apr 2019), production suspended (Jan 2020); by Jul 2020 target was 31/mo by end-2022

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So this is kind of a peak year for us on, I'll say, cash usage on 777 combined with 777X.
finding: Smith first forecast 2019 as the peak cash-use year for 777/777X. As the schedule slipped he moved the peak to 2020, and in 2021 he still called 2020 the peak.
response: Peak moved to 2020 (Oct 2019); reaffirmed Jan/Apr 2021 with EIS late 2023

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So that playbook, you should just think of that as the same no matter what the mix. So we don't let mix be the deciding factor. Mix is mix. It's our job to try to offset that or use that to our advantage the best way possible.
finding: Smith ran one margin and productivity playbook whatever the program mix, treating an unfavourable mix as something to offset, not as an excuse.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And what are some best practices within industrials, outside the industrials, how we bring them back into Boeing, make it part of our operating rhythm and hold ourselves to a standard that is not necessarily industry? It could be that it's best-in-class. ... So we don't really have a cap, I think I would say.
finding: Smith benchmarked cost and capital efficiency against best-in-class industrials rather than aerospace peers, and put no ceiling on productivity targets.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: While our organic investment remains the primary engine for growth, we may partner with other industry players ... as demonstrated by the proposed strategic partnership with Embraer, which, assuming all approvals are received in a timely manner, we expect to close by the end of the year.
finding: Smith treated organic R&D as the main growth engine, with partnerships and joint ventures such as Embraer used to add capability, and gave a dated closing target.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We don't spend money just to spend money. Trust me. But I can tell you that it's the timing of potential newer airplanes plays right into the 777X kind of ramping down.
finding: Smith wanted to hold R&D roughly flat as a share of sales, with new-airplane spending sequenced behind 777X, rather than lifting the R&D envelope to fund overlapping programs.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So while we've committed to spend money on R&D and you get 6 months into it and you realize maybe that's not as good maybe as we thought it was, we're stopping. We're reallocating that to something that's even -- sees more potential going forward.
finding: Smith ran R&D as a portfolio with stop-loss reviews: projects that underperform after about six months are cut and the money reallocated.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But I will tell you, we're doubling down on integration. So if you look at the amount of effort and the operating rhythm around integrating KLX, I would argue is far greater than you've ever seen in the past. That's intentional, absolutely intentional and holding ourselves accountable to that original business case.
finding: Smith backed bolt-on M&A that met the criteria (KLX), then held the deal accountable to its original business case through heavy integration oversight.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So when you kind of step back and look at this, again, right where I started, this is very much an execution. It's doing what we said we would do.
finding: Smith presented the cash-growth story as pure execution of milestones already promised. His signature framing was 'doing what we said we would do'.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So I think we got a good plan in place. I wouldn't tell you that we see anything that's been outside the norm of what we've normally been through in our certification of our other aircraft.
finding: In February 2019, between the two MAX accidents, Smith called 777X certification business as usual. A year later he said the opposite (see 2020-02-12).
response: By Feb 2020: 'we're not assuming business as usual certify the aircraft'

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And this year will be a milestone of deciding whether, as we -- Dennis talked in the call, whether we get the authority and ask for the authority to offer it in the market. And if we do, does that meet our criteria? And then from there, there'll be a decision whether we formally launch or not.
finding: Smith said 2019 would bring the NMA authority-to-offer decision. No offer was made, and in January 2020 Boeing stepped back to reassess its whole commercial product strategy.
response: NMA set aside; 'step back and reassess' announced 2020-01-29

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So it's probably a long way of saying that there's a lot of criteria, and we're being very disciplined, and we're going to go when we're ready, but we're staying very engaged with our customer throughout this process
finding: Smith's stance on launching the NMA was 'go when we're ready': process discipline came first and customer pressure on timing second.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So certainly, the market demand is there. We're in a oversold position. So it's not the market that's driving -- it's driving the rate increases certainly in that demand. It's really more in the production system.
finding: Smith treated narrowbody rate as limited by supply, not demand: the 737 was oversold, and the binding constraints were the factory and suppliers such as CFM.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: very focused on cash, ultimately cash, and efficiency, back to not only how we're generating to cash but being very prudent about how we're deploying it as well
finding: Cash generation and disciplined deployment were Smith's top-line metrics even in the boom years.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we got to work through those gates, and it's a pass or fail. So if it's a fail, you got to kind go back and meet the criteria and a lot of people obviously involved in these gates to get through them.
finding: For a new airplane (NMA), Smith described a strengthened stage-gate process with pass/fail criteria covering technology, business case, pricing and engines. The gates, not the market's timing, set the pace.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: You could buy a seat manufacturer. You could become one or you could partner. We chose to partner.
finding: Smith filled capability gaps through an explicit build/buy/partner choice and picked partnerships when they offered a 'win-win' at lower capital risk.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So again, talk about a lesson learned, concurrent development of big major development programs. So we're not going to do that, and we've made that clear.
finding: Smith set a hard rule against running major development programs concurrently: NMA spending would be timed to follow the 777X development ramp-down.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: One score. So everybody's compensated on one score: free cash flow, earnings and revenue. And each of us individually on our behaviors is rated on how we're planning to make Boeing better.
finding: Smith tied executive incentives to enterprise free cash flow, earnings and revenue ('One Boeing') rather than to divisional results, to force best-practice sharing across units.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And until we have clarity on the 737 MAX return to service, we have temporarily paused our share repurchase program. However, our long-term balance cash deployment strategy and commitment remains unchanged.
finding: Smith's first crisis lever was the buyback: he paused it within weeks while saying the long-term shareholder-return commitment was intact.
response: Buyback paused (April 2019)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And remember, too, back then, we didn't have a share repurchase program. And so that is a lever for us today that we can utilize to help navigate through this, but again, not losing sight in our long-term commitment around repo.
finding: Smith saw the buyback program as a discretionary shock absorber to cut first in a crisis, unlike the 787-era balance sheet of ten years earlier.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: given the dynamic of 737 MAX return-to-service time line in activities, we are not in a position today to provide a forecast of the impacts of the 737 MAX grounding on our full year 2019 financials.
finding: Faced with an open-ended crisis, Smith withdrew full-year guidance rather than offer a range, and promised a separate call once there was clarity.
response: 2019 guidance withdrawn; no formal guidance reissued through April 2021 in slice

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: From Day 1 of the grounding, we've been doing detailed scenario planning around return to service and production rates, including analyzing the implications on our supply chain, customer fleet and deliveries to fully understand the range of financial outcomes.
finding: Smith's first move after the grounding was scenario planning on return to service and production rates, mapping the range of financial outcomes.
response: Scenario planning; rate cut 52->42; buyback paused

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We will continue to assess our production plans going forward and have established waypoint milestones along our plan. This will allow us to make decisions based on information we have at that point on whether to further adjust production rates as required.
finding: Smith made decisions at pre-set 'waypoint' milestones: each production-rate call was deferred to a defined checkpoint and taken on the information available then, not pre-committed.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But we also are holding on to head count. Remember, we were at 52, going down to 42. We've held that head count in factory, and what we've been doing with that is really working the jobs behind schedule and any jobs that are out of position in getting things back into position in the factory.
finding: When the rate was cut, Smith kept the factory workforce in place and used the slack to clear traveled work, accepting higher period costs to protect a smooth future ramp.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So again, going into the supply chain, rather than pulling everybody down to 42, let's go through and understand liquidity within each of those suppliers, where -- who needs help, who doesn't, who is on schedule, who can we use to get this opportunity to get back on schedule.
finding: Smith managed suppliers case by case rather than with a blanket cut: lagging suppliers were kept at 52 to catch up, and help went where liquidity was weak.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we're clear-eyed about what we know and what we don't know and the range of possibilities or outcomes and how would we manage it and how do we get ahead of it. And we're very much in a mindset of getting ahead of it and frankly playing on the side of being conservative at this point
finding: In a crisis Smith deliberately leaned conservative on cash and liquidity. 'Clear-eyed' and 'getting ahead of it' were his recurring phrases.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Long pole in the tent right now is GE engine. There's some challenges they're working through there on testing. ... As we see it today, we still expect to fly this year and entry into service in 2020.
finding: Smith committed to 777X first flight in 2019 and entry into service in 2020. First flight slipped to January 2020, and EIS moved to 2021 and then to late 2023.
trigger: GE9X engine issues; post-MAX certification scrutiny
response: EIS 2021 (Jan 2020), late 2023 with $6.5bn charge (Jan 2021)
lag: 7 months to first slip; ~19 months to 2023 reset

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Look, that is -- we're very clear-eyed on the brand. And so we're putting whatever resource is required inside and outside the company to help us restore the MAX brand and then, obviously, work on the company brand. So that's going to take whatever it's going to take. That's the top priority for us.
finding: Smith treated MAX brand repair as an uncapped spend and brought in outside crisis and brand experts.
response: Outside brand/crisis experts hired; brand made a daily swim lane

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
