quote: But to get to 57, and I'll say not be healthy and have an optimized production system, isn't the right answer. So we're going to take these in increments and monitor health and then make the next rate break, monitor health, next rate break. Not a demand issue, right?
finding: Smith would leave demand unmet rather than ramp into an unhealthy system. Rate breaks were incremental, each gated on a health check.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: looking at the timing also and the demand for the Dash 8 and see if that still makes sense and do we want to push that out and how do we want to manage that.
finding: Smith was willing to defer a weaker-demand variant (777-8) to protect the program's economics and focus on the core model.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And I think as you see, when we're in the marketplace with the 787, the airplane is certainly -- our sales folks have done their job, but the airplane is really selling itself. The operating economics of that airplane are unmatchable.
finding: Smith saw the 787 as superior to competing widebodies and spoke of it in absolute terms ('unmatchable'), not relative to Airbus products by name.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Outside of that, we've got a daily operating rhythm that I participate on as does Dennis and a lot of the other executive council and the whole team. So we've got about 7 swim lanes that we cover every morning and go through and get a status
finding: Smith ran the MAX crisis through a centralised daily executive 'operating rhythm' with about seven swim lanes, in which the CFO took part directly alongside the CEO.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I maybe step back a little bit and take the MAX out of the equation for a second and tell you that the balance of the company and, I'd say, the key puts and takes that we saw pre-MAX remain intact.
finding: Smith handled bad news by isolating it: the MAX was framed as the single outlier while the 'fundamentals remain intact' everywhere else.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: For the purpose of our second quarter financial results, we have assumed that the regulatory approval in the U.S. and other jurisdictions begin early in fourth quarter 2019.
finding: Smith's return-to-service accounting assumption slipped every quarter: early Q4 2019, then Q4 2019, mid-2020, Q3 2020 and Q4 2020. Deliveries finally resumed in December 2020.
response: Assumption moved 5 times; deliveries restarted Dec 2020

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: BCA revenue and earnings were reduced by $5.6 billion of pretax charge related to our estimate of potential concessions and other considerations to customers ... we will deal with the impact individually, customer by customer, and we will look at various forms of economic value that we can provide.
finding: Smith booked the full estimated customer-compensation liability up front in one quarter and settled customer by customer in mixed forms (cash and in-kind) over several years.
response: $5.6bn charge Q2 2019; liability raised to $8.3bn (Q4 2019), $9.6bn (2020)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We will continue to assess our current production plans and incorporate any new insights ... to help inform us on whether further rate reduction or other options, including a temporary shutdown of the MAX production, are needed.
finding: Smith flagged a production shutdown as a live option about six months before Boeing took it, preparing investors in stages rather than with a sudden reversal.
response: MAX production suspended January 2020

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: we're disappointed by where we are with that -- with this engine. So we're trying to get ahead of this, Cai, and putting mitigating actions in place and really, again, minimize the impact on us and ultimately, on our customers.
finding: Smith publicly pinned the 777X delay on the GE engine and said Boeing was disappointed in the engine maker, while framing the response as joint mitigation.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think don't anticipate share repo until we've got return to service. We're executing on the production rates and reaching the stability that we expect. And once we get to that level, then we'll reassess our cash deployment efforts.
finding: Smith put buybacks behind a sequence of conditions (return to service, production rates, stability) and added debt reduction to the queue.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: However, in the near term, managing our liquidity and balance sheet leverage are top priorities and will continue to be so until the 737 MAX deliveries resume, we execute the 737 production rate increases and see stability in the production system.
finding: Smith's financial priorities moved from shareholder returns to liquidity and leverage, with explicit exit conditions: deliveries resume, rates rise, the system is stable.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And as I said, we do have additional balance sheet levers. If we need to pull additional levers, we'll do that. We don't see that over the short term.
finding: In October 2019 Smith saw no near-term need for more liquidity levers. Within three months Boeing lined up a $12 billion-plus term loan, and in 2020 it drew $13.8 billion and issued $25 billion of bonds.
response: $12bn+ term loan commitment (Jan 2020), drawn $13.8bn (Mar 2020), $25bn bond (May 2020)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Now having said all that, as I've said and Dennis has said many times, the regulators pace this. We don't pace it.
finding: Smith's standard line on the MAX timeline was that the regulators set the pace, avoiding public timing commitments while the accounting still carried dated assumptions.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So it's hurtful, I think, to all of us 150,000 when you hear people say, "Well, there must be a trade-off there." There's no trade-offs that take place there. That's the priority. That's always been the priority, and that will continue to be.
finding: When asked whether Boeing traded safety for cost or schedule, Smith flatly denied that any trade-off had ever happened, defending the culture instead of conceding a systemic problem.
trigger: Press reports questioning cost/schedule versus safety trade-offs

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We're going through the regulatory approval process. We expect to -- probably early next year, that will be brought to a conclusion.
finding: Smith moved the Embraer closing from end-2019 to early 2020. The slice shows Cai von Rumohr in February 2020 still referring to Embraer as pending ('You've got Embraer to do'), and after that it says nothing more about the deal.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And so we'll go through that engine integration process and get that in place and then start to go into the pretesting and still kind of looking at a window of early next year where we'll have first flight.
finding: Smith's reset 777X first-flight window (early 2020) was met: he reported first flight completed in January 2020.
response: First flight completed January 2020 (reported 2020-01-29)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Those are some hard lessons learned there that we're addressing and are addressing. And we own it, and we're putting those fixes in place. And our job is to ensure that nothing like that ever happens again.
finding: Smith accepted ownership of the MAX failures ('we own it') while defending Boeing's safety culture.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: So we'll move up from 42, we'll hold for a period of time, we'll monitor the health across the board, and then we'll move up. ... But I think the big message here is we're not going to go up in rate until we're ready.
finding: Smith described a 'step, hold, assess, step' production-rate algorithm, with readiness rather than calendar or demand as the trigger.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And stability is going to be a real key, I'll say, enabler as we move up in rate, maintaining stability and predictability within the supply chain and within our own factories and then ultimately to our customer. ... If we're not stable, we're not going up.
finding: 'If we're not stable, we're not going up' sums up Smith's rate rule: rate increases are gated on demonstrated stability in Boeing's own factory and in the supply chain.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And not having a China order in a couple of years, certainly, now we're at that point of lead time away where we'd have to implement that airplane, made the decision to bring the rate down for a couple of years. ... But ultimately, we want to make sure we get to the right rate and maintain that rate, not overproduce.
finding: Smith cut 787 production from 14 to 12 a month on order-book lead time (no China orders) and said Boeing would not overproduce. Rate followed the visible skyline, not hoped-for orders.
trigger: US-China trade tensions; no China widebody orders in ~2 years

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And then off-line, we go through -- I go through liquidity analysis with the team, supplier status, where we need to help suppliers, where they are with inventory rates, where we're storing inventory, how we're storing inventory
finding: Smith owned liquidity, supplier health and inventory storage within the CEO-CFO daily crisis rhythm, so his remit went beyond finance into operations.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Our debt level has been elevated during the grounding, and we are planning to immediately reduce it once our cash flow generation returns to a more normalized level. ... Investing in our business and repaying debt will remain our cash deployment priority for the next few years.
finding: Smith reordered capital priorities to invest first, repay debt second and return capital to shareholders later, for a multi-year horizon.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As we're in the planning window of a rate decision and to reduce risk in the '21 and 2022 skyline, we've decided to further reduce the rate to 10 per month in early '21 before returning to 12 per month in 2023.
finding: Smith cut the 787 rate in steps: 14 to 12 (October 2019), 10 (January 2020), 6 (2020) and 5 (December 2020). Each cut was framed as prudent and as the last needed.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Now we will -- currently, we're looking at starting the line earlier than the actual lifting of the grounding. But again, think of that as a risk mitigator.
finding: Smith planned to restart production ahead of regulatory clearance, gated on confidence in the timing, to de-risk the ramp. This is a calculated lead rather than waiting until approval was certain.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: This includes costs related to our decision to maintain the 737 production infrastructure, including labor during the suspension and low rate production. As you may recall, this decision is part of our efforts to sustain the gains in the production system and supply chain quality and health made over the last several months.
finding: Smith chose to keep the 737 workforce and infrastructure through the production suspension, accepting about $4 billion of abnormal costs (later $5 billion) to protect stability gains.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We've asked the team to step back and reassess our commercial product development strategy to determine what family of airplanes will be needed in the future. The team will build on the work we have done as part of the NMA design and production system analysis as we move forward.
finding: In the crisis Smith announced that the NMA was shelved in favour of a broader reassessment of a future 'family of airplanes', keeping the NMA design and production work as input.
trigger: MAX crisis, balance-sheet strain, CEO change
response: NMA stopped; product strategy reassessment

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We will take a measured approach to the 777X rate ramp, and we will look to minimize the amount of change in corporation work by managing the number of aircraft produced prior to entry into service.
finding: Smith cut concurrency risk on 777X by limiting how many aircraft were built before certification, to reduce later change-incorporation costs.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We are mindful of the impacts the additional debt has on our credit ratings. Currently at A-, A3, but confident we have the sufficient balance sheet flexibility and operational levers to navigate this challenging time.
finding: Smith accepted rating erosion as the price of debt-funded liquidity while signalling the ratings mattered.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Clearly, our narrowbody delivery market share has been and will continue to be impacted by the MAX. ... The limited production slot availability of aircraft from both Boeing and our competitor affords us ample time to double down on improving operating efficiency in order to mitigate some of these challenges
finding: Smith conceded narrowbody delivery share to Airbus but argued the competitor's sold-out slots limited the lasting damage, giving Boeing time to fix its operations.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: On the supply-demand, China is a big deal. Don't mistake it. It's a big deal, and that's a big play in these production rates. Outside of that, as you've seen, when we've been going head-to-head with the 787, we've been winning the marketplace.
finding: Smith said the 787 wins head-to-head widebody campaigns against Airbus and named China orders, not competitive losses, as the swing factor for widebody rates.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I have a lot of respect for Dave and look forward to the continued partnership. And I can tell you, we are completely 100% aligned on our priorities and the path forward for our company.
finding: After his brief stint as interim CEO, Smith publicly backed Calhoun and stressed full CEO-CFO alignment.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: First and foremost, to pay down the debt. ... But clearly, this has caused us to re-shift that balanced approach and primarily pay down a significant amount of this debt, and then we'll reassess where we are and decide how to move forward with a more balanced deployment.
finding: Smith formally suspended the 'balanced deployment' model: debt paydown came first, and shareholder returns would be reconsidered only after substantial deleveraging.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And like I said, we'll paint a picture and let you know what's in there, what isn't in there, what are the key drivers within there, what are the watch items, so everybody is kind of well-informed to understand the puts and takes.
finding: Smith's guidance style was conditional, laying out drivers, 'puts and takes' and watch items. In the crisis he withheld formal numbers until clarity on return to service, customer sequencing and production.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As I said on the earnings call, we're trying to front load that and get these behind us on behalf of the airline and for ourselves.
finding: Smith chose to front-load MAX customer settlements to clear the liability quickly, accepting near-term cash pain.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: And that's what we're getting in the -- we're right in that sweet spot on the lead time where we have to make a decision, and we think it's a prudent thing to do. But like I said, if we see a marketplace different or there's different dynamics, we'll assess them, and we'll make a different decision.
finding: Smith timed rate decisions by supplier lead times: he cut when the lead-time window forced a choice, and kept the option to reverse if the market changed.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: because, in some cases, we gave everybody a green light, "Hey, go continue to produce." So we got inventory to build -- burn off once we come back up in rate.
finding: Smith let many suppliers keep producing during the 737 pause, absorbing inventory to keep them healthy, at the cost of a slower inventory burn-off on restart.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I think one of the things that we learned is when you're at a rate of 52 and a fuselage is a day late, it makes a big difference. And we don't want work out of position, so making up for it out on the ramp is not something we want to get in. So let's relook at the buffer.
finding: From the 2018 737 disruption Smith learned that high rates leave no slack. He pushed for more buffer inventory and work kept in position instead of lean just-in-time at 52 or more a month.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: It's -- get the MAX safely back up into the air and certainly focus on the balance sheet, get the balance sheet healthy and then don't lose sight of the competitive dynamics and how we would address that.
finding: Smith ranked his early-2020 priorities: (1) MAX return to service, (2) repair the balance sheet, (3) keep watch on competitive dynamics.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: I mean priority one is MAX and has been and needs to be certainly versus the next product. Now having said that, not that we're not thinking about the next product, but we use this as an opportunity to step back from what we were, I'll say, specifically focused on the NMA and relook at the commercial product landscape
finding: Smith explicitly ranked fixing the MAX above any new airplane. The NMA was paused in favour of a wider look at the product landscape and competitive dynamics.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Look, we're not assuming business as usual certify the aircraft, nor should we. Do we have specifics on what exactly might change? Not specifics, but we're anticipating them.
finding: After the MAX, Smith built extra certification time and test points into 777X plans, a turn away from his early-2019 'nothing outside the norm' view.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Fixed-price development better than what it was but still not where it needs to be. ... Not only are they fixed-priced, we're dealing with a lot of technology in these products and risk that we've got to manage well in advance.
finding: Smith admitted that fixed-price development contracts (tanker, Starliner) were still a source of losses and treated fixed-price development risk as a continuing priority.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As far as the marketplace goes, look, like I said, think of a campaign where the 87 hasn't won, and you'll be thinking a long time.
finding: Smith claimed near-total 787 win rates in widebody campaigns, which shows his confidence that Boeing's widebody position against Airbus was secure.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: not to say we're not focused on it, but that's not taking up a significant amount of our time, meaning our time, me, Dave, Stan. We've got the teams focused on that, day in and day out.
finding: Smith said future-product work was delegated to the product-development team while the CEO, CFO and BCA head focused on the MAX and the balance sheet.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: In March 2020, we suspended payment of our dividend until further notice. Since April 2019, we've suspended our share repurchase program. And in March 2020, our Board of Directors terminated its prior authorization to repurchase shares of the company's common stock.
finding: As the crisis deepened, Smith's order of cuts was buyback paused (April 2019), then dividend suspended and buyback authorization terminated (March 2020).
trigger: COVID-19 on top of MAX grounding
response: Dividend suspended; buyback authorization terminated

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We expect to gradually increase the production rate to 31 during 2021 and expect further gradual increases to correspond with market demand. We've assumed that the timing of the regulatory approvals will enable the 737 MAX deliveries to resume during the third quarter of 2020.
finding: After COVID hit, Smith reset the 737 plan to 31 a month during 2021 with deliveries from Q3 2020. Three months later both slipped, to 31 by end-2022 and deliveries in Q4 2020.
response: 31/mo by end-2022 and Q4 2020 deliveries (Jul 2020)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: Our current forecast, based on all the rate discussions we just had today, is a positive 2021 cash flow.
finding: In April 2020 Smith forecast positive 2021 cash flow. By October 2020 it had slipped to 2022, and by January 2021 he guided that 2021 would be a use of cash.
response: Positive cash moved to 2022 (Oct 2020); 2021 a use of cash (Jan 2021)

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As you know, 777X is a use of cash this year, will peak this year. We expect it to be a use of cash next year. But then, it's cash flow-positive in the following year.
finding: Smith forecast 777X cash-positive in 2022. After the late-2023 EIS reset he said cash positive one to two years after first delivery.
response: Jan 2021: cash positive 1-2 years after late-2023 first delivery

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: We believe that government's support will be critical to ensuring our industry's access to liquidity, and we continue to evaluate options in the capital markets as well as funding options from the U.S. government via the U.S. Treasury and various federal reserve programs.
finding: In April 2020 Smith kept government funding open as an option alongside the capital markets. Boeing then raised $25 billion in bonds and credited government action for reopening credit markets.
response: $25bn bond issued May 2020

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: But at the end of the day, it's going to be what it's going to be on the investment grade. But certainly, we'd prefer to stay investment grade.
finding: Smith treated investment grade as a strong preference, not a hard constraint. He would not sacrifice liquidity to defend the rating.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Performance & Strategy
quote: As part of that, I'm excited to take on a new role and work closely with our teams across the business units to drive operational excellence and restore production and supply chain health
finding: Under Calhoun, Smith's remit widened from finance to enterprise operations (production and supply-chain health), making the CFO a co-owner of factory performance.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Operations, Finance & Strategy
quote: In May, we completed a $25 billion bond issuance and the strong investor response on the bond validates the confidence we have in our future.
finding: Smith funded the COVID crisis through public debt markets ($25 billion bond) rather than equity or direct government aid, and presented the oversubscription as a vote of confidence.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Operations, Finance & Strategy
quote: In some cases, we would have liked to bring production rate down sooner to match near-term demand. However, there's a number of key factors that need to take into consideration, including orderly supply chain transition and production system stability.
finding: Smith accepted building ahead of demand (finished-goods inventory) rather than cutting rates abruptly. He put supply-chain orderliness ahead of matching demand.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO and Executive VP of Enterprise Operations, Finance & Strategy
quote: We worked hard to derisk the past decade by addressing a number of different areas, including pension funding risk, labor stability, product development sequencing and raising the bar on productivity, safety and cash management discipline.
finding: Smith described his decade as CFO as a derisking program covering pension, labour contracts and sequencing of development programs, and saw that preparation as the foundation for surviving the crisis.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: And have we sharpened our pencil on all that? Absolutely, in delaying some things and refining some of those investments, again, with a keen eye towards liquidity. But we're continuing to fund the key franchises that we got in the pipeline, 777X, 737-10, Starliner, and so on
finding: During COVID Smith trimmed and delayed investment but protected funding for in-development franchises (777X, 737-10, Starliner). He ranked finishing existing programs above starting new ones.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: But as we outlined last week, we see and IATA sees this kind of taking around 3 years to return to 2019 levels.
finding: Smith anchored Boeing's COVID production rates on a recovery to 2019 traffic in about three years (around 2023), taken from IATA's view.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Well, look, as you said, in mid-March, we advanced our bank loan of $13.8 billion, which some would have, at the time, may be viewed early. We viewed it as trying to be prudent and then issuing the $25 billion to ensure that we had appropriate liquidity to get through this period.
finding: Smith moved early and decisively on liquidity, drawing the full $13.8 billion term loan in mid-March 2020 before markets froze. He accepted the carrying cost to secure the cash.
response: Full term-loan drawdown, then $25bn bond

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: But I think on the supply chain, absolutely big focus. They're an extension of our factory. ... For every dollar we spend, $0.70 goes to the supply chain. And we've continued to fund the supply chain through this pandemic to keep them healthy
finding: Smith treated suppliers as an extension of Boeing's factory and kept funding them through COVID, because about 70% of Boeing's spend flows to them.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Again, we want to be positioned for strength coming out of this. Right now, it's getting through this period. And cash will be ... continue to be king, and we'll manage that very tightly, but smartly as well and stay ahead of it on the liquidity actions.
finding: 'Cash is king' captures Smith's crisis ranking: survival liquidity first, managed 'smartly' so as not to damage future position.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: But look, we'll continue to evaluate the product strategy in this, obviously, very dynamic environment and remain mindful what's happening on the competitive landscape. So like I said, we haven't lost sight of it, and we won't. And we'll make the right investments at the right time to maintain a competitive advantage
finding: On new airplanes Smith stayed noncommittal through COVID: he would watch competitors and invest 'at the right time', with no launch timing given.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: So we've got the baseline plan we talked about last week, but we are running scenarios and have for quite some time on a more severe downside or stress case. And just again, this is treated us well, this discipline, getting ahead of it and not just looking at a baseline plan
finding: Smith ran downside and stress-case liquidity scenarios alongside the baseline and sized actions to the stress case.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: We originally plan to invest over $6 billion this year. Through prioritization, we have pared back these investments by approximately $2 billion.
finding: Smith cut planned 2020 investment by about a third through prioritisation rather than across-the-board cuts.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: In addition, we've decided to use Boeing's stock rather than cash to fund our company contribution to employees' 401(k) plans for the foreseeable future. This will preserve approximately $1 billion of cash gradually over the next 12 months.
finding: Smith used Boeing stock instead of cash for 401(k) matching and a $3 billion pension prefunding, a quiet form of equity issuance to save cash without a public raise.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: While we're still aiming to turn cash positive in late '21, the recovery and the continued elevated virus cases make the path much more challenging. Based on what we know today, it's looking more likely that we will be cash flow-positive in the 2022 time frame.
finding: Smith reset the cash-positive target from 2021 to 2022 gradually: he kept the old target as an aspiration while signalling the new one as 'more likely'.
response: 2022 reaffirmed Jan and Apr 2021

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: We are being and will continue to be proactive and look around corners to assess risk factors and take appropriate action. We've been focused on derisking our business and a disciplined cash management for some time, and COVID-19 has accelerated these efforts further.
finding: 'Look around corners' was Smith's signature phrase for anticipating risks early. He described his crisis decisions as continuing a long-running derisking agenda.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Also, through our 787 study, it became evident that the consolidation to a single production location in South Carolina will make us more efficient and lower production and better positioned for the future. As a result, earlier this month, we made the decision to consolidate the 787 production in South Carolina by mid-'21.
finding: Smith backed a study-led structural move, consolidating 787 final assembly in South Carolina, to cut cost at low rates and capture efficiency when rates recover.
response: 787 consolidated to Charleston by mid-2021

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: The reality is that our industry as a whole will simply build less over the coming years. And we have to help our industry partners recalibrate to that lower demand in the near term, while maintaining stability as much as possible
finding: Smith accepted a multi-year lower-volume reality and steered the supply chain through a managed recalibration rather than abrupt cuts.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: So that's going to continue to be our discipline, but we're, again, very diligently focused on it. And if we have to make further adjustments down, then we certainly will to match the demand.
finding: Smith signalled more 787 cuts were possible if risk-assessed demand weakened. He made one five weeks later (to 5 a month).

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Our guiding principle here is that every decision we make must help us navigate through this difficult period while also not diminishing our future competitiveness.
finding: Smith's stated test for crisis decisions had two parts: it must aid survival now and must not erode future competitiveness.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: The enterprise operations team successfully launched the formation of 4 company-wide process councils around supply chain, program management, quality and manufacturing. ... We have simplified our structure to allow the process councils to lead on driving accountability and decision-making closer to the work that's being performed.
finding: As head of enterprise operations, Smith pushed decision rights down to cross-company process councils and cut management layers.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: it will be all about paying down that debt. ... got to get this debt balance down. And we'll look for every opportunity to do that in the most efficient way, including equity. So nothing's off the table.
finding: Asked directly about equity issuance, Smith did not rule it out ('nothing's off the table') but framed it only as a tool for paying down debt.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: So as a result of that, we've made a modest adjustment to the 787 production rate from what we had previously announced rate of 6 aircraft a month beginning in mid-'21 to a rate of 5 per month by mid-'21.
finding: Smith called the latest 787 cut 'modest' after a series of reductions from 14 a month, framing each step as small.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: And again, as any development program, there is inherent risk that can affect schedule. And the timing of EIS will ultimately be influenced by the certification requirements defined by regulators.
finding: Before the 777X reset, Smith prepared investors by stressing development risk and regulator control without giving a date. The 2023 delay and $6.5 billion charge followed seven weeks later.
response: Late 2023 EIS announced 2021-01-27

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: And as we rebuild trust 1 airplane at a time, we will be laser-focused on, again, safety, quality and transparency.
finding: On the MAX ungrounding, Smith framed recovery as rebuilding trust 'one airplane at a time', echoing Calhoun's language.
response: Deliveries restarted Dec 2020

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: So while the additional time for inspection is impacting deliveries, conducting the comprehensive reviews is absolutely the right thing to do for our customers and for the long-term health of the program.
finding: Smith accepted halting 787 deliveries for quality inspections at a large near-term cash cost, putting quality ahead of delivery timing.
response: Zero 787 deliveries in Nov 2020; inventory unwound through 2021

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: As Dave mentioned, we expect first delivery of the 777X to now occur in late 2023, and we recorded a $6.5 billion reach-forward loss on the program. Our decision to implement certain modifications to the aircraft design has added time to the schedule and result in additional costs.
finding: Smith delivered the 777X reset as one large charge ($6.5 billion) with a new late-2023 date, after earlier commitments of 2020 and then 2021.
trigger: Certification requirements and design modifications; COVID demand
response: EIS late 2023; accounting quantity cut to 350

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Bringing this all together, based on what we know today, we continue to expect 2021 to still be a use of cash and to be cash flow positive in 2022.
finding: Smith's reset commitment was a 2021 cash use and positive cash in 2022, reaffirmed in April 2021. The slice ends before 2022 results.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: As a reminder, initial accounting quantity doesn't represent the long-term potential size of the program. We see replacement demand for over 1,500 larger widebody aircraft, which will be well suited to the 777X.
finding: Smith defended the long-term 777X business case against a cut accounting quantity by pointing to large-widebody replacement demand.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: Once cash flow generation returns to more normal levels, reducing our debt level will be our top priority. We believe we currently have sufficient liquidity and are not planning to increase our debt levels.
finding: Smith's capital order on leaving was unchanged: debt reduction as top priority once cash normalised, and no new borrowing.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: And I'd say even in some cases, we've made more investment like on the 737 line in order to capture stability on the other end, as Dave indicated. ... So in a lot of cases, we've moved money or shifted money or even added money in some cases because we're playing a long game here.
finding: Even in the downturn Smith added investment where it bought production stability (737 line), consistent with his 'playing a long game' stance.

speaker: Gregory D. Smith, CFO & Executive VP of Enterprise Operations
quote: we're looking around corners and playing out options and making sure we have them and understanding the second and third order effect. And to your point, some of them -- sequence of these sometimes matters and the timing of them matters.
finding: Smith approached capital-structure moves as sequenced options, weighing second- and third-order effects and timing before acting.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & Corporate Audit and CFO
quote: Our investment-grade credit rating is very important to us, and we will consider all aspects of our capital structure to strengthen our balance sheet.
finding: From his first call he named the investment-grade rating as the constraint on capital-structure choices.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & Corporate Audit and CFO
quote: We know where the vast majority of the airplanes are going given the demand, and we anticipate delivering most of these airplanes by the end of 2023. This assumes we resume delivery to our customers in China during the first quarter of 2022.
finding: His first inventory forecast depended on China resuming in Q1 2022. China did not resume, and the target slipped to 2024 (July 2022), to 2025 for some aircraft (October 2022) and to 'more likely to slip into 2025' (October 2023).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & Corporate Audit and CFO
quote: We currently anticipate total 787 abnormal costs to be approximately $1 billion.
finding: His first 787 cost estimate was a large underestimate. It was raised to about $2B one quarter later, to about $2.8B in January 2023 and to $3B in October 2023.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & Corporate Audit and CFO
quote: We still expect full year 2021 to be a use of cash and turn cash flow positive in 2022.
finding: This was a dated cash commitment, and he kept it: 2022 free cash flow came in at +$2.3B (reported January 2023).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & Corporate Audit and CFO
quote: In the short time I've been here, the priorities couldn't be more clear: Deliver for our customers, drive the highest levels of safety, quality and stability in all we do, innovate for the future and generate positive, sustainable free cash flow.
finding: On his first call he adopted the house ranking: customers, safety, quality and stability first, then innovation, with sustainable free cash flow as the financial goal.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: With this backdrop, we think of 2022 in 3 parts. First, we'll focus on reaching key milestones so that we can resume 737 deliveries to Chinese customers and restart 787 deliveries.
finding: Instead of numeric guidance he set out a year gated by milestones (787 restart, China MAX), and gave numbers only once those milestones were met.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It is important to keep in mind that from an economic standpoint, cash margins on the 787 remain positive.
finding: He reframes accounting charges in cash terms to soften bad news. He repeats the line quarter after quarter on the 787.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It's not a smidge over 0, I promise you that. And we're not going to be as descriptive as you might want.
finding: He uses colloquial assurances ('I promise you') in place of numbers, and says openly that he is holding back detail.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we now anticipate 787 abnormal costs will be approximately $2 billion, with most being incurred by the end of 2023. This estimate increased by approximately $1 billion from last quarter due to the additional rework requirements and lower production rates continuing longer than previously expected.
finding: One quarter after giving it, he doubled the 787 abnormal-cost estimate. He reset the number openly and put the cause on scope (rework) and on duration.
response: estimate raised ~$1B to ~$2B

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We are still anticipating delivery of the first airplane in late 2023.
finding: In January 2022 he held the 777X first delivery at late 2023. Three months later he moved it to 2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: While this effort has inevitably impacted our deliveries to customers and our near-term financial performance, we are fully confident it is the right thing to do for our future.
finding: He presented the 787 delivery halt and the $3.5B charge as a long-term investment in quality rather than as a failure.
response: accepts near-term cost for conformance

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We don't have the time frame, but we think that the first step is getting the first one out the door.
finding: He refuses to give dates for regulator-gated events and commits only to the next concrete step.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: the supply chain is currently not a constraint. However, as we look forward to the industry recovering and future production rate increases, our supply chain remains a key watch item due to raw material and labor availability as well as logistical challenges.
finding: Early 2022 he described the supply chain as only a watch item. Within months it became his main explanation for missed delivery targets.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: one priority is to take leverage down, but also a priority is to make sure we're going to be ready to invest in that next airplane at the right moment. ... nothing would suggest we wouldn't want to be investors for the right airplane.
finding: He treats deleveraging and keeping the means to fund a future new airplane as two priorities that must be kept in balance, but leaves the timing open ('at the right moment').

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I think recency effect, it seems like it's in that $10 billion to $12 billion, but it's too hard to tell right now given it's a dynamic world.
finding: He put the minimum cash needed to run Boeing at about $10-12B, a liquidity floor that limits how much cash can be deployed.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: As we manage the company for cash flow, we're adjusting our 777-9 production rate, including a temporary pause due 2023. This move will minimize inventory, reduce the number of airplanes requiring change in corporation and avoid capitalizing costs on the balance sheet. ... We believe this is the best allocation of resources and cash.
finding: He met the 777X slip by pausing production to protect cash and limit rework inventory, and accepted about $1.5B of abnormal costs to do so.
response: pause 777-9 production

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Based on an updated assessment of the time required to meet certification requirements, we now anticipate delivery of the first 777-9 airplane in 2025.
finding: He reset the 777X first delivery from late 2023 to 2025, about two years, one quarter after reaffirming late 2023, and blamed the certification process.
response: EIS moved late-2023 -> 2025

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we're doing everything we can to complete the certification of the MAX 7 and MAX 10 and ensure their respective first deliveries this year and next.
finding: He committed to MAX 7 first delivery in 2022 and MAX 10 in 2023. By October 2023 neither was certified; MAX 7 had moved to 2023 and MAX 10 to 2024.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We don't need the 10. Believe me, the demand is there. ... for us is to stay focused on that production rate of 31 a month and make it stable and dependable and reliable.
finding: He takes the MAX 10 out of the near-term plan and puts stable rate execution ahead of product breadth.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: given the robust market for freighters, we're leveraging this production pause on the 777-9 to add 777 freighter aircraft in the 2023 to 2026 time frame.
finding: He filled the 777X gap with the legacy 777 freighter, using spare capacity to follow demand for the older airplane.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: all we contemplate having a similar type CapEx levels in the $1 billion, $1.5 billion range, I think it's what it's been historically. ... We have lots of calls on our R&D capital because we are opportunity rich with ideas. What our job is to make sure that we focus in narrowing on the right ones.
finding: He kept capex at its historical $1-1.5B and framed R&D as a rationing job: narrow many ideas down to the right few.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But I will tell you, we are on the verge of turning the corner. We're on the verge of turning the corner and once we do, Boeing is going to do what Boeing does best, which is deliver great airplanes and defense products for our customers.
finding: A signature phrase of 2022 was 'turning the corner', used as confidence language before milestones were reached.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We don't need to tap into our credit lines to fully open. We don't need to take on more debt. We don't need to issue more equity. What we need to is hit those silver milestones, generate stable cash flow.
finding: This is his most categorical 'no equity, no new debt' statement, and it rests on hitting operating milestones. Whether it held is outside this slice, which ends October 2023.

numbers.commitment: no equity, no new debt, no revolver draw

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I can't give you a date. FAA decides, but there continues to be good momentum and people are hard at work. If it was a resource issue, we would have put it on a long time ago.
finding: On the 787 recertification he deferred to the FAA on timing and stressed that money was not the constraint.
response: defer to regulator; no date

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But when we take rate up, it will be a function of our confidence in our supply chain, not the demand signals that you're pointing to.
finding: His rule for raising rates is explicit: supply-chain readiness decides, not the size of the backlog.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But we don't want to do it too quickly. I think, historically, we might have done that before, and it didn't pan out so well. So we just want to make sure stability and discipline are our calling cards and the rate will go up and the demand is there.
finding: He refers to past over-fast ramps as a lesson and makes 'stability and discipline' the condition for any rate increase.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we have to be committed to take a page from the automotive playbook and be willing to slow things down, or in some cases, just pause if all the parts aren't there. Because we can't go back to a world where we are traveling lots of work.
finding: He backed the CEO's rule against travelled work: stop the line rather than build out of sequence, even at the cost of monthly deliveries.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It is delivering 87s. It is delivering more 37s, including ones in China, and sustainably generating cash flow. Those 3 things are the most important elements that we think about day in and day out.
finding: In mid-2022 he narrowed priorities to three operating milestones tied to cash: the 787 restart, MAX deliveries including China, and sustained cash flow.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: given where we're at and probably for a long time, that's the #1 metric that we're all focused on, and that is through the lens of all of our decision-making.
finding: He makes free cash flow the single lens for decisions 'for a long time'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I know that it has some short-term uneasiness, but it's the right decision because that's going to be on for decades.
finding: He defended the 777X delay as an investment in a program that will last decades and accepted the near-term cost.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: the lessons that we learned on the development programs will be ones that we think about how to get better on the bidding process. ... We had issues, took the medicine, move on.
finding: After the fixed-price defense charges he took the losses and drew a bidding lesson. That lesson hardened by 2023 into 'no appetite' for fixed-price development.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: one of the things that Dave has done as he's come in is trying to move all of the decision-making accountability out to the business units and have a much smaller center.
finding: He describes Calhoun's model as decision rights pushed out to the business units with a small corporate center, and backs it.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We now expect delivery to be closer to the low 400s for 2022, short of what we discussed earlier this year as we drive stability and predictability.
finding: He cut the 2022 MAX delivery outlook midyear and blamed the shortfall on putting stability first. He cut again to about 375 in October; actual was 387.
trigger: supply chain, storage flow time, China
response: 2022 737 outlook cut to low 400s

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Given this uncertainty with our customers in China, we now expect more deliveries of airplanes from inventory to shift into 2024.
finding: He formally walked back the 'most inventory delivered by end-2023' target he set in October 2021, nine months later.
response: inventory unwind pushed into 2024

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: To stabilize production and support our supply chain, we're increasing our on-site presence at suppliers, creating teams of experts to address industry-wide shortages, utilizing internal fabrication for search capacity and managing inventory safety stock levels and growing where needed.
finding: His supply-chain response was to put people and inventory into it: on-site teams, in-house fabrication and larger safety stocks, all paid for with working capital.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: With more than 90% share of the freighter market, our lineup is well positioned to capture continued growth.
finding: He presents freighters as a Boeing stronghold where Airbus is not yet a real factor, and builds 777F and 777-8F decisions on that dominance.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Our playbook on capital structure is very straightforward. We deliver airplanes. We generate cash flow. We invest in the organic priorities for the program development, and we pay down debt. It doesn't get any more complicated.
finding: His signature capital-allocation sequence is deliver, generate cash, invest organically, pay down debt. No buybacks or M&A are in it.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So it's a turnaround, make no mistake about it. Some things are going well, and some things are in front of us.
finding: From late 2022 he labels the company openly as 'a turnaround', which lets him explain slips as normal in a turnaround.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: As I think about what normal looks like, for all of you, that would include what we used to have as a credit rating, which was -- which is A-ish range. And there's nothing to suggest that we can't get there.
finding: He set the long-term aim of restoring an A-range credit rating through deleveraging, a goal with no date.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And we talk about when you're going to ramp the rate? Well, when we stabilize on 31. And when there is a moment when we can sit together with our CFM partners and get confidence that we have a delivery schedule that is attainable, and you might have that discussion, but we're not there yet.
finding: A rate increase requires two things: stable output at the current rate and a joint, attainable schedule with the engine supplier.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we have deferred decisions on those planes for a long time. We can't defer that decision forever. So we will begin to remarket some of those airplanes that were otherwise earmarked for our Chinese customers. And we don't do that lightly.
finding: He waited for China as long as he could, then switched to remarketing aircraft for investors' sake. He reports 55 remarketed by July 2023.
response: begin remarketing China-built MAX

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So if I were to call out one bright spot, it would be demand. So overall demand, pretty robust. It's holding up. it's resilient, and that's good for our customers. That's good for our industry, and we see that continuing. So this is not a demand question. This is much more of a supply.
finding: He repeatedly calls Boeing's problem one of supply, not demand, so production capability is what binds.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We still are aiming at our full year target. There's risk in that. But the risk, if we didn't quite get there, is more disappointing our customers. Cash flow will be fine either way.
finding: He keeps the cash commitment separate from the delivery target, so a delivery miss is a customer problem and not a cash-guidance problem.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Because what's important is that this exemption was always intended to include the Dash 7 and the Dash 10, no mistake about it. And if you think about the customer view and our view, is that the commonality of the 737 family is important, and it enhances safety.
finding: He argued publicly for a legislative extension of the MAX 7/10 certification deadline, framing family commonality as a safety benefit.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The real gating item though that we're focused on are the engines on the 37. The engines are behind. CFM has been very collaborative.
finding: He names the CFM LEAP engine supply as the binding constraint on the 737 but keeps the tone collaborative toward GE/Safran.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Now the acceleration will not be as significant as previously anticipated, and our path to recovery is taking a bit longer than expected driven by the challenging macro environment.
finding: He gave this reset of the recovery pace in mild terms and put the cause mainly on the external macro environment.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we feel confident this particular quarter, it really was the recognition of the very rapidly changing environment that is persistent, and can't assume it's going to get better anytime soon.
finding: He took $2.8B of defense charges as a deliberate 'derisk' to reset assumptions and stop assuming conditions would improve.
response: $2.8B charges across 5 fixed-price programs

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And then we also, at the same time, want to continue to invest in the business. $3.5 billion of R&D and $2 billion of CapEx, very much in line with what the business historically done.
finding: He built R&D and capex at historical levels into the long-range plan, not cut to reach the $10B target.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And then any excess cash that we have, we will point towards accelerating debt paydown because investment grade remains a priority for the company.
finding: Excess cash goes to debt reduction before any shareholder return, to protect the investment-grade rating.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: You want realistic and achievable financial metrics, and that is what we intend to do with that range. We believe that the low end is 3. We're aiming at 5.
finding: He guides with a wide range whose floor he treats as the commitment and whose top is aspirational.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Operating cash flow for next year will be between $4.5 billion and $6.5 billion. We'll then reinvest $1.5 billion back into the business through CapEx to get us to free cash flow in the $3 billion to $5 billion range.
finding: His first full-year guide (2023 FCF $3-5B) slid by October 2023 to 'more towards the low end'. The final 2023 result is outside this slice.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The 3,7 deliveries will be somewhere between 400 and 450. Now again, as we try to bound the bottom and give you a high confident set of projections, 400 means that basically next year, all year, we're in the low 30s of deliveries.
finding: He called the 400 floor 'high confident'. By October 2023 the range had been cut to 375-400, below that floor.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And $10 billion reflects our attention to get this place back to normal post the turnaround back to normal, back to the pre-2019 representation. Underlying that assumption of $10 billion, a couple of important points. Revenue for the company will be approximately $100 billion and operating margins of approximately 10%.
finding: His central long-range commitment was about $10B FCF on about $100B revenue and about 10% margin in 2025-26. He reaffirmed it every quarter through October 2023.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The 3,7 in this forecast gets to about 50 a month, which we've done before. The 8,7 gets back to 10 -- gets to 10 a month, and the 777, 777 MAX gets to 4 a month.
finding: He committed to production rates for 2025-26: 737 at 50/month, 787 at 10/month and 777/777X at 4/month, justifying them by past peaks.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On capital structure, the playbook for us is very straightforward: deliver airplanes, generate cash, pay down debt. And I reiterate what Dave said. There's no need and no plans to raise any kind of capital from either the debt or the equity markets. We don't need to.
finding: At Investor Day he restated, with Calhoun, that Boeing would not raise equity or debt. It was the firmest public form of that pledge.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It was 500 at the beginning of this year. And we thought China had a shot at opening up in February, and we also had contemplated a rate increase. ... So we all learned that painfully. ... we try to be a little bit grounded in terms of the numbers that we gave you
finding: He admitted that the 2022 MAX plan of about 500 was badly missed (387 actual) and said he now discounts China and rate assumptions when guiding.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So I just want to be careful that we're not talking ourselves into all of a sudden taking our numbers up. We want to make sure we have the proof points in order for us to make that decision with enough lead time for the engine suppliers, et cetera.
finding: He requires proof points before committing to rate increases and corrected colleagues to stop the market assuming a ramp date.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Free cash flow, our primary financial metric, it's been that for all of this year and as long as Dave has been here.
finding: He confirms free cash flow, not EPS or margin, as Boeing's primary financial metric under Calhoun.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: our priorities are crystal clear. We have to stabilize the business through the course of this turnaround. We have to drive productivity. We have to return value and return value primarily restore that balance sheet.
finding: His ranking is stabilise, then productivity, then 'return value', where returning value means repairing the balance sheet first.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On the 737, that one will be a little bit more pressured largely because, we do have the conversation that we owe customers for the late deliveries as well as we have some customer mix that's going to be unfavorable. So that won't get quite back to the 2018 time frame, margin level.
finding: He says MAX program economics are permanently dented by delay concessions and mix, while the 787 is expected to exceed its prior margins.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: 2020 was a usage of $20 billion of cash, 2021 improved but was still a usage of $4 billion of cash, in 2022, $2.3 billion positive.
finding: He delivered on his October 2021 promise of positive 2022 free cash flow ($2.3B, above the $1.5-2.0B Investor Day estimate).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So production rate at the right moment could get higher. We'll wait and see. We're just going to stick to the range for now.
finding: He holds guidance ranges even when there is upside and would rather wait for evidence than raise early.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: No, no that's not in the playbook. ... the growth has got to be accretive to profit, and it's got to be relatively capital light. And having been in the world before, you can chase revenue and really regret you did, and it wouldn't be good for any of us as investors.
finding: He dropped his predecessors' $50B services revenue goal and set capital-light, profit-accretive growth as the test, citing his own experience.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Similarly, in the commercial side, we're looking to take our rate up, particularly on the 37 from today what's 31 to 50 and on the 87 from which low today to 10. So all of that ramp will happen over the course of the next 2 years.
finding: He committed to taking the 737 from 31 to 50 and the 787 to 10 within about two years (by 2025). The slice ends with the 737 still moving to 38.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So 7, first has been working very hard with the FAA. Our teams can't -- won't predict a time line of a date certain, but a lot of activity and a lot of confidence that, that will get done this year.
finding: He expressed confidence in MAX 7 certification in 2023, after the earlier 2022 date was missed. By October 2023 he reported 'no change' and it had still not happened.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So the good news is that as we think about going from here to there, we have line of sight, and we just have to execute. We just have to go execute. There's no what-ifs in there.
finding: He said the $10B 2025-26 target had 'no what-ifs', a strong certainty claim set against later delivery and defense slips in 2023.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So it's not unprecedented. I acknowledge that the increase is sporty. But we've been looking at this, and there's a lot of confidence that that's the right number. What's important is that, on that 38 for us, the factory space is there. The tooling is there, and the labor is there, right?
finding: He defends the large 31-to-38 step by saying Boeing's own space, tooling and labor are ready and that the risk sits in the supply chain.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And while you can never eliminate risk, we did our very best on the very big assumptions to retire as much risk as we could. And we feel very good about where we are in terms of those products
finding: He said the Q3 2022 charges had retired the fixed-price risk. More charges followed on the tanker (Q1), Commercial Crew, MQ-25 and T-7A (Q2) and the VC-25B (Q3 2023).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We're putting billions in R&D, and we'll spend more R&D money this year than last year, and we'll spend more R&D next year than this year.
finding: Even during the turnaround he committed to rising R&D, spent on capabilities, without launching a new airplane.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: One of those values was transparency. And I have learned over the last 18 months, how important that transparent culture is to our company and is to our industry. And it's not always easy. It -- sometimes it's painful.
finding: He adopted transparency as a working value, linked to the CEO, and uses it to explain disclosing problems early.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And as you know, my accounting doesn't allow me to account for unknowns. So I will deal with it. We'll deal with it. And we'll be fine.
finding: He explains repeated defense charges as accounting that cannot anticipate surprises, and stays matter-of-fact about them.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And again, this word I've said it probably 1,000 times we just got to go execute on that. In terms of what a return to capital discussion might look like, too early. But it'll be there someday.
finding: 'Execute' is his signature word. He keeps deferring shareholder returns until execution is proven.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: An issue was identified. It was escalated quickly. It was reviewed with our regulator and ultimately resolved. That's what we have to do, and I think that all makes us better, and it's behind us, and we're moving forward.
finding: He describes a standard quality-escape sequence (identify, escalate, review with the regulator, resolve) and presents the 787 pause as the system working.
response: pause, regulator review, resume

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: In terms of vertical integration, it's not something that we're focused on. We're focused on stability, and that is job one.
finding: In March 2023 he rejected vertical integration as a remedy for the supply chain. Within this slice Boeing instead advanced cash and signed new commercial terms with Spirit.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we don't want to do thing niche. We want to do something that is step function changing of how our customers are going to be -- get more efficiency, and we'll be better. And right now, anything on that front is next decade, and we've been consistent with that.
finding: His test for a new airplane is a step change in efficiency, not a niche product, and he timed it for the next decade.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I would say, in terms of intervention and investments, so we have put inventory buffer stocks and certain spots to make sure we have stability, predictability, that's all contemplated in our forward look on cash. And even if I had to do a little more of that to get more stable, I'd make that trade and we'd still be fine.
finding: He will spend working capital on buffer inventory to buy stability. Stability outranks short-term cash.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Believe me, there is a different risk tolerance for underwriting in the company, got new team members, new leader of the business. And together as a team, we are getting very clear eyed about risk we're willing to take and not willing to take. And fixed price development work is something that we have no appetite to take.
finding: This is his clearest risk threshold: no new fixed-price development contracts.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Yes. I'm not sure I agree with all of that. But here's what I think about the narrow-body. So the MAX is sold firm through 2026, very good demand. Where we go on the Dash 8, Dash 9 on the MAX competes very well, right? It performs very well. Customers love the airplane, holds its own.
finding: Asked why Boeing does not answer Airbus's narrowbody gains with a new jet, he disputed the premise and pointed to the MAX backlog.
response: defend MAX family, no new jet now

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: it's clearly big enough, bigger than just 1 can handle, right? So we think there's a role in there for the competitors to play. And by the way, the C919, it's not a new competitive entry. We've known about that. We are comfortable with that. Market's big. Let's go compete and win.
finding: He plays down COMAC's C919 as an expected entrant in a China market big enough for several suppliers.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Still a lot of bureaucracy in the company, lot of bureaucracy. And bureaucracy slows everything down, and we are focused on streamlining. I have every intention to try to make the center small and what that means is getting rid of all the nonvalue stuff that corporate functions put upon companies.
finding: He saw corporate bureaucracy as a drag on speed and made shrinking the center part of his own agenda.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I want to work with third-party partners that are better at doing certain things than we'll ever be. ... more engineers, more mechanics, more quality, more supply chain. That's what matters. And I have no problem making that trade all day every day.
finding: He would outsource non-core corporate work and move the savings into engineering, mechanics and quality.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We're supporting Spirit through this recovery, including manufacturing and engineering resources as well as a cash advance. To support overall supply chain stability, we're not changing the master schedule, including anticipated production rate increases and we've contemplated any near-term parts inventory builds into our forward look.
finding: His response to the Spirit vertical-fin escape was to fund and staff the supplier and keep the supply-chain master schedule unchanged so the ramp stayed on track.
response: cash advance, resources, master schedule held

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So when you -- I'll shake that all out, high conviction on the low end of that range of the $3 billion. Is the upper end a bit pressured? Sure. But we have more time to go in the year, and we are committed to delivering that range.
finding: He resets expectations inside the range: 'high conviction on the low end' signals the likely outcome without cutting guidance.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And in terms of the costs, just as a reminder, the cost of this rework was immaterial, and it was booked in the first quarter in our closing position.
finding: He plays down the financial size of quality escapes ('immaterial', 'nonmaterial') to separate operational disruption from the P&L.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Sure. It's all about cash. Yes, I'm for that.
finding: A signature remark: he moves any margin question onto cash.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: current environment, it's pretty good for price realization. And why is that? Because you see the skyline, the deliveries keep moving to the right, which is a good dynamic. We will be disciplined on this topic. ... But I also remind you that every campaign, we compete head to head, and that's the nature of our business.
finding: He sees industry-wide delivery slips, which also hit Airbus, as supporting pricing, but warns that every campaign is head-to-head.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we've lowered our total estimate from $1.5 billion to $1 billion, which reflects plans to resume production later this year rather than early 2024.
finding: This is one of the few cost estimates he cut: 777X abnormal costs came down when he chose to restart production earlier.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Year-to-date, we've repaid $5.1 billion of debt, which is essentially all of our maturities for the year.
finding: He kept his commitment to meet 2023 maturities from cash rather than refinance, with gross debt down to $52.3B.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And then as we exit the year and moving over into the first quarter of next year, those margins will move positive. We're confident in that.
finding: He made a dated promise that BCA operating margins would turn positive by end-2023 or Q1 2024. By October 2023 it had softened to 'in 2024'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: In light of this progress, we are now transitioning production to 38 per month and still plan to increase to 50 per month in the '25, '26 time frame. As we move to the higher rate, we'll continue to prioritize stability, and it will take some time to consistently deliver at 38 per month off the line.
finding: He approved the 38 rate break only after proof points (49 deliveries in June, rework restarted) and warned that output would lag the nominal rate.
response: move to 38/month

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: This includes 85 for customers in China and 55 that have now been remarketed as part of the plan we've previously discussed.
finding: He followed through on the remarketing decision of September 2022: 55 China-built MAX had been placed with other customers.
response: 55 aircraft remarketed

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So I'll take the last one. Our Defense margins have to get better next year, period, full stop.
finding: On defense margins he moved from patience to a flat demand for improvement in 2024.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: In terms of the cash level to run the business, I think $10 billion has always been the number that we've been comfortable with, and I don't see big changes in that.
finding: He restated a minimum operating cash balance of about $10B.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But in terms of what capital deployment looks like once we get out with evidence on that '25/'26 time frame, that's all a discussion that we look forward to have with our investors and our Board, and it's just premature at that time.
finding: Capital returns stay deferred until there is evidence that the 2025-26 targets are met. The Board decides, and he does not pre-commit.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And these are frustrating moments for our customers, for our investors and for our teams. If I think about it, on one hand, it does reflect the transparent culture we're driving. Someone raised their hand, whether it's Boeing or in supply chain and said, something doesn't look right, and that's important.
finding: He presents a quality escape as evidence of a healthy speak-up culture, which owns the problem while giving it a positive spin.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we still are committed to the long-term financial targets that we set out in November of last year at our Investor Day, $10 billion of free cash flow, 50 737 deliveries per month, 10 787 per month in the '25/'26 time frame. So that remains unchanged.
finding: Even after a second Spirit escape he held all the Investor Day targets unchanged, showing he holds long-range commitments steady through near-term shocks.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It will impact about 75% of the 220 airplanes that were inventory -- that were in inventory as of the end of the second quarter. So it's large. In the near term, it will impact deliveries, but we have no intention of changing the master schedule.
finding: On the aft pressure bulkhead escape he again accepted the delivery hit but would not slow the supply chain's master schedule.
response: rework; master schedule unchanged

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And longer term, as we've said before, and we think about that long-range financial framework that we put together in the '25/'26 time frame, we always did that ex China.
finding: He builds plans with uncertain political upside left out (ex-China), a conservative way to underwrite targets.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Yes. I'm not quite there on the upside. I think that the $10 billion reflects a set of assumptions that we feel very confident in and we think are ones -- are numbers that we have ability to meet. When we get closer to that, perhaps we'll relook.
finding: He refused to raise the $10B target toward pre-2019 levels and kept it as the base case he could defend.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: that range of call it, $3 billion, $4-ish billion of R&D, that's going to modestly go up over the next couple of years, but it's not going to do anything to disrupt our free cash flow target.
