finding: He accepted rising R&D for the 777X and 777-8F as compatible with the cash target and called higher R&D 'good news'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: These are disappointing results in the quarter and year-to-date. This performance is below our expectations, and we acknowledge that we aren't as far along in this recovery as we expected to be at this stage.
finding: On defense he plainly owned the miss ('disappointing', 'below our expectations') and then set out a recovery plan.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Considering these latest facts, we expect October deliveries to be in line with September and now expect to deliver between 375 and 400 airplanes for the year.
finding: He cut the 2023 MAX delivery guide below the Investor Day floor of 400 that he had called 'high confident'.
response: 2023 737 guide cut to 375-400

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We still expect most of the MAX inventory aircraft to be delivered by the end of 2024, but more are likely to slip into 2025 tied to the fuselage recovery.
finding: This was the fifth revision of the MAX inventory unwind target since October 2021 (end-2023 at first, now partly 2025).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The total estimate is now $3 billion, up a bit, and we still expect to be largely done by year-end.
finding: The 787 abnormal estimate ended at $3B, three times his first figure of about $1B (October 2021), and he called the latest rise 'up a bit'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I will tell you, in 2024, we expect margins to be positive, and that's going to be underwritten by 2 things primarily BCA.
finding: The BCA margin promise moved from 'exit 2023/Q1 2024' (July) to 'in 2024' (October), a quiet loosening of the date.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The overall financial outlook for 2023 is unchanged from what we previously shared, including $3 billion to $5 billion of free cash flow generation, although the updated 737 deliveries now point more towards the low end of the free cash flow range.
finding: He walked 2023 FCF to the low end of the $3-5B range without formally cutting it. The final result is outside this slice.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Importantly, as Dave mentioned, we recently reached an agreement with Spirit on commercial terms associated with the 737 and 787 programs. We believe this agreement is a win-win for both companies and directly promotes our goal to drive stability and support our airline customers.
finding: He supported renegotiated commercial terms with Spirit, effectively paying for supplier stability.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: the system, as Dave mentioned, has always maintained to be hot because we want to make sure that they know that the demand cycle is there. And we want them to continue focus on that master schedule.
finding: He keeps the supply chain 'hot' at the planned rate even when Boeing's own output falls short, accepting inventory build to protect the ramp.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Perhaps most importantly, we instituted much tighter underwriting standards. As you know, part of the challenge we're dealing with are legacy contracts that we need to get out from under. Rest assured, we haven't signed any fixed price development contracts nor intend to.
finding: He made the ban on fixed-price development contracts explicit and kept to it: none signed under his tenure to date.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And in terms of the $10 billion, we always built that with some understanding that not every piece was going to go exactly correct, there were going to be some puts and takes. And we provide ourselves the room with which we could have certain things not go quite perfectly.
finding: He says contingency was built into the $10B target, which let him absorb the defense shortfalls without changing it.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Our investment-grade credit rating continues to be a priority. And we're developing -- deploying capital in line with the projects we've shared previously: invest in the business and pay down debt.
finding: In the first call after the door plug, West's capital order was the investment-grade rating first, then reinvestment and paying down debt, with no shareholder returns on the list.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: While we're postponing issuing 2024 guidance today, given our current focus, we're committed to sharing timely and transparent updates moving forward.
finding: Faced with the regulator's production cap, West withheld annual guidance entirely rather than publish a range he might have to cut.
trigger: Alaska Airlines 1282 door-plug blowout (2024-01-05) and FAA cap on 737 output at 38/month
response: no 2024 guidance issued

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Yes, we've cycled to 38 per month. We said that. Keep in mind, it always takes time for that to equate it to deliveries, but we're not firing blanks.
finding: His confidence language is colloquial and defensive ('we're not firing blanks'), asserting that the production rate is real even while deliveries lag.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But out of respect for the process that we need to go through the FAA, I just got to steer away from specificity. It's just not the right time.
finding: He used respect for the regulator's process as the reason to refuse numbers, a pattern repeated through 2024.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We're still confident in the goals we laid out for '25, '26 although it may take longer in that window than originally anticipated, and we won't rush the system.
finding: West kept the November 2022 $10bn free-cash-flow goal but softened its timing; the slice shows it pushed 'quite a bit' to the right by September 2024, and 2024 free cash flow ended at minus $14.3bn.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And we're just going to move through this year with real focus in order to be in a position where we start shutting these shadow factories down. And then we're just going to run that play as hard as we can.
finding: Shutting the 737 and 787 rework 'shadow factories' was a fixed 2024 objective, described in his playbook terms ('run that play').

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And in terms of the timeline, I would go back to what we said at earnings, which it will be inside of a year. ... But I wouldn't try to suggest that it's any sooner than 9 months. I think it's between that 9- to 12-month range that we talked about in earnings.
finding: He committed to a 9-12 month fix for the MAX engine anti-ice problem; in July 2025 he said the fix 'has taken us longer' and moved MAX 7/10 certification to 2026.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But when you get out to our time frame of '25, '26, you have a 37 cash margin profile that gets back pretty close to what it was in the '18 time frame. You have a 87 cash margin profile that will be better than what it was in the '18 time frame largely driven by the -10 model mix.
finding: West forecast that 737 cash margins would return close to 2018 levels and 787 margins would beat them by 2025-26; by September 2024 he said both were still 'lower than where they were in 2018'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We kind of kick off negotiations with the IAM in March. The contract expires in September. And we fully expect to get to a point where we have an agreement and work constructively with our partners in IAM.
finding: West was confident of a negotiated IAM deal; members rejected it and struck in September 2024, and the slice shows the factory did not restart until December.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Broadly speaking, on the BDS profile on margins, we still expect them to get to the high single-digit level as we think about our long-term '25, '26 time frame.
finding: His defense-margin commitment was high single digits by 2025-26; BDS then posted minus 15.2% and minus 43.1% margins in 2Q and 3Q 2024, and by 2025 the target had become 'medium to longer term'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But we take full accountability for what's happened here. And we have a comprehensive view of how we go in and help the factory get to a different spot and strengthen quality. And the FAA has increased oversight, and we welcome it.
finding: After the door plug, West's stance was full accountability and welcoming the FAA's tighter oversight rather than resisting it.
trigger: Alaska Airlines 1282 door-plug blowout (2024-01-05) and FAA cap on 737 output at 38/month
response: accept accountability; welcome FAA audit

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So broadly speaking, the cost of an airplane, 60% to 70% are parts. On the labor side, it's less than 15%, and that's touch labor, that's support labor and that's engineering resources.
finding: West's cost model of an airplane: parts dominate and labour is a minor share, which he used to size the exposure to the IAM negotiation.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I view it, yes, as a productivity benefit but it's dwarfed by the quality benefit. By having less traveled work, it's more predictable, it's more steady, it's more repeatable, it's higher quality. And that is our focus.
finding: After the door plug, a finance chief publicly ranked quality above productivity in justifying the cut in traveled work.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So when you consider the resilience of demand and not necessarily having to "worry about that" then you focus all the attention on delivering on the supply side, and that's where we're squarely focused.
finding: West treated demand as a given and put all of his attention on supply, a supply-constrained worldview that shapes his rate and inventory choices.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So holding the rate is a chance for us to double down in stability. ... So it's an investment that we'll make, and we think it's a good investment. And if inventory spikes as it will this year, we feel like we can handle it from a cash flow perspective.
finding: West accepted balance-sheet strain, letting inventory spike while suppliers kept building to the master schedule ('so be it', January), in exchange for a more stable base for future rate breaks.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: They've been knocked around by a variety of supply chain and labor issues that we have to sort our way out for contracts that were written in a different economic environment. ... The good news is, is that we will lapse those contracts in this period, and we'll be able to underwrite it with tighter underwriting disciplines
finding: West blamed defense losses on fixed-price contracts priced in a different economic environment, and made 'tighter underwriting' the remedy.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And it's not going to be outside the envelope of the financials I described. ... And I'll close with, well, we spent $5 billion between R&D and CapEx in 2023. That was 20% plus higher than it was the previous year. So we are investing, and we're ready to do it. What it actually looks like? Too soon to say.
finding: Future-airplane technology spending had to fit within the existing financial envelope; no launch-scale spending was signalled.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We've gotten a bit tighter on capital allocation. We are very focused on accretive offerings, particularly ones that are heavy and intellectual property. And we've also decided no longer to chase aspirational targets that might chase market share.
finding: In services he favoured margin and intellectual-property-heavy offerings over share-driven growth targets.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Yes, we put the customers in a tight spot. The most important thing we do is communicate with them.
finding: On customer harm he admitted it directly and stressed communication over any denial.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And I will say that if a transaction were to occur, we would not use equity, right? We would fund it with a mix of cash and debt.
finding: West ruled out equity for a Spirit deal; in July 2024 Boeing agreed to buy Spirit in an all-stock transaction and later raised $24bn of equity.

numbers.outcome: all-stock Spirit deal announced 2024-07-01 (~$4.7bn equity value)

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And in the quarter, our free cash flow will be a usage of somewhere between $4 billion and $4.5 billion, and that's higher than we originally planned back in January. ... So the full year free cash flow is expected to be in the low single-digit billions of free cash flow generation.
finding: West guided 2024 to positive free cash flow in the low single-digit billions; in May he reset it to a cash use, and 2024 ended at minus $14.3bn.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But we expect BC margins to get better through the year. They'll still be negative in 2024. But if we run the business for the long term, we believe that those margins are going to get to historical levels in the '25, '26 timeframe
finding: West forecast that BCA margins would recover to historical levels by 2025-26; BCA margins were still negative through 2025 (minus 6.6% in 1Q, minus 5.1% in 2Q).

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We ungrounded the entire MAX fleet. We went from producing 0 737s to getting to a rate of the low to mid-30s. ... And it turns out, all of that wasn't enough, and we were reminded of that on January 5.
finding: West conceded that the 2021-23 recovery work had been insufficient, framing the door plug as a reminder rather than an isolated escape.
trigger: Alaska Airlines 1282 door-plug blowout (2024-01-05) and FAA cap on 737 output at 38/month

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But we won't rush or go too fast. In fact, we're deliberately going to slow to get this right. And we are the ones who made the decision to constrain rates on the 737 program below 38 per month until we feel like we're ready.
finding: West said Boeing itself had chosen to produce below the FAA's cap of 38, owning the slowdown as management's own decision.
trigger: Alaska Airlines 1282 door-plug blowout (2024-01-05) and FAA cap on 737 output at 38/month
response: 737 output held below 38/month

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: In fact, starting on March 1 of this year, we no longer travel work between Wichita and our fuselage supplier and Renton. It had been going on too long. So now we will only accept a fully conforming fuselage from Spirit, which means in the near term, there might be variability of supply.
finding: Boeing stopped accepting incomplete Spirit fuselages, knowingly trading near-term supply variability for conformance.
trigger: Alaska Airlines 1282 door-plug blowout (2024-01-05) and FAA cap on 737 output at 38/month
response: no traveled work accepted from Spirit from 2024-03-01

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The path to stable financials is a stable factory, and that's what we're focused on right now.
finding: A signature line: his financial targets were subordinated to factory stability.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We believe and Spirit believes that reintegrating these 2 companies is what's best for safety and for quality for the aerospace industry. We have conviction on that. And without going into the synergies and efficiencies, it's really about focus and running that business not as a business. It was a factory. Run it as a factory
finding: He justified buying Spirit on quality and control rather than synergies, saying Spirit should be run as a captive factory, not a standalone business.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: As it pertains to longer term, there needs to be advanced engine technology and aerodynamic investment in order to get an airplane that's 20% to 30% more efficient than we are today. And that will not be rushed.
finding: West's bar for a new airplane was a 20-30% efficiency gain that depends on new engine technology, and he stressed that it would not be rushed.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: rest assured that we have changed our underwriting standards in our defense business. We will not take on another fixed price development program.
finding: A hard risk threshold: no new fixed-price development contracts in defense.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: For years, we prioritized the movement of the airplane through the factory over getting it done right, and that's got to change.
finding: He openly diagnosed a cultural fault, schedule over conformance, and framed fixing it as a leadership priority.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I always leave specifics to the teams close to the work, but I believe there is a path to a fair and reasonable agreement.
finding: On labour bargaining West delegated to the negotiating teams and offered only optimism.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We're committed to managing the balance sheet in a prudent manner with two main objectives: one, prioritize the investment-grade rating; and two, allow the factory and supply chain to stabilize for a stronger trajectory as we exit this year.
finding: His standing two-part balance-sheet doctrine, which he repeated in near-identical words every quarter to 2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: First of all, it would restore our cash balance to the historical level that you point out, that $10 billion-ish. But it also means that we want to continue our practice to stay well ahead of our near-term maturities. And by near term, I mean roughly the next 12 months.
finding: His liquidity rules were a cash floor of about $10bn and pre-funding roughly 12 months of maturities.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We expect to achieve rate increases, including 10 per month by 2026.
finding: He committed to a 787 rate of 10 a month by 2026; by mid-2025 the program had only reached 7 a month.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Finally, on 777X. We continue to progress along the program time line and still expect first delivery in 2025.
finding: He held the 777X first-delivery date at 2025; it slipped to 2026 in October 2024 and to 2027 in October 2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Longer term, we remain confident in our ability to achieve $10 billion of free cash flow. ... this goal will take us longer than we originally planned and later in the '25, '26 window, primarily tied to the 737 and 787 production delivery ramps of 50 per month and 10 per month, respectively.
finding: The $10bn cash goal was tied to 737 at 50 a month and 787 at 10 a month; by October 2025 the 737 had reached only 38 with approval for 42.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: What our expectation is that over time that while these program margins won't get back to the 2018 levels, they will expand.
finding: Ten weeks after saying 737 cash margins would get 'pretty close' to 2018 levels, he conceded that program margins would not return to 2018 levels; the walk-back came without explicit acknowledgement.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Well, as we stand for what I described in terms of what we're looking at right now, working closely with the rating agencies, we believe we can do the move I described in the near term with market access without that.
finding: Asked whether equity was off the table, West said debt-market access would suffice; within six months Boeing had issued stock for Spirit and raised $24bn including equity.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We believe in the strategic logic of a deal, but we'll take the time needed to get this right before we decide to enter into agreement.
finding: On the Spirit acquisition he combined strategic conviction with patience on terms.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we coordinated with our customers and added more 8s and 9s into the skyline in the near term to mitigate impacts to their fleet needs and stabilize our production plans. And the program margin has been updated to reflect these impacts as well as the slower production ramp.
finding: With the MAX 7/10 delayed, he substituted MAX 8/9s to protect the production rate and took the margin hit.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Well, we've talked about we'll be -- arrive at the optimal funding. Nothing is off the table. We spent time with the rating agencies. And the most important thing is that we're going to maintain investment grade.
finding: Within two months he had moved from 'we would not use equity' to 'nothing is off the table', with the rating as the binding constraint.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Now I also recognize that this can be disruptive, both operationally and financially. And we will, at times, frustrate both our customers and our shareholders. But this is the right time, and this is the right set of actions to take.
finding: He delivered bad news by owning it in advance, warning that both customers and investors would be frustrated.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: as we enter 2025, we'll be more or less in the spot where we thought we were this year but with a much stronger foundation because of the work we're doing right now.
finding: He framed the setback as about a one-year slip; the strike and a $14.3bn cash use in 2024 made the reset larger.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We expect the full year now to be a use versus generation of cash flow.
finding: He reset 2024 free cash flow from a generation of low single-digit billions (March) to a cash use, ten weeks after the March guide.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And I understand everyone would wish it would go faster, but it's a long-cycle business and we have to be disciplined. We can't rush. We can't push the factory too hard or the system too hard because the payoff, if we do this right, is going to be big beyond 2025
finding: A patient, long-cycle style: he refused to push the factory despite investor impatience.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But we believe that we've got a path forward. We don't believe we need to make unnecessary trades.
finding: Despite delivery delays, he refused concessionary backlog 'trades', preferring to reshuffle delivery slots.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So the signals continue to be pretty good. And the product line holds up really well competitively. And we'll continue to compete campaign by campaign in this demand environment.
finding: West's competitive view was benign: he claimed the product line holds up well and treated competition as campaign by campaign, without naming Airbus.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I also think, importantly, we commend this colleague. This is exactly the kind of thing we want our people to do is raise their hand in an open culture if they see something that does not look right
finding: When a 787 employee flagged skipped conformance tests, West publicly praised the person who spoke up, signalling a speak-up culture.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And we tell them what we consistently said to everyone, the investment grade is the #1 priority. And as we regularly monitor our liquidity, if we are able to bump up against maturities we're going to do what it takes to protect that rating, period. And we've been consistent since April 2020 on that front
finding: His one unconditional commitment was to protect the investment-grade rating 'period', a stance he dated back to April 2020.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And we will not be shy or bashful with any investments that are needed in order for long-term stability.
finding: He signalled open-ended willingness to spend on Spirit after closing for the sake of stability.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Yes, David, I'm just not smart enough right at this moment to say whether it's $5 billion or $10 billion. As you know, as we ramp deliveries, it's pretty meaningful movement in our cash balance. So I'm going to steer away from trying to get more specific.
finding: He deflected a request for a cash-burn number with self-deprecation, and the year ended at a $14.3bn use.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: First, prioritize the investment grade rating; and second, allow the factory and supply chain to reset, both of which were supported by our decision to acquire Spirit with all stock financing.
finding: West recast the July 2024 all-stock Spirit purchase ($4.7bn equity value, $8.3bn EV) as serving the rating priority, reversing his March 2024 'we would not use equity': protecting the rating outranked the earlier statement.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On the free cash flow outlook for the year, we are now expecting a larger use of cash than previously forecasted.
finding: This was the second downward reset of 2024 cash guidance in four months, again given without a number.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So we feel good about the progress we've made, and we've got proof points that says we've got a real ability to hit our 38 per month as we exit the year.
finding: He committed to 38 a month on the 737 by the end of 2024; the strike intervened, and 38 was not reached until May 2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Now we also know that it will turn positive about a year after EIS as deliveries begin to ramp. And that will play out in a very normal way that most development programs play out.
finding: West's model of the 777X business case was a standard development-program J-curve, turning cash-positive about a year after entry into service.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So we are perfectly comfortable to supplement our liquidity position to support these two objectives. And we're constantly evaluating our capital structure and liquidity levels to ensure that we could satisfy our debt maturities over the next 18 months while keeping confidence in our credit rating as investment grade.
finding: During the strike his liquidity rule widened from 12 to 18 months of maturities covered, and he signalled a capital raise.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: This strike injects so much uncertainty, that is a very difficult question to answer, and I'm not going to do that today. ... So again, I won't try to predict it either for this year or next, it's just -- it's too soon. It's just too soon.
finding: Under acute uncertainty he withdrew from any forward numbers for 2024 or 2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We thought we had what was an unprecedented offer to hit the things that we knew or understood, members care about was around wage increases, around supplements to health care, supplements to retirement and job security. And we put our best foot forward, and that's what was unanimously endorsed until it wasn't.
finding: He admitted that management had misread the membership: an offer endorsed by union leadership was rejected by the workers.
trigger: IAM machinists rejected the contract and struck from 2024-09-13

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So the long-term fundamentals of the business that we've discussed and I've discussed over time, that hasn't changed. What's changed is it's moved to the right quite a bit.
finding: This was his first admission that the 2025-26 targets (the $10bn of free cash flow, BCA and BDS margins) had moved 'quite a bit' to the right; he kept the claim that the fundamentals were intact and stopped dating BDS's high-single-digit margin goal.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Near term, the 737 and the 787 cash margins are positive, but they're lower than where they were in 2018 from a variety of drivers, including lower production rates. ... And there's no magic here. We just have to execute.
finding: He conceded that cash margins were below 2018 levels while keeping the long-run return-to-2018 thesis; 'no magic... just execute' was a recurring line.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: strike will impact production and deliveries and operations and will jeopardize our recovery. So our immediate focus is to the laser-like focused on actions to conserve cash, and we will.
finding: On the first day of the strike West moved straight to conserving cash.
trigger: IAM machinists rejected the contract and struck from 2024-09-13
response: cash conservation actions

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we discovered damage on one of the thrust links on the flight test aircraft and immediately paused the flight test program. ... We have to give the team time to assess the situation and then a path forward.
finding: On the 777X thrust-link finding the response was an immediate pause and no schedule claim until the root cause was found; the delay later fed the 2026 slip.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And now based on where we are with the work stoppage, specifically for the non-787 programs, it will be very specific that if you're not behind, we have safety stock, don't deliver anymore.
finding: When cash became the constraint during the strike, he reversed the keep-suppliers-ahead policy and halted shipments from suppliers holding safety stock.
trigger: IAM machinists rejected the contract and struck from 2024-09-13
response: stop non-787 supplier shipments where safety stock exists

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The priorities for the company broadly are very clear. First, we've got to recover our commercial business. Secondly, we've got to bring stability and derisk our defense business. And third, our capital structure has to reflect the investment grade credit rating.
finding: His explicit ranking under the new CEO: recover commercial, then derisk defense, then a capital structure consistent with investment grade.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On the 777, we expect lower deliveries than last year, driven to a large extent by engine availability. That has been a constraint.
finding: He named the engine makers' supply as a binding widebody constraint, one of his few references to engine suppliers.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: new CEO is bringing different perspectives. And being from the industry and knowing the company, his instincts are spot on, and he's digging in deep for sure. ... He is focused on getting close to that factory floor, and that started from day 1, from day 1. So he is expecting that from all of us.
finding: West aligned publicly with Ortberg's factory-floor leadership style and said the whole leadership team was expected to follow it.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The actions we've recently taken, including establishing the universal shelf registration, which is now effective, directly support these priorities, and we have a plan to comprehensively address the balance sheet in the near term that could include an offering of equity and equity-linked securities.
finding: Once the rating was at risk he turned to issuing equity, the option he had ruled out in March; the $24bn raise closed in October and year-end cash was $26.3bn, including early repayment of a $3.5bn 2025 bond.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We're focused on maintaining $10 billion of cash in addition to our revolver capacity as we historically have.
finding: This restated his explicit cash floor: about $10bn plus undrawn revolvers.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: the $2.6 billion pretax charge primarily reflects our latest assessment of the certification time lines to address the delays in flight testing of the 777-9 as well as anticipated delays associated with the IAM work stoppage. ... and now expect first delivery in 2026.
finding: The 777X first delivery slipped from 2025 to 2026 with a $2.6bn charge, confirming that his reaffirmations in April-July 2024 had been wrong.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: As it pertains to 2025, 2025 free cash flow will be significantly better than 2024. And we expect the first half to be a cash usage and the second half to turn positive and then build real momentum as we exit the year
finding: He forecast that 2025 cash would be much better than 2024, turning positive in the second half; the slice shows 3Q25 at plus $238m and the full year guided to about minus $2.5bn, against minus $14.3bn in 2024.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We continue to take the tough but necessary actions to preserve cash and safeguard our future. We've worked across our supply chain partners to significantly reduce expenditures while balancing the associated trade-offs. We shared plans to reduce our workforce to align with our financial reality and a more focused set of priorities.
finding: He answered the strike-driven cash drain with supplier spending cuts, workforce reductions and lower discretionary spending.
trigger: IAM machinists rejected the contract and struck from 2024-09-13
response: supplier spend cuts, workforce reduction, discretionary cuts

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: CapEx investments stepped up last year and could increase by approximately $500 million in 2025 to support planned growth across both the commercial and defense businesses.
finding: Even while burning cash, he raised capex for growth, protecting investment in capacity.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So as we sit here today, we've got a lot of work in front of us. 2025, in some ways, could look like 2023, maybe a bit better if things go our way.
finding: He anchored 2025 expectations conservatively to 2023, with upside conditional on execution.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On the -7-10, inventory levels were stable at approximately 35 airplanes and testing on the anti-icing design solution is ongoing with certification expected to follow later in the year.
finding: He forecast MAX 7/10 certification in 2025; in July 2025 he moved it to 2026.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We are intent on ensuring the production system and the supply chain demonstrate stability prior to making the next increase on rates sometime this year.
finding: Gated rate increases: demonstrate stability first, then step up the rate. The 787 reached 7 a month by mid-2025.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: But in terms of the longer-term profile, the IAM agreement did put pressure. But keep in mind, we're talking about a cost that's less than 5% of the airplane.
finding: He sized the strike settlement as below 5% of airplane cost, small next to the productivity from closing the shadow factories.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: In terms of the inventory, we've got $87.5 billion worth of inventory in the company right now. That is too much. Now it's been an investment and stability, and we are committed to make that investment so that we can get the factories in the right spot.
finding: He called the $87.5bn inventory 'too much' yet defended it as a deliberate investment in stability.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I will tell you, though, as we move forward, we will expect any kind of inflation pressure to be offset by an expectation that we continue to drive productivity.
finding: With supply contracts and escalation fixed, he expected productivity, not price, to absorb inflation.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: our objective has always been to get the 15% of the portfolio that's wrapped up in these fixed price development programs, including T7 to not be a drag to just be neutral, right, to be at the 0 profit and not consume cash.
finding: For the legacy fixed-price defense programs his ambition was only breakeven, which shows how much risk he had written off.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So as we said at earnings, this isn't going to be a major restructuring of the Boeing company. This is an area where you could prune things that might not be as core, partly to finish the supplementation of the balance sheet that was anchored in the equity raise. ... But mostly, this is about just focus and simplicity.
finding: West framed divestitures as limited pruning for focus and to finish the post-equity-raise balance-sheet repair, not a breakup; in January he had flagged 'portfolio decisions', and in April Boeing agreed to sell parts of Digital Aviation Solutions for $10.55bn.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We still expect to close the deal sometime this summer, middle of the year.
finding: He guided the Spirit closing to mid-2025; in July it moved to 'later in the year', and in October 2025 it was still 'expected to close this year'.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So we can't wait to move our way now that we're in the second phase of certification and get ourselves to the point where we could get this in service next year. So far, so good.
finding: He reaffirmed 777X service entry in 2026; in October 2025 a $4.9bn charge moved first delivery to 2027.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: And then we see no reason why the business can't get back to historical financials once we get through stability. ... So it's not a complicated play. We just have to go execute.
finding: His recurring thesis, repeated to his last call in July 2025: there is no structural impairment and recovery is pure execution ('not a complicated play').

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: we deliberately wanted, once everybody got back in the factory after the strike, we wanted to make sure it was a very methodical way to bring people back in, get them trained, get them certified before they touch the airplane.
finding: After the strike he described a slow, training-gated restart rather than a rush to recover volume.
trigger: IAM machinists rejected the contract and struck from 2024-09-13

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It's really quantitative, and we can't wait until when we show stability over the course of time that we're going to then be allowed to move up to higher rates beyond 38.
finding: Rate increases depended on six FAA-agreed key performance indicators (rework, escapes, traveled work, shortages, training, ticketing), so the decision rule was quantitative and external.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Given our elevated inventory levels, that I'll probably keep talking about, we don't see -- we see neither a near-term impact on production, nor do we see an impact on us getting to 38 per month on the 37 and 7 per month on the 87.
finding: He cited the buffer inventory as insurance when a supplier fire hit, presenting it as a payoff of the 2024 policy.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: We are going to be able to take a much broader time horizon in terms of investments, right? We want to invest in quality, stability, innovation, and we'll do it in ways that perhaps they couldn't have done by themselves. ... One team, faster decision-making, less bureaucracy.
finding: His case for vertical integration was longer-horizon investment and faster decisions inside one company.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So the first priority is to finish the certification deliveries of our current development programs. I got -7, -10, 777X, we have finished that, right? ... So that's job one, and we can't take our eye off that ball.
finding: Before any new airplane, the priority was certifying the MAX 7, MAX 10 and 777X.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Now it's a ways off, and there's been no timetable set. And it's a ways off for a variety of reasons that we don't need to go into, but we just don't want to rush a decision for a product that's going to be out there for 50 years, right? It's a really important decision.
finding: On a new airplane he set no timetable and stressed the 50-year consequence of the decision, a clear wait-until-ready stance.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: What we do worry about is availability of parts because this is a broad complicated supply chain and people have different levels of exposure to it. And we want to make sure that we're really transparent with the supply chain, so that we're not making suboptimal trades in the supply chain for the short term.
finding: West's main concern on tariffs was part availability rather than cost, and he warned against short-term trade-offs in the supply chain.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: It's not going to be a slogan. It's not going to be a poster. It's going to be things we really believe in. And then once that gets distilled from this working team and disseminated, it will get embedded everywhere. It will get embedded in performance management systems
finding: He backed embedding the CEO's culture reset in performance-management systems rather than in slogans.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: As you saw yesterday, we entered into an agreement to sell portions of our Digital Aviation Solutions business for $10.55 billion, which is an important component of our strategy to focus on our core businesses and strengthen the balance sheet.
finding: He sold a high-margin software asset to strengthen the balance sheet, delivering the 'portfolio decisions' he had flagged in January.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Regarding free cash flow, we set a conservative plan for the year and had a strong start operationally, which we believe puts us in a position to largely offset any potential cash flow impact of China deliveries this year as well as higher expected input costs due to tariffs.
finding: By 2025 he had moved to deliberately conservative plans that leave room to absorb shocks.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: the net annual impact of higher tariffs on our input costs is manageable and within our plan, it's less than $500 million annually.
finding: He quantified the tariff hit on input costs as under $500m a year.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: I'd also say that keep in mind that over time, any input-related costs will work its way through to price escalators. So it should mostly neutralize over time.
finding: He expected contractual price escalators to pass cost inflation through to airline customers over time.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: Specifically on China, it represents approximately 10% of our commercial backlog. And if we need to redirect supply to more stable demand, the strong market backdrop across the rest of the world still supports our planned production rate increases.
finding: When China halted deliveries over tariffs, his response was to redirect airplanes to other customers rather than cut production rates.
trigger: China halted Boeing deliveries amid April 2025 US-China tariff escalation
response: redirect China airplanes; hold rate plan

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: On production, the factory steadily increased rate during the quarter, with monthly production reaching 38 per month in May, and the team remains intent on stabilizing at that level.
finding: The 737 reached 38 a month in May 2025, about five months after his original exit-2024 target, delayed by the strike.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: The engine anti-ice solution has taken us longer, and we now expect certification next year.
finding: He conceded plainly that the anti-ice fix, promised in 9-12 months in February 2024, had slipped and pushed MAX 7/10 certification to 2026.

speaker: Brian J. West, Executive VP of Finance & CFO
quote: So when I put all that together, I think your number there of $3 billion is pretty reasonable for the full year.
finding: He endorsed a full-year 2025 cash use of about $3bn and promised a positive 4Q, conditional on trade and deliveries; cash turned positive one quarter early (3Q25 at $238m) and his successor improved the year to about minus $2.5bn.
